originalAbstract: We propose a new scheme to construct neural networks to classify pat(cid:173) terns. The new scheme has several novel features : We focus attention on the important attributes of patterns in ranking order. Extract the most important ones first and the less important ones later. In training we use the information as a measure instead of the error

paragraphs: The paper proposes a way to construct neural networks for pattern classification around an ordered sequence of attributes. The network gives attention first to the attributes regarded as most important, then extracts less important ones later. Classification is therefore organized around a ranking of the information available in a pattern.

The sequence is central to the proposal. Attributes do not all receive the same position in the decision process: their relative importance determines when they are considered. This provides a concrete interpretation of sequential decision making in the paper, namely arranging the examination of a pattern so that its more important characteristics come earlier.

The second stated feature concerns training. The authors use information as the training measure instead of error, linking the learning procedure to the informative content of pattern attributes. Together, these choices describe a classifier whose construction emphasizes both what to examine and the order in which to examine it. The contribution presented in the abstract is this proposed learning scheme and its organizing principles.
summary.tldr: The proposed classifier examines attributes in importance order and trains using an information measure rather than error.

title: A Novel Net that Learns Sequential Decision Process

abstract: A higher order single layer recursive network easily learns to simulate a deterministic finite state machine and recognize regular grammars. When an enhanced version of this neural net state machine is connected through a common error term to an external analog stack memory, the combination can be interpreted as a neural net pushdown automata. The neural net finite state machine is given the primitives, push and POP. and is able to read the top of the stack. Through a gradient descent learning rule derived from the common error function, the hybrid network learns to effectively use the stack actions to manipUlate the stack memory and to learn simple contextfree grammars.

paragraphs: The paper examines how a recurrent neural network can learn grammatical structure. A higher-order network with a single layer learns to simulate a deterministic finite-state machine and recognize regular grammars. This connects the network's changing internal state to a formal machine that processes a sequence through successive state transitions.

The authors then extend the model by attaching an external analog stack. The network can read the top of this memory and receives push and pop operations for adding and removing stored information. An enhanced neural state machine and the stack share an error term, allowing their combined behavior to be trained toward the same objective.

A gradient-descent rule derived from that error function teaches the network to use the stack operations effectively. The resulting hybrid learns simple context-free grammars and can be interpreted as a neural pushdown automaton. The key contribution is learned coordination between a neural controller and an explicit memory structure, extending grammatical capabilities beyond those demonstrated by the finite-state network alone.
summary.tldr: A recurrent neural state machine learns simple context-free grammars when trained to control an external stack.

title: Higher Order Recurrent Networks and Grammatical Inference

abstract: A routing scheme that uses a neural network has been developed that can aid in establishing point-to-point communication routes through multi(cid:173) stage interconnection networks (MINs). The neural network is a network of the type that was examined by Hopfield (Hopfield, 1984 and 1985). In this work, the problem of establishing routes through random MINs (RMINs) in a shared-memory, distributed computing system is addressed. The performance of the neural network routing scheme is compared to two more traditional approaches - exhaustive search routing and greedy rout(cid:173) ing. The results suggest that a neural network router may be competitive for certain RMIN s.

paragraphs: This paper applies a neural network to finding communication routes through multistage interconnection networks. The setting is a shared-memory distributed computing system, where point-to-point communication must pass through a network with multiple stages. The specific routing problem concerns random multistage interconnection networks.

The proposed router uses a Hopfield-type neural network to help establish routes. Its purpose is computational: the neural network acts as part of the procedure for finding a path through the interconnection structure. The study therefore examines a neural approach to a systems problem rather than a recognition or prediction task.

The authors compare its performance with exhaustive-search routing and greedy routing. Their results suggest that the neural router may be competitive for certain random multistage networks. That qualification is central to the finding: the reported promise applies to particular network cases. The contribution is evidence that neural-network computation can be a viable routing alternative within the class of interconnection systems examined.
summary.tldr: A Hopfield-type neural router shows potential to compete with traditional routing methods on certain random multistage networks.

title: Neural Network Routing for Random Multistage Interconnection Networks

abstract: The fundamental backpropagation (BP) algorithm for training ar(cid:173) tificial neural networks is cast as a deterministic nonmonotone per(cid:173) turbed gradient method. Under certain natural assumptions, such as the series of learning rates diverging while the series of their squares converging, it is established that every accumulation point of the online BP iterates is a stationary point of the BP error func(cid:173) tion. The results presented cover serial and parallel online BP, modified BP with a momentum term, and BP with weight decay.
originalAbstract: The fundamental backpropagation (BP) algorithm for training ar(cid:173) tificial neural networks is cast as a deterministic nonmonotone per(cid:173) turbed gradient method. Under certain natural assumptions, such as the series of learning rates diverging while the series of their squares converging, it is established that every accumulation point of the online BP iterates is a stationary point of the BP error func(cid:173) tion. The results presented cover serial and parallel online BP, modified BP with a momentum term, and BP with weight decay.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes the convergence of online backpropagation by placing it within a broader mathematical framework for gradient methods. The framework allows updates to contain perturbations and does not require the error to decrease at every step. This matters because understanding a training sequence requires accounting for its overall behavior, even when individual updates are not improvements.

Under specified assumptions, every accumulation point of the weight sequence is a stationary point of the backpropagation error function. An accumulation point is a location approached by some subsequence of updates; stationary means that the error's gradient vanishes there. The result therefore describes possible limiting locations without identifying them as globally optimal solutions.

One stated condition requires learning rates whose sum diverges while the sum of their squares converges. These paired requirements constrain how the update sizes decrease over training. The analysis covers serial and parallel online backpropagation, as well as versions with momentum and weight decay, bringing several training variants under a common convergence account.
summary.tldr: Under learning-rate and other assumptions, online backpropagation and several variants have only stationary points as accumulation points.

title: Backpropagation Convergence Via Deterministic Nonmonotone Perturbed Minimization

abstract: I propose a learning algorithm for learning hierarchical models for ob(cid:173) ject recognition. The model architecture is a compositional hierarchy that represents part-whole relationships: parts are described in the lo(cid:173) cal context of substructures of the object. The focus of this report is inducing the structure of learning hierarchical models from data, i.e. model prototypes from observed exemplars of an object. At each node in the hierarchy, a probability distribution governing its parameters must be learned. The connections between nodes reflects the structure of the object. The formulation of substructures is encouraged such that their parts become conditionally independent. The resulting model can be interpreted as a Bayesian Belief Network and also is in many respects similar to the stochastic visual grammar described by Mjolsness.

paragraphs: This paper proposes an algorithm for learning hierarchical object models from observed examples. The representation organizes an object through part-whole relationships, with each part described in the local context of a larger substructure. The learning problem includes discovering the structure of this hierarchy, so the organization of the model is itself learned from data.

Each node has parameters governed by a probability distribution that must be estimated. Connections between nodes express the object's structure. The algorithm encourages substructures whose component parts become conditionally independent: once the relevant substructure is taken into account, the model can treat its parts independently within that context.

This criterion gives the formation of substructures a probabilistic purpose. Grouping parts is tied to how their dependencies can be represented, rather than simply placing them into a hierarchy. The resulting model can be interpreted as a Bayesian belief network and also resembles a stochastic visual grammar. The contribution is a way to induce object prototypes that jointly capture part organization and variation across observed examples.
summary.tldr: A learning algorithm discovers probabilistic part-whole hierarchies for object recognition directly from examples.

title: Learning in Compositional Hierarchies: Inducing the Structure of Objects from Data

abstract: Backpropagation learning algorithms typically collapse the network's structure into a single vector of weight parameters to be optimized. We suggest that their performance may be improved by utilizing the structural information instead of discarding it, and introduce a framework for ''tempering'' each weight accordingly. In the tempering model, activation and error signals are treated as approximately independent random variables. The characteristic scale of weight changes is then matched to that ofthe residuals, allowing structural properties such as a node's fan-in and fan-out to affect the local learning rate and backpropagated error. The model also permits calculation of an upper bound on the global learning rate for batch updates, which in turn leads to different update rules for bias vs. non-bias weights. This approach yields hitherto unparalleled performance on the family relations benchmark, a deep multi-layer network: for both batch learning with momentum and the delta-bar-delta algorithm, convergence at the optimal learning rate is sped up by more than an order of magnitude.

paragraphs: Backpropagation often treats all network weights as one parameter vector, setting aside information about where each connection sits. This paper proposes tempering weight updates according to network structure. The aim is to make learning reflect differences among connections, including how many inputs and outputs their associated nodes have.

The model treats activation and error signals as approximately independent random variables. It matches the characteristic size of weight changes to the scale of residual errors. This allows fan-in and fan-out to influence local learning rates and backpropagated errors. The analysis also gives an upper bound on the global batch-learning rate and leads to different update rules for bias and non-bias weights.

On the deep multilayer family-relations benchmark, tempering speeds convergence by more than an order of magnitude at the optimal learning rate, for both batch learning with momentum and delta-bar-delta. The result supports using structural information to scale learning updates, with the approximate independence assumption providing the foundation for the proposed calculation.
summary.tldr: Structure-aware scaling of backpropagation updates yields more than a tenfold convergence speedup on the family-relations benchmark.

title: Tempering Backpropagation Networks: Not All Weights are Created Equal

abstract: We consider the solution to large stochastic control problems by means of methods that rely on compact representations and a vari(cid:173) ant of the value iteration algorithm to compute approximate cost(cid:173) to-go functions. While such methods are known to be unstable in general, we identify a new class of problems for which convergence, as well as graceful error bounds, are guaranteed. This class in(cid:173) volves linear parameterizations of the cost-to- go function together with an assumption that the dynamic programming operator is a contraction with respect to the Euclidean norm when applied to functions in the parameterized class. We provide a special case where this assumption is satisfied, which relies on the locality of transitions in a state space. Other cases will be discussed in a full length version of this paper.

paragraphs: The paper studies large stochastic control problems using compact approximations to the cost-to-go function, which represents expected future cost. A variant of value iteration updates these approximations. Although compact representations make large problems more manageable, the authors note that such approximate dynamic programming methods can be unstable in general.

They identify a class of problems where convergence and controlled error bounds are guaranteed. The representation must be linear in its parameters, and the dynamic programming operator must be a contraction in Euclidean norm when applied to functions in the chosen class. Informally, the contraction requirement means that the update shrinks differences measured in that norm.

The authors provide a special case satisfying the condition through locality of transitions in the state space. This ties the guarantee to the structure of the control problem as well as the approximation scheme. The result gives a concrete route to stable approximate value iteration, with the convergence and error claims depending on the stated contraction assumption.
summary.tldr: Linear approximate value iteration has convergence and error guarantees under a Euclidean contraction condition satisfied by a local-transition special case.

title: Stable LInear Approximations to Dynamic Programming for Stochastic Control Problems with Local Transitions

abstract: This paper compares three penalty terms with respect to the effi(cid:173) ciency of supervised learning, by using first- and second-order learn(cid:173) ing algorithms. Our experiments showed that for a reasonably ade(cid:173) quate penalty factor, the combination of the squared penalty term and the second-order learning algorithm drastically improves the convergence performance more than 20 times over the other com(cid:173) binations, at the same time bringing about a better generalization performance.
originalAbstract: This paper compares three penalty terms with respect to the effi(cid:173) ciency of supervised learning, by using first- and second-order learn(cid:173) ing algorithms. Our experiments showed that for a reasonably ade(cid:173) quate penalty factor, the combination of the squared penalty term and the second-order learning algorithm drastically improves the convergence performance more than 20 times over the other com(cid:173) binations, at the same time bringing about a better generalization performance.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how the choice of penalty term interacts with the learning algorithm in supervised training. It compares three penalty terms using both first-order and second-order learning methods. The experimental question concerns combinations: the effectiveness of a penalty is assessed together with the optimization procedure used to train the model.

The strongest reported result comes from combining a squared penalty term with the second-order algorithm. With a reasonably appropriate penalty factor, this pairing improves convergence performance by more than twentyfold relative to the other tested combinations. The penalty factor is therefore part of the stated condition under which the large improvement appears.

The same combination also produces better generalization in the reported experiments. The outcome connects two goals of supervised learning: reaching a solution efficiently and obtaining a solution that performs well beyond training. The contribution is evidence that these goals can improve together through a suitable pairing of penalty and learning method, with the reported advantage specifically tied to the squared-penalty, second-order combination.
summary.tldr: With a suitable penalty factor, squared penalties paired with second-order learning improve convergence by more than twentyfold and also improve generalization.

title: Second-order Learning Algorithm with Squared Penalty Term

abstract: We have a developed an analog VLSI system that models the coordina(cid:173) tion of neurobiological segmental oscillators. We have implemented and tested a system that consists of a chain of eleven pattern generating cir(cid:173) cuits that are synaptically coupled to their nearest neighbors. Each pat(cid:173) tern generating circuit is implemented with two silicon Morris-Lecar neurons that are connected in a reciprocally inhibitory network. We dis(cid:173) cuss the mechanisms of oscillations in the two-cell network and explore system behavior based on isotropic and anisotropic coupling, and fre(cid:173) quency gradients along the chain of oscillators.

Each pat(cid:173) tern generating circuit is implemented with two silicon Morris-Lecar neurons that are connected in a reciprocally inhibitory network. paragraphs: This paper builds an analog hardware model of how repeated biological segments coordinate rhythmic activity. The implemented system contains eleven pattern-generating circuits arranged in a chain. Each circuit communicates through synaptic connections only with its immediate neighbors, so coordination is studied through local interactions between adjacent oscillators.

Each pattern generator contains two silicon implementations of Morris-Lecar neurons. The neurons inhibit one another, creating a small reciprocal network whose oscillation mechanisms the authors examine. This two-cell circuit supplies the repeating unit for the larger chain, connecting the behavior of an individual rhythm generator to the behavior of the coordinated system.

The authors test the hardware and explore how its behavior changes with isotropic or anisotropic coupling and with frequency gradients along the chain. These variations examine the roles of directional coupling and differences in oscillator frequency. The work therefore provides a physical platform for investigating how local neural connections can organize rhythms across multiple segments, with explicit control over several features of those connections.
summary.tldr: An eleven-stage analog neural circuit models rhythmic coordination through interactions between neighboring oscillators.

title: Analog VLSI Model of Intersegmental Coordination with Nearest-Neighbor Coupling

The result is obtained in a PAC- Bayesian framework and is based on geometrical arguments in the space of linear classifiers. The new bound constitutes an exponential improvement of the so far tightest margin bound by Shawe-Taylor et al. [8] and scales logarithmically in the inverse margin. paragraphs: The paper develops a bound on the generalization error of linear classifiers using a refined measure of training margin. Its PAC-Bayesian analysis relies on geometry in the space of possible classifiers. The authors argue that the classical margin is too coarse to capture the relevant ratio between the full hypothesis space and the portion consistent with the training data.

The new bound improves exponentially on the previous tightest margin bound identified in the abstract and depends logarithmically on inverse margin. Sufficiently large margins can give nontrivial bounds even when the number of training examples is smaller than the number of input dimensions. This provides a more favorable theoretical account of classification in that setting.

The analysis also gives a qualification about support vector machines: an SVM is optimal with respect to this bound only when feature vectors have equal length. The authors consequently recommend normalizing feature vectors before using SVMs. Experiments on two benchmark datasets support that recommendation, linking the geometric result to a concrete preprocessing choice.
summary.tldr: A refined PAC-Bayesian margin bound strengthens generalization guarantees and supports using SVMs with normalized feature vectors.

title: A PAC-Bayesian Margin Bound for Linear Classifiers: Why SVMs work

abstract: In this work, we introduce an Interactive Parts (IP) model as an alternative to Hidden Markov Models (HMMs). We tested both models on a database of on-line cursive script. We show that im(cid:173) plementations of HMMs and the IP model, in which all letters are assumed to have the same average width, give comparable results. However , in contrast to HMMs, the IP model can handle duration modeling without an increase in computational complexity.

We show that im(cid:173) plementations of HMMs and the IP model, in which all letters are assumed to have the same average width, give comparable results. However , in contrast to HMMs, the IP model can handle duration modeling without an increase in computational complexity.

paragraphs: The paper introduces the Interactive Parts model as an alternative to hidden Markov models for recognizing online cursive handwriting. Both approaches are tested on a database of cursive script. The comparison focuses on recognition behavior and on the computational consequences of modeling how long individual parts of the writing extend.

Under the assumption that every letter has the same average width, the tested implementations produce comparable results. That assumption is important to the reported comparison: it specifies the setting in which the two models perform similarly. The abstract therefore supports comparable recognition under that shared condition, rather than a general claim that one model recognizes handwriting better.

The distinguishing capability is duration modeling. The authors state that the Interactive Parts model can include it without increasing computational complexity, in contrast to HMMs. This makes the contribution about the cost of representing duration as well as recognition itself. The model offers a way to accommodate that aspect of cursive script while retaining the stated computational complexity.
summary.tldr: Interactive Parts matches HMM recognition under a shared letter-width assumption while supporting duration modeling without added computational complexity.

title: Interactive Parts Model: An Application to Recognition of On-line Cursive Script

abstract: We propose a novel method for the analysis of sequential data that exhibits an inherent mode switching. In particular, the data might be a non-stationary time series from a dynamical system that switches between multiple operating modes. Unlike other ap(cid:173) proaches, our method processes the data incrementally and without any training of internal parameters. We use an HMM with a dy(cid:173) namically changing number of states and an on-line variant of the Viterbi algorithm that performs an unsupervised segmentation and classification of the data on-the-fly, i.e. the method is able to pro(cid:173) cess incoming data in real-time. The main idea of the approach is to track and segment changes of the probability density of the data in a sliding window on the incoming data stream. The usefulness of the algorithm is demonstrated by an application to a switching dynamical system.

paragraphs: The paper addresses sequential data generated by a system that switches between operating modes. Such changes can make a time series non-stationary: its statistical behavior varies as the system changes mode. The goal is to identify and classify segments while observations arrive, rather than waiting for the complete sequence.

The method uses a hidden Markov model whose number of states can change dynamically. An online version of the Viterbi algorithm assigns structure to the incoming sequence, producing an unsupervised segmentation and classification. Its central signal is a change in the probability density of observations within a sliding window over the data stream.

This design connects local statistical changes with a changing representation of the system’s modes. The authors state that it operates incrementally, requires no training of internal parameters, and can process incoming observations in real time. An application to a switching dynamical system demonstrates its usefulness for the kind of mode changes the method is designed to detect.
summary.tldr: A dynamically changing hidden Markov model segments and classifies switching time series as observations arrive.

title: A Dynamic HMM for On-line Segmentation of Sequential Data

abstract: We describe a Markov chain method for sampling from the distribution of the hidden state sequence in a non-linear dynamical system, given a sequence of observations. This method updates all states in the sequence simultaneously using an embedded Hidden Markov Model (HMM). An update begins with the creation of “pools” of candidate states at each time. We then deﬁne an embedded HMM whose states are indexes within these pools. Using a forward-backward dynamic programming algo- rithm, we can efﬁciently choose a state sequence with the appropriate probabilities from the exponentially large number of state sequences that pass through states in these pools. We illustrate the method in a simple one-dimensional example, and in an example showing how an embed- ded HMM can be used to in effect discretize the state space without any discretization error. We also compare the embedded HMM to a particle smoother on a more substantial problem of inferring human motion from 2D traces of markers.

We then deﬁne an embedded HMM whose states are indexes within these pools. Using a forward-backward dynamic programming algo- rithm, we can efﬁciently choose a state sequence with the appropriate probabilities from the exponentially large number of state sequences that pass through states in these pools. paragraphs: The paper addresses inference of an entire hidden state sequence in a nonlinear dynamical system from observed data. It introduces a Markov chain sampling method that updates all times together, allowing a proposed trajectory to be selected as a connected sequence rather than as separate state choices.

Each update first creates a pool of candidate states at every time. The authors then construct an embedded hidden Markov model whose state labels identify entries in those pools. A forward-backward dynamic programming procedure selects a sequence with the appropriate probabilities. This avoids explicitly enumerating the exponentially many trajectories that can be formed by combining pool entries across time.

The method is illustrated with a one-dimensional example and another example showing how the embedded model can effectively discretize the state space without introducing discretization error. A larger application compares it with a particle smoother for recovering human motion from two-dimensional marker traces. These examples connect the sequence-sampling construction to both its handling of continuous states and a substantial motion-inference task.
summary.tldr: An embedded hidden Markov model efficiently samples whole hidden trajectories from pools of candidate states in nonlinear systems.

title: Inferring State Sequences for Non-linear Systems with Embedded Hidden Markov Models

abstract: We consider the problem of detecting humans and classifying their pose from a single image. Specifically, our goal is to devise a statistical model that simultaneously answers two questions: 1) is there a human in the image? and, if so, 2) what is a low-dimensional representation of her pose? We investigate models that can be learned in an unsupervised manner on unlabeled images of human poses, and provide information that can be used to match the pose of a new image to the ones present in the training set. Starting from a set of descriptors recently proposed for human detection, we apply the Latent Dirichlet Allocation framework to model the statistics of these features, and use the resulting model to answer the above questions. We show how our model can efficiently describe the space of images of humans with their pose, by providing an effective representation of poses for tasks such as classification and matching, while performing remarkably well in human/non human decision problems, thus enabling its use for human detection. We validate the model with extensive quantitative experiments and comparisons with other approaches on human detection and pose matching.

We show how our model can efficiently describe the space of images of humans with their pose, by providing an effective representation of poses for tasks such as classification and matching, while performing remarkably well in human/non human decision problems, thus enabling its use for human detection. We validate the model with extensive quantitative experiments and comparisons with other approaches on human detection and pose matching.

paragraphs: The paper seeks to answer two connected questions from a single image: whether a person is present and how that person's pose can be represented compactly. A useful representation should also allow a new pose image to be compared with examples in a training collection, connecting detection with pose classification and matching.

The authors begin with image descriptors developed for human detection and model their statistics using Latent Dirichlet Allocation. They investigate learning this model without pose labels from images of human poses. The learned structure supplies a low-dimensional description that can support both recognition of human images and comparisons among their poses.

Extensive quantitative experiments and comparisons examine human detection and pose matching. The authors report an effective representation for pose classification and matching, together with strong human-versus-nonhuman decisions. These results support the idea that one statistical model of image features can serve both tasks, so that representing pose contributes to a broader account of what human images look like.
summary.tldr: An unsupervised feature model learns compact pose representations that also support human detection in single images.

title: Detecting Humans via Their Pose

abstract: This paper presents the first data-dependent generalization bounds for non-i.i.d. settings based on the notion of Rademacher complexity. Our bounds extend to the non-i.i.d. case existing Rademacher complexity bounds derived for the i.i.d. setting. These bounds provide a strict generalization of the ones found in the i.i.d. case, and can also be used within the standard i.i.d. scenario. They apply to the standard scenario of beta-mixing stationary sequences examined in many previous studies of non-i.i.d. settings and benefit form the crucial advantages of Rademacher complexity over other measures of the complexity of hypothesis classes. In particular, they are data-dependent and measure the complexity of a class of hypotheses based on the training sample. The empirical Rademacher complexity can be estimated from finite samples and lead to tighter bounds.

paragraphs: Generalization bounds connect performance on training data with performance beyond that sample. Many familiar results assume examples are independent and identically distributed. This paper extends Rademacher-complexity bounds beyond that setting, allowing analysis of dependent observations while preserving a measure of complexity tied to the observed data.

The bounds apply to stationary sequences satisfying beta-mixing conditions. These conditions provide a structured setting for dependence rather than covering every possible dependent process. The results strictly generalize the corresponding independent-data bounds, meaning the framework also remains applicable when the standard independent and identically distributed assumptions do hold.

A central advantage is that the complexity of the hypothesis class is assessed through the training sample. Empirical Rademacher complexity can be estimated from a finite sample and can yield tighter bounds. The contribution is therefore more than accommodating dependence: it carries a data-dependent approach to generalization analysis into that setting, preserving a useful connection between the observed sample and the strength of the resulting guarantee.
summary.tldr: Rademacher-complexity generalization bounds extend to stationary beta-mixing data while retaining sample-dependent complexity estimates.

title: Rademacher Complexity Bounds for Non-I.I.D. Processes

abstract: Regularized Least Squares (RLS) algorithms have the ability to avoid over-fitting problems and to express solutions as kernel expansions. However, we observe that the current RLS algorithms cannot provide a satisfactory interpretation even on a constant function. On the other hand, while kernel-based algorithms have been developed in such a tendency that almost all learning algorithms are kernelized or being kernelized, a basic fact is often ignored: The learned function from the data and the kernel fits the data well, but may not be consistent with the kernel. Based on these considerations and on the intuition that a good kernel-based inductive function should be consistent with both the data and the kernel, a novel learning scheme is proposed. The advantages of this scheme lie in its corresponding Representer Theorem, its strong interpretation ability about what kind of functions should not be penalized, and its promising accuracy improvements shown in a number of experiments. Furthermore, we provide a detailed technical description about heat kernels, which serves as an example for the readers to apply similar techniques for other kernels. Our work provides a preliminary step in a new direction to explore the varying consistency between inductive functions and kernels under various distributions.

paragraphs: Regularized least squares can control overfitting and express a learned function as a kernel expansion. The authors nevertheless identify an interpretive problem, including for constant functions: fitting observations well does not necessarily make the learned function consistent with the kernel. They propose treating consistency with both the data and the kernel as a learning objective.

The new scheme comes with a corresponding representer theorem and an interpretation of which kinds of functions should remain unpenalized. This connects the regularization rule to the behavior the method intends to preserve. The emphasis is therefore on the relationship between a kernel, its associated learning function, and the penalty used during fitting.

The authors present that treatment as a guide for adapting similar techniques to other kernels. They describe the work as a preliminary step toward understanding how function-kernel consistency varies under different distributions, rather than as a completed general account.
summary.tldr: A kernel learning scheme aligns fitted functions with both observations and kernel structure, clarifying penalties and showing promising accuracy gains.

title: Learning with Consistency between Inductive Functions and Kernels

abstract: The Random Projection Tree (RPTree) structures proposed in [Dasgupta-Freund-STOC-08] are space partitioning data structures that automatically adapt to various notions of intrinsic dimensionality of data. We prove new results for both the RPTree-Max and the RPTree-Mean data structures. Our result for RPTree-Max gives a near-optimal bound on the number of levels required by this data structure to reduce the size of its cells by a factor s >= 2. We also prove a packing lemma for this data structure. Our final result shows that low-dimensional manifolds possess bounded Local Covariance Dimension. As a consequence we show that RPTree-Mean adapts to manifold dimension as well.

Our result for RPTree-Max gives a near-optimal bound on the number of levels required by this data structure to reduce the size of its cells by a factor s >= 2. paragraphs: Random Projection Trees divide a data space into progressively smaller cells and can adapt to the data's intrinsic dimensionality. This paper strengthens the theoretical understanding of two versions, RPTree-Max and RPTree-Mean. Its focus is how the geometry of the data influences the behavior of these partitioning structures.

For RPTree-Max, the authors prove a near-optimal bound on how many tree levels are needed to shrink cell size by a chosen factor of at least two. They also establish a packing lemma for the structure. These results sharpen the account of how its partitions become smaller and how the resulting cells are organized geometrically.

The final result connects low-dimensional manifolds to bounded Local Covariance Dimension. That connection establishes that RPTree-Mean adapts to manifold dimension as well. The contribution is theoretical: it extends the guarantees for these existing data structures and links their adaptive behavior to another important description of low-dimensional structure in data.
summary.tldr: New proofs sharpen RPTree-Max partition guarantees and establish that RPTree-Mean adapts to manifold dimension.

title: Random Projection Trees Revisited

abstract: The sequence memoizer is a model for sequence data with state-of-the-art performance on language modeling and compression. We propose a number of improvements to the model and inference algorithm, including an enlarged range of hyperparameters, a memory-efficient representation, and inference algorithms operating on the new representation. Our derivations are based on precise definitions of the various processes that will also allow us to provide an elementary proof of the mysterious" coagulation and fragmentation properties used in the original paper on the sequence memoizer by Wood et al. (2009). We present some experimental results supporting our improvements."

Our derivations are based on precise definitions of the various processes that will also allow us to provide an elementary proof of the mysterious" coagulation and fragmentation properties used in the original paper on the sequence memoizer by Wood et al. (2009). We present some experimental results supporting our improvements."

paragraphs: The sequence memoizer is a model for sequential data with strong established performance in language modeling and compression. This paper improves both the model and the procedures used to perform inference with it. Its focus is on making an already effective approach more flexible, more memory-efficient, and more clearly grounded mathematically.

The proposed changes enlarge the range of available hyperparameters and introduce a representation that uses memory more efficiently. The authors also develop inference algorithms that operate on this new representation. These changes address linked aspects of the method: what model settings can be expressed, how the model is stored, and how calculations are performed.

The derivations begin with precise definitions of the underlying processes. Those definitions also support an elementary proof of the coagulation and fragmentation properties used in the original sequence memoizer. Experimental results provide support for the proposed improvements. The paper therefore contributes both practical modifications and a clearer explanation of mathematical properties on which the model depends.
summary.tldr: The paper expands the sequence memoizer’s hyperparameters, improves its memory representation and inference, and clarifies its mathematical foundations.

title: Improvements to the Sequence Memoizer

abstract: We introduce a new Bayesian nonparametric approach to identification of sparse dynamic linear systems. The impulse responses are modeled as Gaussian processes whose autocovariances encode the BIBO stability constraint, as defined by the recently introduced “Stable Spline kernel”. Sparse solutions are obtained by placing exponential hyperpriors on the scale factors of such kernels. Numerical experiments regarding estimation of ARMAX models show that this technique provides a definite advantage over a group LAR algorithm and state-of-the-art parametric identification techniques based on prediction error minimization.

Numerical experiments regarding estimation of ARMAX models show that this technique provides a definite advantage over a group LAR algorithm and state-of-the-art parametric identification techniques based on prediction error minimization.

paragraphs: This paper studies the identification of sparse dynamic linear systems: learning a system's response while favoring a representation with fewer active components. It proposes a Bayesian nonparametric approach that combines two requirements in the statistical model. One concerns the stability of the learned responses, and the other concerns sparsity.

The system's impulse responses are modeled as Gaussian processes. Their autocovariances use the Stable Spline kernel to encode bounded-input, bounded-output stability, meaning that bounded inputs should produce bounded outputs. The authors then place exponential hyperpriors on the kernel scale factors to obtain sparse solutions. Stability is therefore represented through the covariance structure, while sparsity is encouraged through the scales controlling those structures.

Numerical experiments on ARMAX model estimation show an advantage over a group LAR algorithm and parametric identification methods based on prediction error minimization. These results support the proposed combination in the tested identification setting. The methodological contribution is to bring stability constraints and sparse estimation into one Bayesian framework for learning dynamic responses.
summary.tldr: Stable Spline kernels and exponential scale hyperpriors combine stability and sparsity in Bayesian system identification, with advantages in reported ARMAX experiments.

title: Learning sparse dynamic linear systems using stable spline kernels and exponential hyperpriors

abstract: We introduce HD (or ``Hierarchical-Deep'') models, a new compositional learning architecture that integrates deep learning models with structured hierarchical Bayesian models. Specifically we show how we can learn a hierarchical Dirichlet process (HDP) prior over the activities of the top-level features in a Deep Boltzmann Machine (DBM). This compound HDP-DBM model learns to learn novel concepts from very few training examples, by learning low-level generic features, high-level features that capture correlations among low-level features, and a category hierarchy for sharing priors over the high-level features that are typical of different kinds of concepts. We present efficient learning and inference algorithms for the HDP-DBM model and show that it is able to learn new concepts from very few examples on CIFAR-100 object recognition, handwritten character recognition, and human motion capture datasets.

We present efficient learning and inference algorithms for the HDP-DBM model and show that it is able to learn new concepts from very few examples on CIFAR-100 object recognition, handwritten character recognition, and human motion capture datasets.

paragraphs: This paper introduces Hierarchical-Deep models, which combine deep learning with structured hierarchical Bayesian modeling. The objective is to learn new concepts from very few examples by organizing what has already been learned at several levels. The concrete model places a hierarchical Dirichlet process prior over the activities of top-level features in a Deep Boltzmann Machine.

The architecture brings together three forms of reusable knowledge. Low-level features capture generic patterns, higher-level features capture correlations among those patterns, and a category hierarchy shares prior information about which high-level features are typical of different kinds of concepts. This hierarchy gives new concepts access to information learned across related categories.

The authors provide efficient learning and inference algorithms for the combined HDP-DBM model. They demonstrate learning from very few examples on CIFAR-100 object recognition, handwritten character recognition, and human motion capture datasets. These results support the proposed combination of learned representations and shared category priors as a way to transfer useful knowledge into new concept-learning problems.
summary.tldr: A combined HDP-DBM model shares hierarchical feature knowledge to learn new concepts from very few examples.

title: Learning to Learn with Compound HD Models

abstract: We introduce a new discrepancy score between two distributions that gives an indication on their \emph{similarity}. While much research has been done to determine if two samples come from exactly the same distribution, much less research considered the problem of determining if two finite samples come from similar distributions. The new score gives an intuitive interpretation of similarity; it optimally perturbs the distributions so that they best fit each other. The score is defined between distributions, and can be efficiently estimated from samples. We provide convergence bounds of the estimated score, and develop hypothesis testing procedures that test if two data sets come from similar distributions. The statistical power of this procedures is presented in simulations. We also compare the score's capacity to detect similarity with that of other known measures on real data.

paragraphs: This paper distinguishes asking whether two datasets come from exactly the same distribution from asking whether their distributions are similar. With finite samples, similarity is a useful target in its own right. The authors introduce a discrepancy score, perturbed variation, intended to express that relationship directly.

The score interprets similarity through an optimal perturbation that makes the distributions fit each other as well as possible. Although defined for distributions, it can be estimated efficiently from observed samples. The authors provide convergence bounds for the estimate, linking the sample-based calculation to the distribution-level quantity it aims to measure.

They also develop hypothesis tests for whether two datasets come from similar distributions. Simulations examine the tests’ statistical power, and real-data comparisons assess how the score detects similarity relative to other measures. These evaluations accompany a contribution that spans a definition of similarity, an efficient estimator, and statistical testing procedures, making the proposed notion usable with finite observations.
summary.tldr: Perturbed variation measures distributional similarity through optimal perturbations and supports efficient estimation and hypothesis testing from samples.

title: The Perturbed Variation

abstract: In Compressive Sensing Magnetic Resonance Imaging (CS-MRI), one can reconstruct a MR image with good quality from only a small number of measurements. This can significantly reduce MR scanning time. According to structured sparsity theory, the measurements can be further reduced to $\mathcal{O}(K+\log n)$ for tree-sparse data instead of $\mathcal{O}(K+K\log n)$ for standard $K$-sparse data with length $n$. However, few of existing algorithms has utilized this for CS-MRI, while most of them use Total Variation and wavelet sparse regularization. On the other side, some algorithms have been proposed for tree sparsity regularization, but few of them has validated the benefit of tree structure in CS-MRI. In this paper, we propose a fast convex optimization algorithm to improve CS-MRI. Wavelet sparsity, gradient sparsity and tree sparsity are all considered in our model for real MR images. The original complex problem is decomposed to three simpler subproblems then each of the subproblems can be efficiently solved with an iterative scheme. Numerous experiments have been conducted and show that the proposed algorithm outperforms the state-of-the-art CS-MRI algorithms, and gain better reconstructions results on real MR images than general tree based solvers or algorithms.

paragraphs: The paper develops a method for reconstructing magnetic resonance images from relatively few measurements. Collecting fewer measurements can substantially shorten scanning time, provided the reconstruction retains good image quality. The authors investigate whether incorporating tree structure into the reconstruction model can improve CS-MRI beyond approaches that mainly use wavelet sparsity and total variation.

The motivation comes from structured sparsity theory. For data of length n with K nonzero entries, the abstract contrasts measurement requirements of order K + K log n for standard sparsity with order K + log n for tree sparsity. This theoretical advantage applies to tree-sparse data; it motivates using relationships among coefficients alongside sparsity itself.

They report that numerous experiments produced better reconstructions than leading CS-MRI methods and general tree-based solvers. These findings support incorporating tree structure within a model that also accounts for the other forms of sparsity.
summary.tldr: The paper combines wavelet, gradient, and tree sparsity in an efficient convex optimization method that reports improved MRI reconstruction from limited measurements.

title: Compressive Sensing MRI with Wavelet Tree Sparsity

abstract: We study the problem of reconstructing low-rank matrices from their noisy observations. We formulate the problem in the Bayesian framework, which allows us to exploit structural properties of matrices in addition to low-rankedness, such as sparsity. We propose an efficient approximate message passing algorithm, derived from the belief propagation algorithm, to perform the Bayesian inference for matrix reconstruction. We have also successfully applied the proposed algorithm to a clustering problem, by formulating the problem of clustering as a low-rank matrix reconstruction problem with an additional structural property. Numerical experiments show that the proposed algorithm outperforms Lloyd's K-means algorithm.
originalAbstract: We study the problem of reconstructing low-rank matrices from their noisy observations. We formulate the problem in the Bayesian framework, which allows us to exploit structural properties of matrices in addition to low-rankedness, such as sparsity. We propose an efficient approximate message passing algorithm, derived from the belief propagation algorithm, to perform the Bayesian inference for matrix reconstruction. We have also successfully applied the proposed algorithm to a clustering problem, by formulating the problem of clustering as a low-rank matrix reconstruction problem with an additional structural property. Numerical experiments show that the proposed algorithm outperforms Lloyd's K-means algorithm.

paragraphs: Recovering a low-rank matrix from noisy observations can benefit from knowing more than its rank. This paper uses a Bayesian formulation to incorporate additional structure, such as sparsity, into reconstruction. The aim is to make the assumed properties of the underlying matrix part of inference, allowing information beyond low-rankedness to guide the recovered result.

The authors derive an efficient approximate message passing algorithm from belief propagation to carry out this Bayesian inference. The algorithm provides a computational procedure for reconstructing matrices under the structural model. Its role is to make use of the richer formulation while keeping the inference process efficient.

The same approach is applied to clustering by expressing clustering as low-rank matrix reconstruction with an additional structural property. Numerical experiments show that the proposed method outperforms Lloyd's K-means algorithm. This result supports the usefulness of the reconstruction perspective for the tested clustering problems: cluster discovery can be approached through structured matrix estimation using the same inference machinery.
summary.tldr: Bayesian approximate message passing exploits matrix structure for reconstruction and outperforms Lloyd's K-means in the reported clustering experiments.

title: Low-rank matrix reconstruction and clustering via approximate message passing

abstract: We develop a fast algorithm for the Admixture of Poisson MRFs (APM) topic model and propose a novel metric to directly evaluate this model. The APM topic model recently introduced by Inouye et al. (2014) is the first topic model that allows for word dependencies within each topic unlike in previous topic models like LDA that assume independence between words within a topic. Research in both the semantic coherence of a topic models (Mimno et al. 2011, Newman et al. 2010) and measures of model fitness (Mimno & Blei 2011) provide strong support that explicitly modeling word dependencies---as in APM---could be both semantically meaningful and essential for appropriately modeling real text data. Though APM shows significant promise for providing a better topic model, APM has a high computational complexity because $O(p^2)$ parameters must be estimated where $p$ is the number of words (Inouye et al. could only provide results for datasets with $p = 200$). In light of this, we develop a parallel alternating Newton-like algorithm for training the APM model that can handle $p = 10^4$ as an important step towards scaling to large datasets. In addition, Inouye et al. only provided tentative and inconclusive results on the utility of APM. Thus, motivated by simple intuitions and previous evaluations of topic models, we propose a novel evaluation metric based on human evocation scores between word pairs (i.e. how much one word brings to mind" another word (Boyd-Graber et al. 2006)). We provide compelling quantitative and qualitative results on the BNC corpus that demonstrate the superiority of APM over previous topic models for identifying semantically meaningful word dependencies. (MATLAB code available at: http://bigdata.ices.utexas.edu/software/apm/)"

paragraphs: Topic models describe documents through recurring themes, but models such as LDA assume that words are independent within a topic. The Admixture of Poisson MRFs model, or APM, explicitly represents dependencies between words within each theme. This paper addresses the computational expense of that richer representation and how to evaluate whether its dependencies capture meaning.

APM needs a number of parameters that grows quadratically with vocabulary size. Earlier results were limited to vocabularies of 200 words. The authors develop a parallel training algorithm that alternates Newton-like updates and can handle 10,000 words. This is presented as a substantial step toward larger datasets, rather than a complete solution to scaling.

The paper also introduces an evaluation measure based on human judgments of how strongly one word brings another to mind. That measure directly connects learned word relationships to semantic associations. Quantitative and qualitative results on the BNC corpus favor APM over previous topic models for identifying meaningful dependencies, providing stronger evidence for the model's usefulness than the earlier tentative evaluations.
summary.tldr: Faster training and a human-association evaluation strengthen APM's case for modeling meaningful word dependencies within topics.

title: Capturing Semantically Meaningful Word Dependencies with an Admixture of Poisson MRFs

abstract: We consider the problem of learning the canonical parameters specifying an undirected graphical model (Markov random field) from the mean parameters. For graphical models representing a minimal exponential family, the canonical parameters are uniquely determined by the mean parameters, so the problem is feasible in principle. The goal of this paper is to investigate the computational feasibility of this statistical task. Our main result shows that parameter estimation is in general intractable: no algorithm can learn the canonical parameters of a generic pair-wise binary graphical model from the mean parameters in time bounded by a polynomial in the number of variables (unless RP = NP). Indeed, such a result has been believed to be true (see the monograph by Wainwright and Jordan) but no proof was known. Our proof gives a polynomial time reduction from approximating the partition function of the hard-core model, known to be hard, to learning approximate parameters. Our reduction entails showing that the marginal polytope boundary has an inherent repulsive property, which validates an optimization procedure over the polytope that does not use any knowledge of its structure (as required by the ellipsoid method and others).
originalAbstract: We consider the problem of learning the canonical parameters specifying an undirected graphical model (Markov random field) from the mean parameters. For graphical models representing a minimal exponential family, the canonical parameters are uniquely determined by the mean parameters, so the problem is feasible in principle. The goal of this paper is to investigate the computational feasibility of this statistical task. Our main result shows that parameter estimation is in general intractable: no algorithm can learn the canonical parameters of a generic pair-wise binary graphical model from the mean parameters in time bounded by a polynomial in the number of variables (unless RP = NP). Indeed, such a result has been believed to be true (see the monograph by Wainwright and Jordan) but no proof was known. Our proof gives a polynomial time reduction from approximating the partition function of the hard-core model, known to be hard, to learning approximate parameters. Our reduction entails showing that the marginal polytope boundary has an inherent repulsive property, which validates an optimization procedure over the polytope that does not use any knowledge of its structure (as required by the ellipsoid method and others).

paragraphs: This paper separates two questions about learning an undirected graphical model: whether its parameters are determined by available information, and whether they can be computed efficiently. In a minimal exponential family, mean parameters uniquely determine canonical parameters. That uniqueness makes recovery well-defined, but it does not by itself provide an efficient algorithm.

The main theorem establishes a general computational obstacle. Unless RP equals NP, no algorithm can recover canonical parameters from mean parameters for generic pairwise binary graphical models in time polynomial in the number of variables. This is a general hardness result, rather than a claim that every particular model is difficult.

The proof reduces a known hard problem—approximating the hard-core model's partition function—to approximate parameter learning. An efficient solution to the latter would therefore solve the former. The reduction also establishes a repulsive property of the marginal polytope's boundary, supporting an optimization procedure that does not need knowledge of the polytope's structure. The result shows why statistical identifiability alone cannot guarantee computational feasibility.
summary.tldr: Recovering graphical-model parameters from their means is generally computationally intractable unless RP equals NP, even when the parameters are uniquely determined.

title: Hardness of parameter estimation in graphical models

abstract: We consider the Principal Component Analysis problem for large tensors of arbitrary order k under a single-spike (or rank-one plus noise) model. On the one hand, we use information theory, and recent results in probability theory to establish necessary and sufficient conditions under which the principal component can be estimated using unbounded computational resources. It turns out that this is possible as soon as the signal-to-noise ratio beta becomes larger than C\sqrt{k log k} (and in particular beta can remain bounded has the problem dimensions increase). On the other hand, we analyze several polynomial-time estimation algorithms, based on tensor unfolding, power iteration and message passing ideas from graphical models. We show that, unless the signal-to-noise ratio diverges in the system dimensions, none of these approaches succeeds. This is possibly related to a fundamental limitation of computationally tractable estimators for this problem. For moderate dimensions, we propose an hybrid approach that uses unfolding together with power iteration, and show that it outperforms significantly baseline methods. Finally, we consider the case in which additional side information is available about the unknown signal. We characterize the amount of side information that allow the iterative algorithms to converge to a good estimate.
originalAbstract: We consider the Principal Component Analysis problem for large tensors of arbitrary order k under a single-spike (or rank-one plus noise) model. On the one hand, we use information theory, and recent results in probability theory to establish necessary and sufficient conditions under which the principal component can be estimated using unbounded computational resources. It turns out that this is possible as soon as the signal-to-noise ratio beta becomes larger than C\sqrt{k log k} (and in particular beta can remain bounded has the problem dimensions increase). On the other hand, we analyze several polynomial-time estimation algorithms, based on tensor unfolding, power iteration and message passing ideas from graphical models. We show that, unless the signal-to-noise ratio diverges in the system dimensions, none of these approaches succeeds. This is possibly related to a fundamental limitation of computationally tractable estimators for this problem. For moderate dimensions, we propose an hybrid approach that uses unfolding together with power iteration, and show that it outperforms significantly baseline methods. Finally, we consider the case in which additional side information is available about the unknown signal. We characterize the amount of side information that allow the iterative algorithms to converge to a good estimate.

paragraphs: The paper studies principal component estimation for tensors under a model consisting of one rank-one signal plus noise. It separates two questions: whether the signal can be estimated at all, and whether particular computationally efficient algorithms can estimate it. This distinction exposes a gap between information available in the data and information accessible through the analyzed methods.

With unrestricted computation, the authors establish necessary and sufficient conditions for estimation. In particular, estimation is possible when the signal-to-noise ratio exceeds C times the square root of k log k, where k is tensor order; for fixed order, this ratio can remain bounded as dimensions grow. The polynomial-time methods analyzed, based on unfolding, power iteration, and message passing, instead require the ratio to grow with dimension.

The authors suggest that this gap may reflect a fundamental computational limitation, without establishing that conclusion for every efficient estimator. They also propose an unfolding-and-power-iteration hybrid that substantially improves on baselines at moderate dimensions, and characterize how much side information enables iterative methods to reach a good estimate.
summary.tldr: A rank-one tensor model reveals a gap between statistical recoverability and the signal strength required by several efficient estimation algorithms.

title: A statistical model for tensor PCA

abstract: In many applications, the data is of rich structure that can be represented by a hypergraph, where the data items are represented by vertices and the associations among items are represented by hyperedges. Equivalently, we are given an input bipartite graph with two types of vertices: items, and associations (which we refer to as topics). We consider the problem of partitioning the set of items into a given number of parts such that the maximum number of topics covered by a part of the partition is minimized. This is a natural clustering problem, with various applications, e.g. partitioning of a set of information objects such as documents, images, and videos, and load balancing in the context of computation platforms.In this paper, we focus on the streaming computation model for this problem, in which items arrive online one at a time and each item must be assigned irrevocably to a part of the partition at its arrival time. Motivated by scalability requirements, we focus on the class of streaming computation algorithms with memory limited to be at most linear in the number of the parts of the partition. We show that a greedy assignment strategy is able to recover a hidden co-clustering of items under a natural set of recovery conditions. We also report results of an extensive empirical evaluation, which demonstrate that this greedy strategy yields superior performance when compared with alternative approaches.

paragraphs: The paper studies partitioning items linked by shared associations, represented as a hypergraph or an item-topic bipartite graph. Its objective is to minimize the largest number of topics covered by any partition. This makes the most heavily burdened part the focus, with applications including clustering information objects and balancing computational loads.

The setting is streaming: items arrive one at a time, and each assignment must be made immediately and cannot be reversed. Memory is limited to at most a linear function of the number of partitions. These requirements make scalability part of the problem definition, ruling out reliance on retaining and repeatedly reorganizing the full input.

The authors analyze a greedy assignment strategy and prove that it recovers a hidden co-clustering under a stated set of recovery conditions. The guarantee is conditional, rather than applying to arbitrary streams. An extensive empirical evaluation also finds superior performance over the alternatives considered. The results show how a simple assignment rule can combine strict streaming constraints with useful structural recovery.
summary.tldr: A memory-efficient greedy streaming rule partitions hypergraph items and recovers hidden co-clustering under specified conditions.

title: Streaming Min-max Hypergraph Partitioning

abstract: Elicitation is the study of statistics or properties which are computable via empirical risk minimization. While several recent papers have approached the general question of which properties are elicitable, we suggest that this is the wrong question---all properties are elicitable by first eliciting the entire distribution or data set, and thus the important question is how elicitable. Specifically, what is the minimum number of regression parameters needed to compute the property?Building on previous work, we introduce a new notion of elicitation complexity and lay the foundations for a calculus of elicitation. We establish several general results and techniques for proving upper and lower bounds on elicitation complexity. These results provide tight bounds for eliciting the Bayes risk of any loss, a large class of properties which includes spectral risk measures and several new properties of interest.

paragraphs: Elicitation asks which statistical properties can be computed through empirical risk minimization. This paper argues that a simple yes-or-no answer misses the main issue: one could first recover the entire distribution or dataset and then compute the desired property. The more informative question is how many regression parameters are needed to obtain it.

The authors formalize that question through a notion of elicitation complexity. They develop general results and techniques for proving upper and lower bounds on the number of required parameters. An upper bound shows that a representation of a certain size suffices; a lower bound establishes that a smaller one cannot suffice within the framework.

These techniques yield tight bounds for eliciting the Bayes risk of any loss, a class that includes spectral risk measures and additional properties studied in the paper. Tight bounds identify matching requirements and constructions rather than merely demonstrating feasibility. The contribution establishes foundations for reasoning systematically about the size of the intermediate prediction problem needed to recover a statistical quantity.
summary.tldr: Elicitation complexity measures the minimum number of regression parameters needed to recover a statistical property through risk minimization.

title: On Elicitation Complexity

abstract: Most robots lack the ability to learn new objects from past experiences. To migrate a robot to a new environment one must often completely re-generate the knowledge- base that it is running with. Since in open-ended domains the set of categories to be learned is not predefined, it is not feasible to assume that one can pre-program all object categories required by robots. Therefore, autonomous robots must have the ability to continuously execute learning and recognition in a concurrent and interleaved fashion. This paper proposes an open-ended 3D object recognition system which concurrently learns both the object categories and the statistical features for encoding objects. In particular, we propose an extension of Latent Dirichlet Allocation to learn structural semantic features (i.e. topics) from low-level feature co-occurrences for each category independently. Moreover, topics in each category are discovered in an unsupervised fashion and are updated incrementally using new object views. The approach contains similarities with the organization of the visual cortex and builds a hierarchy of increasingly sophisticated representations. Results show the fulfilling performance of this approach on different types of objects. Moreover, this system demonstrates the capability of learning from few training examples and competes with state-of-the-art systems.

Topics are learned independently for each category through an unsupervised process and updated incrementally as new object views arrive. These features form a hierarchy of increasingly sophisticated representations, with similarities to the organization of the visual cortex.

The reported results show successful performance across different object types, learning from few training examples, and competitiveness with state-of-the-art systems. The contribution connects ongoing category learning with ongoing representation learning. This combination addresses the need for recognition systems whose knowledge can grow as they encounter additional objects and views.
summary.tldr: An open-ended 3D recognition system incrementally learns both object categories and hierarchical features, with competitive results from few training examples.

title: Hierarchical Object Representation for Open-Ended Object Category Learning and Recognition

abstract: While neural machine translation (NMT) is making good progress in the past two years, tens of millions of bilingual sentence pairs are needed for its training. However, human labeling is very costly. To tackle this training data bottleneck, we develop a dual-learning mechanism, which can enable an NMT system to automatically learn from unlabeled data through a dual-learning game. This mechanism is inspired by the following observation: any machine translation task has a dual task, e.g., English-to-French translation (primal) versus French-to-English translation (dual); the primal and dual tasks can form a closed loop, and generate informative feedback signals to train the translation models, even if without the involvement of a human labeler. In the dual-learning mechanism, we use one agent to represent the model for the primal task and the other agent to represent the model for the dual task, then ask them to teach each other through a reinforcement learning process. Based on the feedback signals generated during this process (e.g., the language-model likelihood of the output of a model, and the reconstruction error of the original sentence after the primal and dual translations), we can iteratively update the two models until convergence (e.g., using the policy gradient methods). We call the corresponding approach to neural machine translation \emph{dual-NMT}. Experiments show that dual-NMT works very well on English$\leftrightarrow$French translation; especially, by learning from monolingual data (with 10\% bilingual data for warm start), it achieves a comparable accuracy to NMT trained from the full bilingual data for the French-to-English translation task.

paragraphs: Neural translation depends heavily on paired sentences in two languages, which are costly to label. This paper develops dual-NMT to learn from monolingual text by connecting translation in opposite directions. An English-to-French model and a French-to-English model form a loop, creating feedback that can train both systems without a human labeling each new example.

The two models act as agents that teach one another through reinforcement learning. Feedback includes how plausible a translation looks to a language model and how well translating it back reconstructs the original sentence. Policy-gradient methods can use these signals to update the models iteratively, making the reverse translation task part of the learning process.

Experiments report strong results for translation between English and French. Specifically, for French-to-English translation, learning from monolingual data after a warm start using 10% of the bilingual data achieves accuracy comparable to training NMT on the full bilingual set. That result supports reducing paired-data requirements in the tested setting while retaining a bilingual initialization.
summary.tldr: Dual-NMT trains opposite translation directions together, using monolingual text and round-trip feedback to reduce reliance on bilingual training pairs.

title: Dual Learning for Machine Translation

abstract: Several works have shown that deep CNN classifiers can be easily transferred across datasets, e.g. the transfer of a CNN trained to recognize objects on ImageNET to an object detector on Pascal VOC. Less clear, however, is the ability of CNNs to transfer knowledge across tasks. A common example of such transfer is the problem of scene classification that should leverage localized object detections to recognize holistic visual concepts. While this problem is currently addressed with Fisher vector representations, these are now shown ineffective for the high-dimensional and highly non-linear features extracted by modern CNNs. It is argued that this is mostly due to the reliance on a model, the Gaussian mixture of diagonal covariances, which has a very limited ability to capture the second order statistics of CNN features. This problem is addressed by the adoption of a better model, the mixture of factor analyzers (MFA), which approximates the non-linear data manifold by a collection of local subspaces. The Fisher score with respect to the MFA (MFA-FS) is derived and proposed as an image representation for holistic image classifiers. Extensive experiments show that the MFA-FS has state of the art performance for object-to-scene transfer and this transfer actually outperforms the training of a scene CNN from a large scene dataset. The two representations are also shown to be complementary, in the sense that their combination outperforms each of the representations by itself. When combined, they produce a state of the art scene classifier.
