paragraphs: Recognizing an entire scene from object-based features requires transferring knowledge across tasks. This paper argues that conventional Fisher vectors are ineffective for the high-dimensional, nonlinear features produced by modern CNNs. It attributes much of the problem to diagonal-covariance Gaussian mixtures, which have limited ability to represent second-order relationships among feature dimensions.

The proposed replacement is a mixture of factor analyzers, which approximates a nonlinear data manifold through multiple local subspaces. The authors derive its Fisher score and use that score as an image representation for holistic classification. The modeling change aims to preserve richer relationships in object features when summarizing them for scene recognition.

Experiments show state-of-the-art object-to-scene transfer, with performance exceeding training a scene CNN on a large scene dataset in the reported evaluation. The two representations also provide complementary information: combining them outperforms either alone and yields a state-of-the-art scene classifier. The findings support both improving the statistical model behind transferred features and combining those features with a representation learned directly for scenes.
summary.tldr: Fisher scores from mixtures of factor analyzers improve object-to-scene transfer and complement scene-trained CNN representations.

title: Object based Scene Representations using Fisher Scores of Local Subspace Projections

abstract: In this work we develop a theory of hierarchical clustering for graphs. Our modelling assumption is that graphs are sampled from a graphon, which is a powerful and general model for generating graphs and analyzing large networks. Graphons are a far richer class of graph models than stochastic blockmodels, the primary setting for recent progress in the statistical theory of graph clustering. We define what it means for an algorithm to produce the ``correct" clustering, give sufficient conditions in which a method is statistically consistent, and provide an explicit algorithm satisfying these properties.
originalAbstract: In this work we develop a theory of hierarchical clustering for graphs. Our modelling assumption is that graphs are sampled from a graphon, which is a powerful and general model for generating graphs and analyzing large networks. Graphons are a far richer class of graph models than stochastic blockmodels, the primary setting for recent progress in the statistical theory of graph clustering. We define what it means for an algorithm to produce the ``correct" clustering, give sufficient conditions in which a method is statistically consistent, and provide an explicit algorithm satisfying these properties.

paragraphs: The paper develops a statistical theory of hierarchical graph clustering. A hierarchy describes groups at multiple levels, so evaluating a clustering algorithm requires a target that captures more than one partition. The authors address this foundational question by defining what it means for a graph-clustering hierarchy to be correct.

Their modeling assumption is that the observed graph is sampled from a graphon. The abstract describes graphons as a general framework for generating graphs and studying large networks, richer than stochastic block models. This broadens the modeling setting beyond the block-model framework that had supported much of the statistical theory of graph clustering.

Within that setting, the authors provide sufficient conditions for statistical consistency and give an explicit algorithm satisfying them. The conditions establish a route to correctness; they are not presented as requirements that every successful algorithm must obey. The contribution connects three pieces that need to agree: a graph-generating model, a definition of the desired hierarchy, and a procedure with a corresponding statistical guarantee.
summary.tldr: The paper defines correct hierarchical clustering for graphon-generated graphs and supplies an algorithm satisfying sufficient conditions for consistency.

title: Graphons, mergeons, and so on!

abstract: Previous studies have proposed image-based clutter measures that correlate with human search times and/or eye movements. However, most models do not take into account the fact that the effects of clutter interact with the foveated nature of the human visual system: visual clutter further from the fovea has an increasing detrimental influence on perception. Here, we introduce a new foveated clutter model to predict the detrimental effects in target search utilizing a forced fixation search task. We use Feature Congestion (Rosenholtz et al.) as our non foveated clutter model, and we stack a peripheral architecture on top of Feature Congestion for our foveated model. We introduce the Peripheral Integration Feature Congestion (PIFC) coefficient, as a fundamental ingredient of our model that modulates clutter as a non-linear gain contingent on eccentricity. We finally show that Foveated Feature Congestion (FFC) clutter scores (r(44) = −0.82 ± 0.04, p < 0.0001) correlate better with target detection (hit rate) than regular Feature Congestion (r(44) = −0.19 ± 0.13, p = 0.0774) in forced fixation search; and we extend foveation to other clutter models showing stronger correlations in all cases. Thus, our model allows us to enrich clutter perception research by computing fixation specific clutter maps. Code for building peripheral representations is available.

paragraphs: Visual clutter can make a target difficult to find, but its effect depends on where a person is looking. Human vision treats the center of gaze differently from the periphery, and clutter farther from the center can interfere more strongly with perception. An image-wide clutter score can overlook this dependence on fixation.

The paper extends the Feature Congestion clutter measure with a peripheral representation. Its Peripheral Integration Feature Congestion coefficient adjusts clutter through a nonlinear gain that depends on distance from the fixation point. This produces Foveated Feature Congestion scores and allows clutter maps to be computed for particular gaze locations.

In a search task where participants held their gaze fixed, the foveated scores correlated substantially more strongly with target detection rates than ordinary Feature Congestion scores. The authors also applied foveation to other clutter models and reported stronger correlations in every tested case. These findings support incorporating peripheral vision into clutter measurement for the studied task. They show why predicting search difficulty can benefit from knowing both the image contents and the observer's fixation.
summary.tldr: Accounting for peripheral vision makes clutter scores more closely track target detection in a fixed-gaze search task.

title: Can Peripheral Representations Improve Clutter Metrics on Complex Scenes?

abstract: Determining how much of the sensory information carried by a neural code contributes to behavioral performance is key to understand sensory function and neural information flow. However, there are as yet no analytical tools to compute this information that lies at the intersection between sensory coding and behavioral readout. Here we develop a novel measure, termed the information-theoretic intersection information $\III(S;R;C)$, that quantifies how much of the sensory information carried by a neural response $R$ is used for behavior during perceptual discrimination tasks. Building on the Partial Information Decomposition framework, we define $\III(S;R;C)$ as the part of the mutual information between the stimulus $S$ and the response $R$ that also informs the consequent behavioral choice $C$. We compute $\III(S;R;C)$ in the analysis of two experimental cortical datasets, to show how this measure can be used to compare quantitatively the contributions of spike timing and spike rates to task performance, and to identify brain areas or neural populations that specifically transform sensory information into choice.

paragraphs: A neural response can carry information about a sensory stimulus, but determining how much of that information contributes to behavior is a separate problem. This paper introduces intersection information, a measure designed to connect sensory coding with behavioral choice during perceptual discrimination tasks. It focuses on information shared across the stimulus, neural response, and subsequent decision.

The measure builds on Partial Information Decomposition. Starting with the mutual information between a stimulus and a neural response, it identifies the portion that also informs the behavioral choice. This provides a quantitative way to study the overlap between what neural activity represents about the stimulus and what is relevant to the animal's decision.

The authors apply the measure to two experimental cortical datasets. They demonstrate how it can compare contributions from spike timing and spike rates to task performance. They also show its use in identifying brain areas or neural populations that transform sensory information into choice. The contribution is an analytical tool for studying where sensory representation and behavioral readout intersect.
summary.tldr: Intersection information quantifies the portion of sensory information in neural responses that also informs behavioral choice.

title: Quantifying how much sensory information in a neural code is relevant for behavior

abstract: Black box variational inference (BBVI) with reparameterization gradients triggered the exploration of divergence measures other than the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence, such as alpha divergences. In this paper, we view BBVI with generalized divergences as a form of estimating the marginal likelihood via biased importance sampling. The choice of divergence determines a bias-variance trade-off between the tightness of a bound on the marginal likelihood (low bias) and the variance of its gradient estimators. Drawing on variational perturbation theory of statistical physics, we use these insights to construct a family of new variational bounds. Enumerated by an odd integer order $K$, this family captures the standard KL bound for $K=1$, and converges to the exact marginal likelihood as $K\to\infty$. Compared to alpha-divergences, our reparameterization gradients have a lower variance. We show in experiments on Gaussian Processes and Variational Autoencoders that the new bounds are more mass covering, and that the resulting posterior covariances are closer to the true posterior and lead to higher likelihoods on held-out data.

paragraphs: Variational inference approximates a difficult posterior by optimizing a more manageable distribution. This paper interprets generalized-divergence versions of black-box variational inference as biased importance-sampling estimates of marginal likelihood. That interpretation exposes a trade-off between obtaining a tighter bound and keeping the gradient estimates used for optimization sufficiently stable.

Drawing on perturbation theory from statistical physics, the authors construct a family of variational bounds indexed by an odd integer K. At K equal to one, the family recovers the standard KL bound. As K tends to infinity, it converges to the exact marginal likelihood. The proposed reparameterization gradients also have lower variance than those associated with alpha divergences.

Experiments on Gaussian processes and variational autoencoders show more mass-covering approximations, meaning the fitted distributions represent posterior probability more broadly. The resulting posterior covariances are closer to the true posterior, and held-out likelihoods improve. These findings connect the new objectives to both uncertainty estimation and predictive performance, while exact marginal-likelihood recovery is specifically a limiting statement.
summary.tldr: Perturbation-based variational bounds balance approximation and gradient noise, improving posterior coverage and held-out likelihood in reported experiments.

title: Perturbative Black Box Variational Inference

abstract: We show that gradient descent on full-width linear convolutional networks of depth $L$ converges to a linear predictor related to the $\ell_{2/L}$ bridge penalty in the frequency domain. This is in contrast to linearly fully connected networks, where gradient descent converges to the hard margin linear SVM solution, regardless of depth.
originalAbstract: We show that gradient descent on full-width linear convolutional networks of depth $L$ converges to a linear predictor related to the $\ell_{2/L}$ bridge penalty in the frequency domain. This is in contrast to linearly fully connected networks, where gradient descent converges to the hard margin linear SVM solution, regardless of depth.

paragraphs: This paper examines how network architecture influences the linear predictor reached by gradient descent. Its comparison involves full-width linear convolutional networks and linear fully connected networks. Although both settings produce linear predictors, the stated results show that the training process selects solutions with different mathematical characterizations. The architecture therefore matters even in this linear setting.

For a convolutional network of depth L, the limiting predictor is related to an ℓ_(2/L) bridge penalty in the frequency domain. The dependence on L is central: changing depth changes the exponent in the penalty associated with the learned predictor. The result describes a relationship between optimization, depth, and the frequency-domain form of the solution.

For linear fully connected networks, gradient descent instead converges to the hard-margin linear support vector machine solution, regardless of depth. This comparison gives a precise example of implicit bias: the structure used to represent a predictor affects the solution training reaches. The stated convolutional result concerns full-width linear networks, and its characterization is a relation to the bridge penalty.
summary.tldr: Gradient descent has a depth-dependent frequency-domain bias in full-width linear convolutional networks, unlike linear fully connected networks.

title: Implicit Bias of Gradient Descent on Linear Convolutional Networks

abstract: The basic principles in designing convolutional neural network (CNN) structures for predicting objects on different levels, e.g., image-level, region-level, and pixel-level, are diverging. Generally, network structures designed specifically for image classification are directly used as default backbone structure for other tasks including detection and segmentation, but there is seldom backbone structure designed under the consideration of unifying the advantages of networks designed for pixel-level or region-level predicting tasks, which may require very deep features with high resolution. Towards this goal, we design a fish-like network, called FishNet. In FishNet, the information of all resolutions is preserved and refined for the final task. Besides, we observe that existing works still cannot \emph{directly} propagate the gradient information from deep layers to shallow layers. Our design can better handle this problem. Extensive experiments have been conducted to demonstrate the remarkable performance of the FishNet. In particular, on ImageNet-1k, the accuracy of FishNet is able to surpass the performance of DenseNet and ResNet with fewer parameters. FishNet was applied as one of the modules in the winning entry of the COCO Detection 2018 challenge. The code is available at https://github.com/kevin-ssy/FishNet.

This paper designs FishNet around their combined needs, including tasks that require deep representations while retaining high spatial resolution.

The challenge result describes FishNet's role within a larger system rather than an isolated evaluation of the backbone.
summary.tldr: FishNet preserves and refines features across resolutions to support classification, detection, and segmentation with a shared backbone design.

title: FishNet: A Versatile Backbone for Image, Region, and Pixel Level Prediction

abstract: We present a novel approach for nonparametric regression using wavelet basis functions. Our proposal, waveMesh, can be applied to non-equispaced data with sample size not necessarily a power of 2. We develop an efficient proximal gradient descent algorithm for computing the estimator and establish adaptive minimax convergence rates. The main appeal of our approach is that it naturally extends to additive and sparse additive models for a potentially large number of covariates. We prove minimax optimal convergence rates under a weak compatibility condition for sparse additive models. The compatibility condition holds when we have a small number of covariates. Additionally, we establish convergence rates for when the condition is not met. We complement our theoretical results with empirical studies comparing waveMesh to existing methods.

paragraphs: The paper introduces waveMesh, a nonparametric regression method using wavelet basis functions. It accommodates observations that are not equally spaced and does not require the sample size to be a power of two. These properties broaden the data arrangements to which the proposed wavelet regression approach can be applied.

The authors develop an efficient proximal gradient descent algorithm for computing the estimator and establish adaptive minimax convergence rates. They also extend the approach to additive and sparse additive models, potentially involving many covariates. This makes the method relevant beyond a single regression input, including settings where only some covariates contribute to the fitted relationship.

For sparse additive models, minimax-optimal rates require a weak compatibility condition. The authors state that this condition holds with a small number of covariates and also derive convergence rates when it does not hold. Empirical comparisons with existing methods complement the theory. The result combines flexible data handling and computation with guarantees whose strength depends on the stated setting.
summary.tldr: waveMesh extends wavelet regression to irregularly spaced data and sparse additive models, with efficient optimization and conditional optimal convergence guarantees.

title: Wavelet regression and additive models for irregularly spaced data

abstract: We explore the use of Vector Quantized Variational AutoEncoder (VQ-VAE) models for large scale image generation. To this end, we scale and enhance the autoregressive priors used in VQ-VAE to generate synthetic samples of much higher coherence and fidelity than possible before. We use simple feed-forward encoder and decoder networks, making our model an attractive candidate for applications where the encoding and/or decoding speed is critical. Additionally, VQ-VAE requires sampling an autoregressive model only in the compressed latent space, which is an order of magnitude faster than sampling in the pixel space, especially for large images. We demonstrate that a multi-scale hierarchical organization of VQ-VAE, augmented with powerful priors over the latent codes, is able to generate samples with quality that rivals that of state of the art Generative Adversarial Networks on multifaceted datasets such as ImageNet, while not suffering from GAN's known shortcomings such as mode collapse and lack of diversity.

Strengthening these learned priors and organizing the codes into a multiscale hierarchy allows the system to produce images with greater coherence and fidelity than earlier versions of the approach.

The architecture separates image encoding and decoding from sequential generation. Simple feed-forward networks perform the encoding and decoding, while the autoregressive model operates only in the compressed latent space. The authors report that this sampling process is an order of magnitude faster than generating directly in pixel space, with particular benefits for large images.

On complex datasets such as ImageNet, the hierarchical model generates samples whose quality rivals state-of-the-art generative adversarial networks. The authors also report avoiding GAN-associated problems such as mode collapse and insufficient diversity. The results show how powerful priors over compressed representations can combine high image quality, diverse outputs, and a more efficient location for the sequential sampling work.
summary.tldr: VQ-VAE-2 generates diverse, high-quality images by sampling powerful hierarchical priors in a compressed representation.

title: Generating Diverse High-Fidelity Images with VQ-VAE-2

abstract: We propose a new approach to graph compression by appeal to optimal transport. The transport problem is seeded with prior information about node importance, attributes, and edges in the graph. The transport formulation can be setup for either directed or undirected graphs, and its dual characterization is cast in terms of distributions over the nodes. The compression pertains to the support of node distributions and makes the problem challenging to solve directly. To this end, we introduce Boolean relaxations and specify conditions under which these relaxations are exact. The relaxations admit algorithms with provably fast convergence. Moreover, we provide an exact O(d log d) algorithm for the subproblem of projecting a d-dimensional vector to transformed simplex constraints. Our method outperforms state-of-the-art compression methods on graph classification.

The formulation supports both directed and undirected graphs. Its dual description uses distributions over nodes, making the support of those distributions—the nodes receiving nonzero mass—the central object of compression.

Choosing that support makes the optimization difficult to solve directly. The authors introduce Boolean relaxations and give conditions under which the relaxed formulations are exact. This conditional exactness matters because it identifies when the more tractable formulation retains the solution of the original problem. The resulting relaxations support algorithms with provably fast convergence.

In experiments, the compression method outperforms state-of-the-art alternatives on graph classification. The work therefore combines a transport-based compression model, theoretical treatment of its relaxations, and evidence of usefulness for a downstream graph task.
summary.tldr: An optimal-transport formulation compresses graphs through tractable relaxations and improves reported graph-classification performance.

title: Solving graph compression via optimal transport

abstract: We study the loss surface of a feed-forward neural network with ReLU non-linearities, regularized with weight decay. We show that the regularized loss function is piecewise strongly convex on an important open set which contains, under some conditions, all of its global minimizers. This is used to prove that local minima of the regularized loss function in this set are isolated, and that every differentiable critical point in this set is a local minimum, partially addressing an open problem given at the Conference on Learning Theory (COLT) 2015; our result is also applied to linear neural networks to show that with weight decay regularization, there are no non-zero critical points in a norm ball obtaining training error below a given threshold. We also include an experimental section where we validate our theoretical work and show that the regularized loss function is almost always piecewise strongly convex when restricted to stochastic gradient descent trajectories for three standard image classification problems.

paragraphs: Neural network loss surfaces are generally difficult to optimize, but their geometry can have more structure within particular regions. This paper studies feed-forward networks with ReLU activations and weight decay. It shows that the regularized loss is piecewise strongly convex on an important open set, which contains every global minimizer under additional conditions.

Within that set, the authors prove that local minima are isolated and every differentiable critical point is a local minimum. These are regional statements about the regularized objective, rather than a claim that the entire network loss is convex. For linear neural networks, they also rule out nonzero critical points satisfying a specified training-error threshold within a norm ball.

Experiments on three standard image classification problems examine the geometry encountered along stochastic gradient descent trajectories. The authors find the regularized loss almost always exhibits piecewise strong convexity along those trajectories. This empirical observation complements the theory by suggesting that the analyzed geometry appears during training, while the formal conclusions remain tied to the stated set and conditions.
summary.tldr: Weight-decayed ReLU networks have piecewise strongly convex loss geometry on a specified region, yielding conditional guarantees about critical points.

title: Piecewise Strong Convexity of Neural Networks

abstract: Facial action units (AUs) recognition is essential for emotion analysis and has been widely applied in mental state analysis. Existing work on AU recognition usually requires big face dataset with accurate AU labels. However, manual AU annotation requires expertise and can be time-consuming. In this work, we propose a semi-supervised approach for AU recognition utilizing a large number of web face images without AU labels and a small face dataset with AU labels inspired by the co-training methods. Unlike traditional co-training methods that require provided multi-view features and model re-training, we propose a novel co-training method, namely multi-label co-regularization, for semi-supervised facial AU recognition. Two deep neural networks are used to generate multi-view features for both labeled and unlabeled face images, and a multi-view loss is designed to enforce the generated features from the two views to be conditionally independent representations. In order to obtain consistent predictions from the two views, we further design a multi-label co-regularization loss aiming to minimize the distance between the predicted AU probability distributions of the two views. In addition, prior knowledge of the relationship between individual AUs is embedded through a graph convolutional network (GCN) for exploiting useful information from the big unlabeled dataset. Experiments on several benchmarks show that the proposed approach can effectively leverage large datasets of unlabeled face images to improve the AU recognition robustness and outperform the state-of-the-art semi-supervised AU recognition methods.

paragraphs: Recognizing facial action units supports emotion and mental-state analysis, but producing accurate action-unit labels requires expertise and time. This paper combines a small labeled face dataset with a large collection of unlabeled web images. Its semi-supervised approach draws on co-training while learning the different feature views within the model.

Two deep networks generate representations for labeled and unlabeled faces. A multi-view loss is designed to encourage conditionally independent representations, while a separate co-regularization loss brings the networks’ predicted action-unit probability distributions closer together. The method therefore seeks distinct representations that nonetheless agree about the action units present.

A graph convolutional network incorporates prior knowledge about relationships among action units, adding structure to how information from unlabeled images is used. Across several benchmarks, the authors report improved robustness and performance above the state-of-the-art semi-supervised methods considered. The findings support combining learned feature views, agreement between predictions, and known relationships among labels to make unlabeled face images useful for this recognition task.
summary.tldr: Two cooperating networks and a graph of action-unit relationships use unlabeled face images to improve semi-supervised recognition.

title: Multi-label Co-regularization for Semi-supervised Facial Action Unit Recognition

abstract: Ensembles of geophysical models improve projection accuracy and express uncertainties. We develop a novel data-driven ensembling strategy for combining geophysical models using Bayesian Neural Networks, which infers spatiotemporally varying model weights and bias while accounting for heteroscedastic uncertainties in the observations. This produces more accurate and uncertainty-aware projections without sacrificing interpretability. Applied to the prediction of total column ozone from an ensemble of 15 chemistry-climate models, we find that the Bayesian neural network ensemble (BayNNE) outperforms existing ensembling methods, achieving a 49.4% reduction in RMSE for temporal extrapolation, and a 67.4% reduction in RMSE for polar data voids, compared to a weighted mean. Uncertainty is also well-characterized, with 90.6% of the data points in our extrapolation validation dataset lying within 2 standard deviations and 98.5% within 3 standard deviations.

paragraphs: Combining geophysical models can improve projections and represent uncertainty, but the contribution of each model need not be constant across locations or times. This paper introduces BayNNE, a Bayesian neural network approach that learns how to combine models using weights and bias that vary in space and time.

The method also accounts for observation uncertainty that differs across the data, rather than treating all observations as equally uncertain. The authors present this as a way to improve accuracy and uncertainty estimates while preserving interpretability. In their application, BayNNE combines 15 chemistry-climate models to predict total column ozone, allowing the ensemble's combination rule to adapt to the prediction context.

Compared with a weighted mean, BayNNE reduces root mean squared error by 49.4% for temporal extrapolation and 67.4% for polar data voids. The authors also assess uncertainty on the extrapolation validation data: 90.6% of points fall within two standard deviations and 98.5% within three. These results provide evidence for both improved projections and well-characterized uncertainty in the evaluated ozone task, including settings that extend beyond available temporal or regional data.
summary.tldr: BayNNE learns spatially and temporally varying combinations of geophysical models, improving ozone predictions and characterizing their uncertainty.

title: Ensembling geophysical models with Bayesian Neural Networks

abstract: Priority dispatching rule (PDR) is widely used for solving real-world Job-shop scheduling problem (JSSP). However, the design of effective PDRs is a tedious task, requiring a myriad of specialized knowledge and often delivering limited performance. In this paper, we propose to automatically learn PDRs via an end-to-end deep reinforcement learning agent. We exploit the disjunctive graph representation of JSSP, and propose a Graph Neural Network based scheme to embed the states encountered during solving. The resulting policy network is size-agnostic, effectively enabling generalization on large-scale instances. Experiments show that the agent can learn high-quality PDRs from scratch with elementary raw features, and demonstrates strong performance against the best existing PDRs. The learned policies also perform well on much larger instances that are unseen in training.

paragraphs: Job-shop scheduling often relies on priority dispatching rules to decide which operation should proceed next. Designing effective rules requires substantial specialist knowledge, and the resulting rules can still perform poorly. This paper replaces manual rule design with an end-to-end deep reinforcement learning agent that learns a scheduling policy from scratch.

The approach represents the scheduling problem as a disjunctive graph and uses a graph neural network to encode the states encountered while constructing a schedule. The resulting policy network is size-agnostic: its design is not tied to one fixed instance size. This provides a mechanism for applying a learned dispatching policy to larger scheduling problems.

Experiments show that the agent learns high-quality dispatching rules using elementary raw features and performs strongly against the best existing priority rules considered. The learned policies also work well on much larger instances absent from training. These findings matter because they connect automated rule discovery with practical reuse across problem sizes, reducing dependence on hand-designed scheduling expertise in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: A graph-based reinforcement learning agent learns strong scheduling rules that also perform well on much larger unseen job-shop instances.

title: Learning to Dispatch for Job Shop Scheduling via Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Most state-of-the-art deep geometric learning single-view reconstruction approaches rely on encoder-decoder architectures that output either shape parametrizations or implicit representations. However, these representations rarely preserve the Euclidean structure of the 3D space objects exist in. In this paper, we show that building a geometry preserving 3-dimensional latent space helps the network concurrently learn global shape regularities and local reasoning in the object coordinate space and, as a result, boosts performance. We demonstrate both on ShapeNet synthetic images, which are often used for benchmarking purposes, and on real-world images that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art ones. Furthermore, the single-view pipeline naturally extends to multi-view reconstruction, which we also show.

paragraphs: Single-view reconstruction seeks to recover an object's three-dimensional shape from one image. Many deep learning approaches encode the image and then decode a shape representation, but their internal representations rarely preserve the Euclidean structure of the space containing the object. UCLID-Net examines whether preserving that geometry inside the network improves reconstruction.

The method builds a three-dimensional latent space that maintains geometric structure. This gives the network a representation in object coordinates where it can learn overall shape regularities and perform local reasoning together. The paper's central claim is that organizing the learned representation this way helps connect global expectations about shape with local information in the same spatial framework.

The authors report better performance than leading approaches on both synthetic ShapeNet images and real-world images. They also show that the single-view pipeline extends naturally to reconstruction from multiple views. These results support geometry preservation as a useful design choice for the latent representation, with demonstrated benefits across the evaluated image sources and an extension beyond one-view input.
summary.tldr: UCLID-Net improves reported single-image 3D reconstruction by preserving geometry in its latent space and also extends to multiple views.

title: UCLID-Net: Single View Reconstruction in Object Space

abstract: We consider the problem of factorizing a structured 3-way tensor into its constituent Canonical Polyadic (CP) factors. This decomposition, which can be viewed as a generalization of singular value decomposition (SVD) for tensors, reveals how the tensor dimensions (features) interact with each other. However, since the factors are a priori unknown, the corresponding optimization problems are inherently non-convex. The existing guaranteed algorithms which handle this non-convexity incur an irreducible error (bias), and only apply to cases where all factors have the same structure. To this end, we develop a provable algorithm for online structured tensor factorization, wherein one of the factors obeys some incoherence conditions, and the others are sparse. Specifically we show that, under some relatively mild conditions on initialization, rank, and sparsity, our algorithm recovers the factors exactly (up to scaling and permutation) at a linear rate. Complementary to our theoretical results, our synthetic and real-world data evaluations showcase superior performance compared to related techniques.

paragraphs: A three-way tensor organizes information along three dimensions, and CP decomposition expresses it through constituent factors that reveal interactions among those dimensions. Finding the unknown factors leads to a nonconvex optimization problem. The paper addresses limitations of existing guaranteed algorithms, which incur irreducible error and require all factors to follow the same structural pattern.

The proposed online factorization algorithm permits different structures across factors: one satisfies incoherence conditions, while the others are sparse. Under stated conditions on initialization, rank, and sparsity, the authors prove exact recovery at a linear convergence rate. Recovery is understood up to scaling and permutation, preserving the usual ambiguity in how equivalent factors are represented.

Synthetic and real-world evaluations report stronger performance than related techniques, complementing the recovery analysis. The importance of the result is the combination of heterogeneous factor structure and a guarantee without the irreducible bias described for earlier methods. That guarantee depends on the specified structural and initialization conditions; it is not presented as applying to arbitrary tensor factorizations.
summary.tldr: An online tensor factorization algorithm exactly recovers mixed incoherent and sparse factors at a linear rate under stated initialization, rank, and sparsity conditions.

title: Provable Online CP/PARAFAC Decomposition of a Structured Tensor via Dictionary Learning

abstract: We develop an approach for estimating models described via conditional moment restrictions, with a prototypical application being non-parametric instrumental variable regression. We introduce a min-max criterion function, under which the estimation problem can be thought of as solving a zero-sum game between a modeler who is optimizing over the hypothesis space of the target model and an adversary who identifies violating moments over a test function space. We analyze the statistical estimation rate of the resulting estimator for arbitrary hypothesis spaces, with respect to an appropriate analogue of the mean squared error metric, for ill-posed inverse problems. We show that when the minimax criterion is regularized with a second moment penalty on the test function and the test function space is sufficiently rich, then the estimation rate scales with the critical radius of the hypothesis and test function spaces, a quantity which typically gives tight fast rates. Our main result follows from a novel localized Rademacher analysis of statistical learning problems defined via minimax objectives. We provide applications of our main results for several hypothesis spaces used in practice such as: reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, high dimensional sparse linear functions, spaces defined via shape constraints, ensemble estimators such as random forests, and neural networks. For each of these applications we provide computationally efficient optimization methods for solving the corresponding minimax problem (e.g. stochastic first-order heuristics for neural networks). In several applications, we show how our modified mean squared error rate, combined with conditions that bound the ill-posedness of the inverse problem, lead to mean squared error rates. We conclude with an extensive experimental analysis of the proposed methods.

paragraphs: Conditional moment models specify restrictions that should hold on average given other variables. The paper estimates such models through a zero-sum game: a modeler chooses a candidate function, while an adversary searches a test-function space for violated restrictions. Nonparametric instrumental variable regression is a central application of this formulation.

The authors analyze estimation rates for arbitrary hypothesis spaces using an error measure suited to ill-posed inverse problems. When the adversary's objective includes a second-moment penalty and its test-function space is sufficiently rich, the rate scales with the critical radius of the hypothesis and test spaces. Their proof uses a localized Rademacher analysis of minimax learning objectives.

Applications include kernel spaces, sparse linear functions, shape-constrained functions, random forests, and neural networks, with corresponding computational methods. In several applications, further conditions controlling the inverse problem's ill-posedness translate the modified error guarantees into ordinary mean squared error rates. An extensive experimental analysis accompanies the theory. The framework therefore links adversarial fitting, statistical complexity, and practical estimation across several model families.
summary.tldr: Conditional moment estimation becomes a modeler–adversary game with statistical rate guarantees under suitable regularization and test-space richness.

title: Minimax Estimation of Conditional Moment Models

abstract: Although Sinkhorn divergences are now routinely used in data sciences to compare probability distributions, the computational effort required to compute them remains expensive, growing in general quadratically in the size $n$ of the support of these distributions. Indeed, solving optimal transport (OT) with an entropic regularization requires computing a $n\times n$ kernel matrix (the neg-exponential of a $n\times n$ pairwise ground cost matrix) that is repeatedly applied to a vector. We propose to use instead ground costs of the form $c(x,y)=-\log\dotp{\varphi(x)}{\varphi(y)}$ where $\varphi$ is a map from the ground space onto the positive orthant $\RR^r_+$, with $r\ll n$. This choice yields, equivalently, a kernel $k(x,y)=\dotp{\varphi(x)}{\varphi(y)}$, and ensures that the cost of Sinkhorn iterations scales as $O(nr)$. We show that usual cost functions can be approximated using this form. Additionaly, we take advantage of the fact that our approach yields approximation that remain fully differentiable with respect to input distributions, as opposed to previously proposed adaptive low-rank approximations of the kernel matrix, to train a faster variant of OT-GAN~\cite{salimans2018improving}.
originalAbstract: Although Sinkhorn divergences are now routinely used in data sciences to compare probability distributions, the computational effort required to compute them remains expensive, growing in general quadratically in the size $n$ of the support of these distributions. Indeed, solving optimal transport (OT) with an entropic regularization requires computing a $n\times n$ kernel matrix (the neg-exponential of a $n\times n$ pairwise ground cost matrix) that is repeatedly applied to a vector. We propose to use instead ground costs of the form $c(x,y)=-\log\dotp{\varphi(x)}{\varphi(y)}$ where $\varphi$ is a map from the ground space onto the positive orthant $\RR^r_+$, with $r\ll n$. This choice yields, equivalently, a kernel $k(x,y)=\dotp{\varphi(x)}{\varphi(y)}$, and ensures that the cost of Sinkhorn iterations scales as $O(nr)$. We show that usual cost functions can be approximated using this form. Additionaly, we take advantage of the fact that our approach yields approximation that remain fully differentiable with respect to input distributions, as opposed to previously proposed adaptive low-rank approximations of the kernel matrix, to train a faster variant of OT-GAN~\cite{salimans2018improving}.

paragraphs: Sinkhorn divergences compare probability distributions using entropy-regularized optimal transport. Their computation typically involves a kernel matrix containing all pairwise relationships between support points. With n points, this creates a quadratic computational burden, and the matrix must be applied to vectors repeatedly during the iterative solution.

The paper replaces this full representation with positive feature vectors of dimension r, where r is much smaller than n. Kernel values become inner products between those vectors, with corresponding ground costs defined through a negative logarithm. This factorized structure reduces the cost of Sinkhorn iterations to O(nr), making the dependence on support size linear for fixed feature dimension.

The authors show that usual cost functions can be approximated in this form. The approximations also remain fully differentiable with respect to the input distributions, which is useful when distribution comparison forms part of a learning objective. They use that property to train a faster OT-GAN variant, connecting the computational construction to an application that needs gradients through optimal transport.
summary.tldr: Positive low-dimensional features reduce Sinkhorn iteration costs to O(nr) while retaining differentiability for learning applications.

title: Linear Time Sinkhorn Divergences using Positive Features

abstract: Real Time Dynamic Programming (RTDP) is an online algorithm based on Dynamic Programming (DP) that acts by 1-step greedy planning. Unlike DP, RTDP does not require access to the entire state space, i.e., it explicitly handles the exploration. This fact makes RTDP particularly appealing when the state space is large and it is not possible to update all states simultaneously. In this we devise a multi-step greedy RTDP algorithm, which we call $h$-RTDP, that replaces the 1-step greedy policy with a $h$-step lookahead policy. We analyze $h$-RTDP in its exact form and establish that increasing the lookahead horizon, $h$, results in an improved sample complexity, with the cost of additional computations. This is the first work that proves improved sample complexity as a result of {\em increasing} the lookahead horizon in online planning. We then analyze the performance of $h$-RTDP in three approximate settings: approximate model, approximate value updates, and approximate state representation. For these cases, we prove that the asymptotic performance of $h$-RTDP remains the same as that of a corresponding approximate DP algorithm, the best one can hope for without further assumptions on the approximation errors.

The paper extends its usual one-step greedy decisions to an h-step lookahead policy, producing an algorithm called h-RTDP.

For the exact algorithm, the authors prove that longer lookahead improves sample complexity while requiring additional computation. Looking further ahead can therefore reduce the amount of sampled experience needed, at the expense of more planning work. summary.tldr: Longer lookahead in h-RTDP provably improves sample complexity at additional computational cost and matches corresponding approximate dynamic programming asymptotically.

title: Online Planning with Lookahead Policies

abstract: We consider settings in which the data of interest correspond to pairs of ordered times, e.g, the birth times of the first and second child, the times at which a new user creates an account and makes the first purchase on a website, and the entry and survival times of patients in a clinical trial. In these settings, the two times are not independent (the second occurs after the first), yet it is still of interest to determine whether there exists significant dependence "beyond" their ordering in time. We refer to this notion as "quasi-(in)dependence." For instance, in a clinical trial, to avoid biased selection, we might wish to verify that recruitment times are quasi-independent of survival times, where dependencies might arise due to seasonal effects. In this paper, we propose a nonparametric statistical test of quasi-independence. Our test considers a potentially infinite space of alternatives, making it suitable for complex data where the nature of the possible quasi-dependence is not known in advance. Standard parametric approaches are recovered as special cases, such as the classical conditional Kendall's tau, and log-rank tests. The tests apply in the right-censored setting: an essential feature in clinical trials, where patients can withdraw from the study. We provide an asymptotic analysis of our test-statistic, and demonstrate in experiments that our test obtains better power than existing approaches, while being more computationally efficient.

The useful question is whether there is additional dependence beyond that ordering. This paper develops a statistical test for this property, called quasi-independence, with examples including account creation and first purchase, or clinical recruitment and survival.

The proposed nonparametric test considers a potentially infinite collection of alternatives. It can therefore look for dependence without requiring researchers to specify its form beforehand. Familiar procedures, including conditional Kendall’s tau and log-rank tests, emerge as special cases. The method also accommodates right-censored observations, which matter when a study ends or a participant leaves before the event is observed.

The authors analyze the test statistic’s large-sample behavior and evaluate the method experimentally. In those experiments, it detects dependence more effectively than existing approaches while requiring less computation. The contribution is a broader testing framework that preserves the distinction between dependence forced by time ordering and additional relationships that may affect interpretation.
summary.tldr: A nonparametric kernel test detects dependence between event times beyond their required ordering, including with right-censored data.

title: A kernel test for quasi-independence

abstract: We introduce a new public video dataset for action recognition: Anonymized Videos from Diverse countries (AViD). Unlike existing public video datasets, AViD is a collection of action videos from many different countries. The motivation is to create a public dataset that would benefit training and pretraining of action recognition models for everybody, rather than making it useful for limited countries. Further, all the face identities in the AViD videos are properly anonymized to protect their privacy. It also is a static dataset where each video is licensed with the creative commons license. We confirm that most of the existing video datasets are statistically biased to only capture action videos from a limited number of countries. We experimentally illustrate that models trained with such biased datasets do not transfer perfectly to action videos from the other countries, and show that AViD addresses such problem. We also confirm that the new AViD dataset could serve as a good dataset for pretraining the models, performing comparably or better than prior datasets. The dataset is available at https://github.com/piergiaj/AViD

paragraphs: AViD is a public action-recognition dataset designed around geographical diversity. Its motivation is that training videos drawn mainly from a few countries may prepare models unevenly for videos from elsewhere. The paper examines this concern and finds that most existing video datasets are statistically concentrated in a limited set of countries.

The dataset collects action videos from many countries, anonymizes face identities, and provides a static collection whose videos carry Creative Commons licenses. These choices combine broader geographical coverage with privacy protection and a fixed collection for training. The contribution therefore concerns how the data is assembled and made available, as well as its usefulness for recognizing actions.

Experiments show that models trained on geographically concentrated datasets transfer imperfectly to videos from other countries, and that AViD addresses this problem. The authors also evaluate its value for pretraining, reporting performance comparable to or better than prior datasets. These findings support broader country coverage as a useful consideration when building action-recognition training resources.
summary.tldr: AViD offers anonymized action videos from diverse countries and shows benefits for cross-country transfer and model pretraining.

title: AViD Dataset: Anonymized Videos from Diverse Countries

abstract: We introduce a novel, end-to-end learnable, differentiable non-rigid tracker that enables state-of-the-art non-rigid reconstruction by a learned robust optimization. Given two input RGB-D frames of a non-rigidly moving object, we employ a convolutional neural network to predict dense correspondences and their confidences. These correspondences are used as constraints in an as-rigid-as-possible (ARAP) optimization problem. By enabling gradient back-propagation through the weighted non-linear least squares solver, we are able to learn correspondences and confidences in an end-to-end manner such that they are optimal for the task of non-rigid tracking. Under this formulation, correspondence confidences can be learned via self-supervision, informing a learned robust optimization, where outliers and wrong correspondences are automatically down-weighted to enable effective tracking. Compared to state-of-the-art approaches, our algorithm shows improved reconstruction performance, while simultaneously achieving 85 times faster correspondence prediction than comparable deep-learning based methods.

paragraphs: Tracking a deforming object requires finding how its surface moves between observations. This paper takes two RGB-D frames, which contain color and depth information, and uses a convolutional network to predict dense correspondences between them. The network also assigns confidence values to those matches, allowing the tracker to distinguish more trustworthy constraints from questionable ones.

The correspondences feed into an as-rigid-as-possible optimization problem that estimates the object's non-rigid motion. The key design choice is to make the weighted nonlinear least-squares solver differentiable. Training can then propagate through the optimization, so the predicted matches and confidence values are learned for their usefulness to the final tracking task. Confidence learning can use self-supervision, automatically reducing the influence of outliers and incorrect matches.

The authors report improved reconstruction performance compared with state-of-the-art approaches. They also report correspondence prediction that is 85 times faster than comparable deep learning methods. That speed claim concerns correspondence prediction specifically. Together, the results support integrating learned matching and robust optimization into a single trainable tracking system.
summary.tldr: A differentiable tracker jointly learns surface matches and their confidence, improving non-rigid reconstruction while greatly accelerating correspondence prediction.

title: Neural Non-Rigid Tracking

abstract: We introduce COPT, a novel distance metric between graphs defined via an optimization routine, computing a coordinated pair of optimal transport maps simultaneously. This gives an unsupervised way to learn general-purpose graph representation, applicable to both graph sketching and graph comparison. COPT involves simultaneously optimizing dual transport plans, one between the vertices of two graphs, and another between graph signal probability distributions. We show theoretically that our method preserves important global structural information on graphs, in particular spectral information, and analyze connections to existing studies. Empirically, COPT outperforms state of the art methods in graph classification on both synthetic and real datasets.

paragraphs: COPT introduces a distance between graphs that also supports learning graph representations without supervision. The aim is to capture information useful for both comparing graphs and constructing graph sketches. Its distance is defined through an optimization problem, making the representation depend on how two graphs can be related through coordinated mappings.

The method jointly computes two optimal transport plans. One relates vertices in the two graphs; the other relates probability distributions of graph signals. Optimizing these plans together coordinates the vertex-level correspondence with the comparison of signal distributions. This paired construction is the central mechanism behind the proposed graph distance.

The authors prove that COPT preserves important information about overall graph structure, including spectral information. They also analyze its relationship to earlier work. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets show better graph classification performance than the state-of-the-art methods used for comparison. Together, the theoretical and empirical results support COPT as a general-purpose representation approach that retains global structure relevant to downstream graph analysis.
summary.tldr: COPT jointly transports vertices and graph-signal distributions to compare graphs while preserving important global structure.

title: COPT: Coordinated Optimal Transport on Graphs

abstract: Federated learning (FL) is a decentralized and privacy-preserving machine learning technique in which a group of clients collaborate with a server to learn a global model without sharing clients' data. One challenge associated with FL is statistical diversity among clients, which restricts the global model from delivering good performance on each client's task. To address this, we propose an algorithm for personalized FL (pFedMe) using Moreau envelopes as clients' regularized loss functions, which help decouple personalized model optimization from the global model learning in a bi-level problem stylized for personalized FL. Theoretically, we show that pFedMe convergence rate is state-of-the-art: achieving quadratic speedup for strongly convex and sublinear speedup of order 2/3 for smooth nonconvex objectives. Experimentally, we verify that pFedMe excels at empirical performance compared with the vanilla FedAvg and Per-FedAvg, a meta-learning based personalized FL algorithm.

paragraphs: Federated learning lets clients collaborate with a server without sharing their data. A shared model can nevertheless serve individual clients poorly when their data distributions differ. This paper proposes pFedMe, an algorithm that combines collaborative learning with models personalized to each client's task.

The method uses Moreau envelopes as regularized client losses. These help separate the optimization of personalized models from learning the global model within a bi-level formulation. This organization makes local adaptation and shared learning distinct parts of the same optimization problem, directly addressing the tension created by statistical diversity across clients.

The authors report state-of-the-art theoretical convergence rates, including quadratic speedup for strongly convex objectives and sublinear speedup of order two-thirds for smooth nonconvex objectives. These are separate claims for different objective classes. Experiments also show better empirical performance than FedAvg and the meta-learning-based personalized method Per-FedAvg. Together, the results support the proposed separation of personal and global optimization through both convergence analysis and observed predictive performance.
summary.tldr: pFedMe uses Moreau-envelope client losses to separate personalized optimization from global federated learning, with convergence guarantees and empirical gains.

title: Personalized Federated Learning with Moreau Envelopes

abstract: Recent empirical work shows that inconsistent results based on choice of hyperparameter optimization (HPO) configuration are a widespread problem in ML research. When comparing two algorithms J and K searching one subspace can yield the conclusion that J outperforms K, whereas searching another can entail the opposite. In short, the way we choose hyperparameters can deceive us. We provide a theoretical complement to this prior work, arguing that, to avoid such deception, the process of drawing conclusions from HPO should be made more rigorous. We call this process epistemic hyperparameter optimization (EHPO), and put forth a logical framework to capture its semantics and how it can lead to inconsistent conclusions about performance. Our framework enables us to prove EHPO methods that are guaranteed to be defended against deception, given bounded compute time budget t. We demonstrate our framework's utility by proving and empirically validating a defended variant of random search.

paragraphs: Comparisons between learning algorithms can reverse when researchers change the hyperparameter search space. One search configuration may favor one algorithm, while another favors its competitor. This paper treats that instability as a problem in how evidence from hyperparameter optimization is converted into conclusions about comparative performance.

The authors call this reasoning process epistemic hyperparameter optimization, or EHPO. They introduce a logical framework that describes what such conclusions mean and how inconsistent conclusions can arise. This shifts attention from merely finding a strong configuration to determining whether the resulting performance claim is defended against the framework's notion of deception.

Within that framework, the paper proves that EHPO methods can be defended against deception given a bounded computation budget. It also constructs a defended version of random search, providing both a proof and empirical validation. The guarantee is tied to the formal setting and budget. Its practical significance is a more rigorous foundation for interpreting algorithm comparisons produced by hyperparameter searches.
summary.tldr: A logical framework formalizes misleading hyperparameter-based comparisons and supports a defended random-search method under a bounded compute budget.

title: Hyperparameter Optimization Is Deceiving Us, and How to Stop It

abstract: Sampling-based motion planning is a popular approach in robotics for finding paths in continuous configuration spaces. Checking collision with obstacles is the major computational bottleneck in this process. We propose new learning-based methods for reducing collision checking to accelerate motion planning by training graph neural networks (GNNs) that perform path exploration and path smoothing. Given random geometric graphs (RGGs) generated from batch sampling, the path exploration component iteratively predicts collision-free edges to prioritize their exploration. The path smoothing component then optimizes paths obtained from the exploration stage. The methods benefit from the ability of GNNs of capturing geometric patterns from RGGs through batch sampling and generalize better to unseen environments. Experimental results show that the learned components can significantly reduce collision checking and improve overall planning efficiency in challenging high-dimensional motion planning tasks.

paragraphs: Sampling-based robot motion planners search for paths through continuous configuration spaces. A major expense is checking whether candidate movements collide with obstacles. This paper aims to reduce that expense by training graph neural networks to guide two stages of planning: exploring possible paths and improving a path after it has been found.

The method operates on random geometric graphs constructed from batches of sampled configurations. During exploration, a learned component repeatedly predicts which edges are collision-free and prioritizes their exploration. A second component smooths the paths produced by the exploration stage. Together, the components apply learned guidance to both discovering a route and refining it.

The authors attribute the approach's benefits to graph networks' ability to capture geometric patterns in these sampled graphs, supporting better generalization to unseen environments. Experiments on challenging high-dimensional motion-planning tasks show substantial reductions in collision checking and improvements in overall planning efficiency. The findings suggest that learning which candidate connections deserve attention can reduce a central computational bottleneck in sampling-based planning.
summary.tldr: Graph neural networks prioritize path exploration and smooth resulting paths, reducing collision checks and improving motion-planning efficiency.

title: Reducing Collision Checking for Sampling-Based Motion Planning Using Graph Neural Networks

abstract: In this work we consider the problem of releasing a differentially private statistical summary that resides on a Riemannian manifold. We present an extension of the Laplace or K-norm mechanism that utilizes intrinsic distances and volumes on the manifold. We also consider in detail the specific case where the summary is the Fr\'echet mean of data residing on a manifold. We demonstrate that our mechanism is rate optimal and depends only on the dimension of the manifold, not on the dimension of any ambient space, while also showing how ignoring the manifold structure can decrease the utility of the sanitized summary. We illustrate our framework in two examples of particular interest in statistics: the space of symmetric positive definite matrices, which is used for covariance matrices, and the sphere, which can be used as a space for modeling discrete distributions.

paragraphs: Some statistical summaries belong to curved geometric spaces rather than unrestricted Euclidean space. This paper studies how to release such summaries with differential privacy while respecting their geometry. Its goal is to preserve useful statistical information when the valid outputs lie on a Riemannian manifold.

The proposed mechanism extends Laplace or K-norm privacy mechanisms using distances and volumes intrinsic to the manifold. The authors examine the Fréchet mean in detail, providing a central example of a statistical summary defined on such a space. Basing the mechanism on the manifold's own geometry makes the structure of the output space part of the privacy procedure.

The authors show that their mechanism is rate optimal and that its performance depends on the manifold's dimension rather than the dimension of an ambient space containing it. They also show that ignoring this structure can reduce the utility of the privatized summary. Examples cover symmetric positive definite matrices, relevant to covariance matrices, and spheres, which can represent discrete distributions.
summary.tldr: A geometry-aware differential privacy mechanism achieves rate-optimal utility governed by a manifold's intrinsic dimension.

title: Differential Privacy Over Riemannian Manifolds

abstract: Exploration methods based on pseudo-count of transitions or curiosity of dynamics have achieved promising results in solving reinforcement learning with sparse rewards. However, such methods are usually sensitive to environmental dynamics-irrelevant information, e.g., white-noise. To handle such dynamics-irrelevant information, we propose a Dynamic Bottleneck (DB) model, which attains a dynamics-relevant representation based on the information-bottleneck principle. Based on the DB model, we further propose DB-bonus, which encourages the agent to explore state-action pairs with high information gain. We establish theoretical connections between the proposed DB-bonus, the upper confidence bound (UCB) for linear case, and the visiting count for tabular case. We evaluate the proposed method on Atari suits with dynamics-irrelevant noises. Our experiments show that exploration with DB bonus outperforms several state-of-the-art exploration methods in noisy environments.

paragraphs: When rewards are sparse, a reinforcement learning agent needs other signals to decide what to explore. Curiosity and transition-count approaches can help, but they may also respond to information unrelated to environmental dynamics, such as white noise. That sensitivity can make irrelevant variation appear worth investigating.

The paper proposes a Dynamic Bottleneck model that uses the information-bottleneck principle to obtain a representation relevant to dynamics. On top of this representation, DB-bonus rewards exploration of state-action pairs with high information gain. The design links the exploration incentive to information about the system’s behavior, addressing the distraction caused by dynamics-irrelevant observations.

The authors establish theoretical connections between DB-bonus and upper confidence bounds in the linear case, and between DB-bonus and visiting counts in the tabular case. These connections relate the new bonus to established exploration ideas under specific settings. Experiments on Atari environments with dynamics-irrelevant noise show that DB-bonus outperforms several leading exploration methods. The stated empirical benefit concerns robustness of exploration in those noisy environments.
summary.tldr: Dynamic Bottleneck learns dynamics-relevant representations and uses information gain to improve exploration in environments containing irrelevant noise.

title: Dynamic Bottleneck for Robust Self-Supervised Exploration

abstract: Robustness of machine learning models is critical for security related applications, where real-world adversaries are uniquely focused on evading neural network based detectors. Prior work mainly focus on crafting adversarial examples (AEs) with small uniform norm-bounded perturbations across features to maintain the requirement of imperceptibility. However, uniform perturbations do not result in realistic AEs in domains such as malware, finance, and social networks. For these types of applications, features typically have some semantically meaningful dependencies. The key idea of our proposed approach is to enable non-uniform perturbations that can adequately represent these feature dependencies during adversarial training. We propose using characteristics of the empirical data distribution, both on correlations between the features and the importance of the features themselves. Using experimental datasets for malware classification, credit risk prediction, and spam detection, we show that our approach is more robust to real-world attacks. Finally, we present robustness certification utilizing non-uniform perturbation bounds, and show that non-uniform bounds achieve better certification.

paragraphs: Adversarial training teaches a model to withstand deliberately altered inputs. Common approaches constrain changes using a uniform norm bound, which is intended to keep adversarial examples close to their originals. This paper argues that such constraints can poorly represent realistic attacks on structured data, where features have meaningful relationships and different levels of importance.

The proposed approach allows non-uniform perturbations during adversarial training. It uses information from the empirical data distribution, including correlations between features and the importance of individual features, to shape the permitted changes. The motivation is to make the training threat model better reflect how related features can change together in the application domain.

Experiments on malware classification, credit risk prediction, and spam detection report greater robustness to real-world attacks. The paper also develops robustness certification using non-uniform perturbation bounds and reports better certification with those bounds. These findings connect the design of permissible input changes to both empirical attack resistance and formal robustness assessment, rather than treating the perturbation constraint as a domain-independent choice.
summary.tldr: Using feature correlations and importance to define non-uniform perturbations improves reported adversarial robustness and robustness certification.

title: Adversarial Robustness with Non-uniform Perturbations

abstract: Optimization algorithms such as projected Newton's method, FISTA, mirror descent and its variants enjoy near-optimal regret bounds and convergence rates, but suffer from a computational bottleneck of computing ``projections" in potentially each iteration (e.g., $O(T^{1/2})$ regret of online mirror descent). On the other hand, conditional gradient variants solve a linear optimization in each iteration, but result in suboptimal rates (e.g., $O(T^{3/4})$ regret of online Frank-Wolfe). Motivated by this trade-off in runtime v/s convergence rates, we consider iterative projections of close-by points over widely-prevalent submodular base polytopes $B(f)$. We develop a toolkit to speed up the computation of projections using both discrete and continuous perspectives. We subsequently adapt the away-step Frank-Wolfe algorithm to use this information and enable early termination. For the special case of cardinality based submodular polytopes, we improve the runtime of computing certain Bregman projections by a factor of $\Omega(n/\log(n))$. Our theoretical results show orders of magnitude reduction in runtime in preliminary computational experiments.

This paper addresses that tradeoff for submodular base polytopes by focusing on repeated projections of points that are close to one another.

The central opportunity is to reuse relevant structure across nearby projection problems instead of treating each as unrelated. They adapt the away-step Frank-Wolfe algorithm to exploit this information and allow early termination, reducing the work involved in obtaining projections.

summary.tldr: Reusing structure across nearby projections accelerates optimization over submodular base polytopes, with a proven speedup for certain cardinality-based cases.

title: Reusing Combinatorial Structure: Faster Iterative Projections over Submodular Base Polytopes

abstract: Gaussian Cox processes are widely-used point process models that use a Gaussian process to describe the Bayesian a priori uncertainty present in latent intensity functions. In this paper, we propose a novel Bayesian inference scheme for Gaussian Cox processes by exploiting a conceptually-intuitive {¥it path integral} formulation. The proposed scheme does not rely on domain discretization, scales linearly with the number of observed events, has a lower complexity than the state-of-the-art variational Bayesian schemes with respect to the number of inducing points, and is applicable to a wide range of Gaussian Cox processes with various types of link functions. Our scheme is especially beneficial under the multi-dimensional input setting, where the number of inducing points tends to be large. We evaluate our scheme on synthetic and real-world data, and show that it achieves comparable predictive accuracy while being tens of times faster than reference methods.

Learning that intensity from observed events requires Bayesian inference, which can be computationally demanding. This paper introduces an inference scheme based on a path-integral formulation of the model.

Its computational cost grows linearly with the number of observed events, and its dependence on the number of inducing points is lower than that of the compared state-of-the-art variational Bayesian schemes. It also accommodates a broad range of link functions, which connect the Gaussian process to the event intensity.

These properties are especially useful for multidimensional inputs, where many inducing points may be needed. On synthetic and real-world datasets, the authors report predictive accuracy comparable to reference methods while running tens of times faster. The results suggest that changing the inference formulation can substantially reduce computation while retaining similar predictive quality in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: A path-integral inference scheme makes Gaussian Cox process learning substantially faster while preserving comparable predictive accuracy in experiments.

title: Fast Bayesian Inference for Gaussian Cox Processes via Path Integral Formulation

abstract: Despite recent advances in its theoretical understanding, there still remains a significant gap in the ability of existing PAC-Bayesian theories on meta-learning to explain performance improvements in the few-shot learning setting, where the number of training examples in the target tasks is severely limited. This gap originates from an assumption in the existing theories which supposes that the number of training examples in the observed tasks and the number of training examples in the target tasks follow the same distribution, an assumption that rarely holds in practice. By relaxing this assumption, we develop two PAC-Bayesian bounds tailored for the few-shot learning setting and show that two existing meta-learning algorithms (MAML and Reptile) can be derived from our bounds, thereby bridging the gap between practice and PAC-Bayesian theories. Furthermore, we derive a new computationally-efficient PACMAML algorithm, and show it outperforms existing meta-learning algorithms on several few-shot benchmark datasets.
