paragraphs: Few-shot meta-learning aims to use experience across tasks to learn effectively on a new task with very few examples. Existing PAC-Bayesian analyses struggled to explain the improvements seen in this setting. The paper identifies a specific mismatch: those theories assume that example counts in previously observed tasks and target tasks follow the same distribution.

The authors relax that assumption and derive two PAC-Bayesian bounds designed for few-shot learning. This makes the theoretical setup better reflect situations where experience comes from tasks with different amounts of data than the eventual target tasks. They also show that the existing MAML and Reptile algorithms can be derived from these bounds, connecting established methods to the revised analysis.

The same framework leads to PACMAML, a new algorithm described as computationally efficient. The authors report that it outperforms existing meta-learning algorithms on several few-shot benchmarks. Together, the results provide a theoretical account of familiar algorithms under more appropriate data-count assumptions and a new method whose reported benchmark performance supports the usefulness of that account.
summary.tldr: Relaxing a task-size assumption yields few-shot PAC-Bayesian bounds that explain MAML and Reptile and motivate the PACMAML algorithm.

title: Bridging the Gap Between Practice and PAC-Bayes Theory in Few-Shot Meta-Learning

abstract: Garments are ubiquitous in both real and many of the virtual worlds. They are highly deformable objects, exhibit an immense variety of designs and shapes, and yet, most garments are created from a set of regularly shaped flat pieces. Exploration of garment structure presents a peculiar case for an object structure estimation task and might prove useful for downstream tasks of neural 3D garment modeling and reconstruction by providing strong prior on garment shapes. To facilitate research in these directions, we propose a method for generating large synthetic datasets of 3D garment designs and their sewing patterns. Our method consists of a flexible description structure for specifying parametric sewing pattern templates and the automatic generation pipeline to produce garment 3D models with little-to-none manual intervention. To add realism, the pipeline additionally creates corrupted versions of the final meshes that imitate artifacts of 3D scanning.With this pipeline, we created the first large-scale synthetic dataset of 3D garment models with their sewing patterns. The dataset contains more than 20000 garment design variations produced from 19 different base types. Seven of these garment types are specifically designed to target evaluation of the generalization across garment sewing pattern topologies.

paragraphs: Garments have highly variable, deformable three-dimensional shapes, yet most originate from collections of flat fabric pieces. This paper uses that relationship to build a synthetic dataset pairing 3D garments with their sewing patterns. Such structural information could provide useful prior knowledge for garment modeling and reconstruction.

The method combines a flexible description format for parameterized sewing-pattern templates with an automated pipeline that generates garment models. It requires little or no manual intervention during generation. The pipeline also creates corrupted mesh versions that imitate artifacts from 3D scanning, adding examples with imperfections relevant to working with scanned shapes.

Using this process, the authors produce more than 20,000 garment design variations from 19 base types. Seven types are specifically designed to evaluate generalization across sewing-pattern topologies, allowing evaluation to address changes in pattern structure. The main contribution is both the paired dataset and a generation method that supports research into the relationship between flat construction patterns and their resulting 3D forms.
summary.tldr: An automated pipeline generates over 20,000 synthetic 3D garments paired with sewing patterns, including scan-like corruptions and topology-generalization cases.

title: Generating Datasets of 3D Garments with Sewing Patterns

abstract: We focus on federated learning in practical recommender systems and natural language processing scenarios. The global model for federated optimization typically contains a large and sparse embedding layer, while each client’s local data tend to interact with part of features, updating only a small submodel with the feature-related embedding vectors. We identify a new and important issue that distinct data features normally involve different numbers of clients, generating the differentiation of hot and cold features. We further reveal that the classical federated averaging algorithm (FedAvg) or its variants, which randomly selects clients to participate and uniformly averages their submodel updates, will be severely slowed down, because different parameters of the global model are optimized at different speeds. More specifically, the model parameters related to hot (resp., cold) features will be updated quickly (resp., slowly). We thus propose federated submodel averaging (FedSubAvg), which introduces the number of feature-related clients as the metric of feature heat to correct the aggregation of submodel updates. We prove that due to the dispersion of feature heat, the global objective is ill-conditioned, and FedSubAvg works as a suitable diagonal preconditioner. We also rigorously analyze FedSubAvg’s convergence rate to stationary points. We finally evaluate FedSubAvg over several public and industrial datasets. The evaluation results demonstrate that FedSubAvg significantly outperforms FedAvg and its variants.

This paper identifies that imbalance as a source of slow optimization when client updates are combined through standard federated averaging.

The proposed method, FedSubAvg, uses the number of clients associated with each feature to correct how submodel updates are aggregated. Its aggregation therefore accounts explicitly for differences in feature participation.

They also analyze its convergence rate to stationary points. Evaluations on public and industrial datasets show significant improvements over FedAvg and its variants, linking the optimization analysis to practical performance in the studied sparse-model settings.
summary.tldr: FedSubAvg corrects federated update aggregation for unequal feature participation, improving optimization in the evaluated sparse-model tasks.

title: Federated Submodel Optimization for Hot and Cold Data Features

abstract: We introduce an additive Gaussian process (GP) framework accounting for monotonicity constraints and scalable to high dimensions. Our contributions are threefold. First, we show that our framework enables to satisfy the constraints everywhere in the input space. We also show that more general componentwise linear inequality constraints can be handled similarly, such as componentwise convexity. Second, we propose the additive MaxMod algorithm for sequential dimension reduction. By sequentially maximizing a squared-norm criterion, MaxMod identifies the active input dimensions and refines the most important ones. This criterion can be computed explicitly at a linear cost. Finally, we provide open-source codes for our full framework. We demonstrate the performance and scalability of the methodology in several synthetic examples with hundreds of dimensions under monotonicity constraints as well as on a real-world flood application.

This paper introduces an additive Gaussian process framework that incorporates such monotonicity constraints while scaling to many input dimensions. The authors show that its constraints hold throughout the input space.

The framework also handles more general linear inequality constraints on individual components, including componentwise convexity. To manage dimensionality, the authors propose additive MaxMod, a sequential procedure that identifies active input dimensions and refines the most important ones. It chooses updates by maximizing a squared-norm criterion that can be computed explicitly at linear cost.

This combination connects structural knowledge about the function with selective refinement of its inputs. The model can enforce its shape requirements while directing refinement toward dimensions identified as important. Demonstrations include synthetic problems with hundreds of dimensions under monotonicity constraints and a real flood application. These results provide evidence for the framework’s performance and scalability in the studied settings, alongside the guarantee that its constraints hold everywhere.
summary.tldr: An additive Gaussian process framework enforces monotonicity throughout the input space and uses sequential dimension selection to scale.

title: High-dimensional Additive Gaussian Processes under Monotonicity Constraints

paragraphs: This paper studies recovering the parameters of a single-layer ReLU network from samples of its output distribution when some samples are arbitrary outliers. The target parameters are the weight matrix and bias vector. The analysis assumes non-negative biases and that the fraction of genuine samples, denoted by p, is greater than two thirds.

The method combines gradient descent with filters based on either a median or a trimmed mean. These filters mitigate the influence of corrupted samples during parameter estimation. This connects an ordinary optimization procedure with robust filtering, allowing the authors to analyze recovery even though the outliers themselves need not follow a specified distribution.

For parameter error ε, the authors prove that sample counts scaling as 1/p² + 1/(ε²p) are sufficient, ignoring logarithmic factors. The sufficient running time has the same dependence multiplied by d², where d is the problem dimension. These are upper bounds under the stated assumptions, rather than claims that every algorithm requires those resources. Theory and simulations together describe how contamination, desired accuracy, and dimension affect the studied recovery procedure.
summary.tldr: Gradient descent with robust filters recovers single-layer ReLU parameters under arbitrary outliers, with proved resource bounds when biases are non-negative and over two thirds of samples are genuine.

title: Learning Distributions Generated by Single-Layer ReLU Networks in the Presence of Arbitrary Outliers

abstract: A surprising phenomenon in modern machine learning is the ability of a highly overparameterized model to generalize well (small error on the test data) even when it is trained to memorize the training data (zero error on the training data). This has led to an arms race towards increasingly overparameterized models (c.f., deep learning). In this paper, we study an underexplored hidden cost of overparameterization: the fact that overparameterized models may be more vulnerable to privacy attacks, in particular the membership inference attack that predicts the (potentially sensitive) examples used to train a model. We significantly extend the relatively few empirical results on this problem by theoretically proving for an overparameterized linear regression model in the Gaussian data setting that membership inference vulnerability increases with the number of parameters. Moreover, a range of empirical studies indicates that more complex, nonlinear models exhibit the same behavior. Finally, we extend our analysis towards ridge-regularized linear regression and show in the Gaussian data setting that increased regularization also increases membership inference vulnerability in the overparameterized regime.

paragraphs: A model can fit its training data perfectly and still predict well on new examples. This paper examines a separate consequence of having many parameters: vulnerability to membership inference. Such an attack tries to determine whether a particular example was used for training, so predictive generalization and protection of training membership are different concerns.

The authors prove that membership-inference vulnerability increases with parameter count for an overparameterized linear regression model with Gaussian data. This gives a theoretical foundation for a relationship previously studied largely through limited empirical evidence. Additional experiments indicate similar behavior in more complex nonlinear models, extending the empirical relevance without making the linear-model theorem universal.

The analysis also considers ridge-regularized linear regression. In the Gaussian-data setting and overparameterized regime, increasing regularization increases membership-inference vulnerability. This result is specifically tied to that setting rather than a claim about every form of regularization. Together, the findings reveal a privacy tradeoff that model accuracy alone does not capture: adding parameters, and even strengthening regularization in the analyzed regime, can make training membership easier to infer.
summary.tldr: The paper proves that more parameters increase membership-inference vulnerability in Gaussian linear regression and finds similar empirical trends in nonlinear models.

title: Parameters or Privacy: A Provable Tradeoff Between Overparameterization and Membership Inference

abstract: In adversarial team games, a team of players sequentially faces a team of adversaries. These games are the simplest setting with multiple players where cooperation and competition coexist, and it is known that the information asymmetry among the team members makes equilibrium approximation computationally hard. Although much effort has been spent designing scalable algorithms, the problem of solving large game instances is open. In this paper, we extend the successful approach of solving huge two-*player* zero-sum games, where a blueprint strategy is computed offline by using an abstract version of the game and then it is refined online, that is, during a playthrough. In particular, to the best of our knowledge, our paper provides the first method for online strategy refinement via subgame solving in adversarial team games. Our method, based on the team belief DAG, generates a gadget game and then refine the blueprint strategy by using column-generation approaches in anytime fashion. If the blueprint is sparse, then our whole algorithm runs end-to-end in polynomial time given a best-response oracle; in particular, it avoids expanding the whole team belief DAG, which has exponential worst-case size. We apply our method to a standard test suite, and we empirically show the performance improvement of the strategies thanks to subgame solving.

paragraphs: Adversarial team games combine cooperation within a team with competition against opponents. Team members may have different information, which makes approximating equilibrium strategies computationally difficult. This paper extends a successful approach from two-player zero-sum games: prepare an approximate blueprint strategy offline, then refine the relevant part while the game is being played.

The method uses a team belief directed acyclic graph to construct an auxiliary gadget game. It then refines the blueprint through column generation, adding strategy components as needed. The process is anytime, allowing refinement to proceed according to the computation available during play.

The computational guarantee has two explicit conditions: the blueprint must be sparse, and a best-response oracle must be available. Under those conditions, the complete algorithm runs in polynomial time and avoids expanding the full team belief graph, whose worst-case size is exponential. Experiments on a standard test suite show improved strategy performance from subgame solving. The contribution is an online refinement method for team games with both conditional scalability guarantees and empirical support.
summary.tldr: An online subgame-solving method improves team-game strategies and runs in polynomial time given a sparse blueprint and a best-response oracle.

title: Subgame Solving in Adversarial Team Games

abstract: Fine-grained categories that largely share the same set of parts cannot be discriminated based on part information alone, as they mostly differ in the way the local parts relate to the overall global structure of the object. We propose Relational Proxies, a novel approach that leverages the relational information between the global and local views of an object for encoding its semantic label. Starting with a rigorous formalization of the notion of distinguishability between fine-grained categories, we prove the necessary and sufficient conditions that a model must satisfy in order to learn the underlying decision boundaries in the fine-grained setting. We design Relational Proxies based on our theoretical findings and evaluate it on seven challenging fine-grained benchmark datasets and achieve state-of-the-art results on all of them, surpassing the performance of all existing works with a margin exceeding 4% in some cases. We also experimentally validate our theory on fine-grained distinguishability and obtain consistent results across multiple benchmarks. Implementation is available at https://github.com/abhrac/relational-proxies.

paragraphs: Fine-grained categories can share nearly all their parts while differing in how those parts relate to the overall object. Recognizing the parts alone can therefore leave the key distinction unresolved. This paper focuses on relationships between local views and global structure as information for identifying such closely related categories.

The authors formalize what it means for fine-grained categories to be distinguishable and prove necessary and sufficient conditions for learning their decision boundaries within that setting. They use those theoretical findings to design Relational Proxies, an approach that encodes semantic labels through relationships between an object's global and local views.

Evaluation on seven fine-grained benchmark datasets produces state-of-the-art results on all seven, with improvements exceeding 4% in some cases. Additional experiments yield results consistent with the distinguishability theory across multiple benchmarks. The contribution links a formal account of what makes these categories separable with a practical method for representing the relevant relationships.
summary.tldr: Relational Proxies uses relationships between local parts and global structure to distinguish fine-grained categories, guided by a formal distinguishability analysis.

title: Relational Proxies: Emergent Relationships as Fine-Grained Discriminators

abstract: Deep learning (DL) algorithms rely on massive amounts of labeled data. Semi-supervised learning (SSL) and active learning (AL) aim to reduce this label complexity by leveraging unlabeled data or carefully acquiring labels, respectively. In this work, we primarily focus on designing an AL algorithm but first argue for a change in how AL algorithms should be evaluated. Although unlabeled data is readily available in pool-based AL, AL algorithms are usually evaluated by measuring the increase in supervised learning (SL) performance at consecutive acquisition steps. Because this measures performance gains from both newly acquired instances and newly acquired labels, we propose to instead evaluate the label efficiency of AL algorithms by measuring the increase in SSL performance at consecutive acquisition steps. After surveying tools that can be used to this end, we propose our neural pre-conditioning (NPC) algorithm inspired by a Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) analysis. Our algorithm incorporates the classifier's uncertainty on unlabeled data and penalizes redundant samples within candidate batches to efficiently acquire a diverse set of informative labels. Furthermore, we prove that NPC improves downstream training in the large-width regime in a manner previously observed to correlate with generalization. Comparisons with other AL algorithms show that a state-of-the-art SSL algorithm coupled with NPC can achieve high performance using very few labeled data.

Comparisons with other AL algorithms show that a state-of-the-art SSL algorithm coupled with NPC can achieve high performance using very few labeled data.

paragraphs: Active learning selects which examples should receive labels, aiming to reduce annotation needs. This paper first questions how that benefit is measured. When evaluation uses supervised learning alone, adding labeled examples changes both the available inputs and their labels. The resulting improvement therefore mixes two sources of benefit, making label efficiency harder to isolate.

The authors propose evaluating acquisition steps through semi-supervised learning, which already uses the unlabeled pool. They then introduce neural pre-conditioning, or NPC, an acquisition algorithm inspired by Neural Tangent Kernel analysis. NPC considers uncertainty about unlabeled examples while penalizing redundant choices within a candidate batch, encouraging informative labels that cover different examples.

The theoretical result concerns networks in the large-width regime: NPC improves downstream training in a way previously associated with generalization. That association is not itself a generalization guarantee. Empirically, combining NPC with a leading semi-supervised learner achieves high performance with very few labels, supporting the value of studying acquisition and unlabeled-data learning together.
summary.tldr: NPC selects uncertain, nonredundant examples for labeling and evaluates label efficiency within semi-supervised learning.

title: A Neural Pre-Conditioning Active Learning Algorithm to Reduce Label Complexity

abstract: Recently, methods such as Decision Transformer that reduce reinforcement learning to a prediction task and solve it via supervised learning (RvS) have become popular due to their simplicity, robustness to hyperparameters, and strong overall performance on offline RL tasks. However, simply conditioning a probabilistic model on a desired return and taking the predicted action can fail dramatically in stochastic environments since trajectories that result in a return may have only achieved that return due to luck. In this work, we describe the limitations of RvS approaches in stochastic environments and propose a solution. Rather than simply conditioning on returns, as is standard practice, our proposed method, ESPER, conditions on learned average returns which are independent from environment stochasticity. Doing so allows ESPER to achieve strong alignment between target return and expected performance in real environments. We demonstrate this in several challenging stochastic offline-RL tasks including the challenging puzzle game 2048, and Connect Four playing against a stochastic opponent. In all tested domains, ESPER achieves significantly better alignment between the target return and achieved return than simply conditioning on returns. ESPER also achieves higher maximum performance than even the value-based baselines.

paragraphs: Some offline reinforcement-learning methods learn to predict actions conditioned on a requested return. In a stochastic environment, however, a high-return trajectory may reflect fortunate events rather than reliably good decisions. Conditioning directly on that outcome can therefore suggest actions that do not deliver the requested performance on average.

ESPER addresses this problem by conditioning on learned average returns that are independent of environmental randomness. The intended distinction is between a result that happened once and performance that can be expected despite chance. This changes the conditioning signal while retaining the broader approach of learning behavior through a prediction task.

The authors evaluate ESPER on several stochastic offline-learning tasks, including 2048 and Connect Four against a stochastic opponent. In every tested domain, it aligns requested and achieved returns significantly better than direct return conditioning. It also achieves higher maximum performance than the evaluated value-based baselines. These findings support separating environmental luck from the target signal when learning policies from recorded trajectories.
summary.tldr: ESPER conditions policies on learned average returns independent of environmental randomness, improving target-performance alignment in tested stochastic tasks.

title: You Can’t Count on Luck: Why Decision Transformers and RvS Fail in Stochastic Environments

abstract: Inductive relation prediction (IRP)---where entities can be different during training and inference---has shown great power for completing evolving knowledge graphs. Existing works mainly focus on using graph neural networks (GNNs) to learn the representation of the subgraph induced from the target link, which can be seen as an implicit rule-mining process to measure the plausibility of the target link. However, these methods are not able to differentiate the target link and other links during message passing, hence the final subgraph representation will contain irrelevant rule information to the target link, which reduces the reasoning performance and severely hinders the applications for real-world scenarios. To tackle this problem, we propose a novel $\textit{single-source edge-wise}$ GNN model to learn the $\textbf{R}$ule-induc$\textbf{E}$d $\textbf{S}$ubgraph represen$\textbf{T}$ations $(\textbf{REST}$), which encodes relevant rules and eliminates irrelevant rules within the subgraph. Specifically, we propose a $\textit{single-source}$ initialization approach to initialize edge features only for the target link, which guarantees the relevance of mined rules and target link. Then we propose several RNN-based functions for $\textit{edge-wise}$ message passing to model the sequential property of mined rules. REST is a simple and effective approach with theoretical support to learn the $\textit{rule-induced subgraph representation}$. Moreover, REST does not need node labeling, which significantly accelerates the subgraph preprocessing time by up to $\textbf{11.66}\times$. Experiments on inductive relation prediction benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our REST.

paragraphs: Inductive relation prediction fills gaps in a knowledge graph even when inference involves entities absent during training. Existing approaches often encode a subgraph around a candidate link using a graph neural network. The paper argues that ordinary message passing can mix evidence relevant to that candidate with unrelated relational rules, weakening the resulting reasoning.

REST makes the candidate link central to representation learning. Its single-source initialization assigns initial edge features only to the target link, which the authors show guarantees relevance between the mined rules and that link. Message passing operates over edges using recurrent functions, allowing the representation to capture the sequential structure of relational rules.

summary.tldr: REST focuses graph message passing on rules relevant to a target relation while substantially reducing subgraph preprocessing.

title: Learning Rule-Induced Subgraph Representations for Inductive Relation Prediction

abstract: We study a general form of Smoothed Online Convex Optimization, a.k.a. SOCO, including multi-step switching costs and feedback delay. We propose a novel machine learning (ML) augmented online algorithm, Robustness-Constrained Learning (RCL), which combines untrusted ML predictions with a trusted expert online algorithm via constrained projection to robustify the ML prediction. Specifically, we prove that RCL is able to guarantee $(1+\lambda)$-competitiveness against any given expert for any $\lambda>0$, while also explicitly training the ML model in a robustification-aware manner to improve the average-case performance. Importantly, RCL is the first ML-augmented algorithm with a provable robustness guarantee in the case of multi-step switching cost and feedback delay. We demonstrate the improvement of RCL in both robustness and average performance using battery management as a case study.

paragraphs: Smoothed online convex optimization involves making sequential decisions while paying costs for changing them. This paper considers a general setting where switching costs depend on multiple steps and feedback arrives late. It asks how machine-learning predictions can improve typical performance while preserving a dependable guarantee when those predictions are unreliable.

Robustness-Constrained Learning, or RCL, combines an untrusted prediction with a trusted expert online algorithm. A constrained projection adjusts the prediction to enforce robustness. For any positive lambda, the authors prove a competitive factor of 1 + lambda relative to the chosen expert. The guarantee is therefore explicitly tied to an expert reference rather than an unrestricted claim of optimality.

RCL also trains the prediction model with awareness of the later robustness adjustment, aiming to improve average-case performance after projection. The authors identify their result as the first provably robust learning-augmented approach covering both multi-step switching costs and delayed feedback. A battery-management case study demonstrates improvements in robustness and average performance, illustrating how the formal protection and learned predictions can work together.
summary.tldr: RCL adjusts learned predictions to guarantee performance relative to an expert while addressing delayed feedback and multi-step switching costs.

title: Robust Learning for Smoothed Online Convex Optimization with Feedback Delay

abstract: Open-world Semi-Supervised Learning (OSSL) is a realistic and challenging task, aiming to classify unlabeled samples from both seen and novel classes using partially labeled samples from the seen classes. Previous works typically explore the relationship of samples as priors on the pre-defined single-granularity labels to help novel class recognition. In fact, classes follow a taxonomy and samples can be classified at multiple levels of granularity, which contains more underlying relationships for supervision. We thus argue that learning with single-granularity labels results in sub-optimal representation learning and inaccurate pseudo labels, especially with unknown classes. In this paper, we take the initiative to explore and propose a uniformed framework, called Taxonomic context prIors Discovering and Aligning (TIDA), which exploits the relationship of samples under various granularity. It allows us to discover multi-granularity semantic concepts as taxonomic context priors (i.e., sub-class, target-class, and super-class), and then collaboratively leverage them to enhance representation learning and improve the quality of pseudo labels.Specifically, TIDA comprises two components: i) A taxonomic context discovery module that constructs a set of hierarchical prototypes in the latent space to discover the underlying taxonomic context priors; ii) A taxonomic context-based prediction alignment module that enforces consistency across hierarchical predictions to build the reliable relationship between classes among various granularity and provide additions supervision. We demonstrate that these two components are mutually beneficial for an effective OSSL framework, which is theoretically explained from the perspective of the EM algorithm. Extensive experiments on seven commonly used datasets show that TIDA can significantly improve the performance and achieve a new state of the art. The source codes are publicly available at https://github.com/rain305f/TIDA.

paragraphs: Open-world semi-supervised learning uses a partially labeled set of known classes to classify unlabeled examples that may also belong to new classes. The paper argues that treating labels at only one level overlooks useful structure. Examples can share relationships at narrower subclass levels and broader superclass levels, even when their target classes differ or are unknown.

The proposed TIDA framework discovers and connects these levels. One module constructs hierarchical prototypes in the learned representation space, providing reference points for subclass, target-class, and superclass concepts. A second module aligns predictions across the hierarchy so that predictions at different levels remain consistent. Those relationships provide additional supervision for learning representations and producing pseudo labels for unlabeled examples.

The authors explain the mutual benefit of discovery and alignment through the expectation-maximization perspective. Experiments on seven commonly used datasets report significant improvements and new state-of-the-art performance. The findings support using relationships across multiple levels of meaning to improve recognition of both known and novel classes, instead of relying entirely on a single set of class boundaries.
summary.tldr: TIDA discovers hierarchical class relationships and aligns predictions across them to improve open-world semi-supervised recognition.

title: Discover and Align Taxonomic Context Priors for Open-world Semi-Supervised Learning

abstract: We introduce AbDiffuser, an equivariant and physics-informed diffusion model for the joint generation of antibody 3D structures and sequences. AbDiffuser is built on top of a new representation of protein structure, relies on a novel architecture for aligned proteins, and utilizes strong diffusion priors to improve the denoising process. Our approach improves protein diffusion by taking advantage of domain knowledge and physics-based constraints; handles sequence-length changes; and reduces memory complexity by an order of magnitude, enabling backbone and side chain generation. We validate AbDiffuser in silico and in vitro. Numerical experiments showcase the ability of AbDiffuser to generate antibodies that closely track the sequence and structural properties of a reference set. Laboratory experiments confirm that all 16 HER2 antibodies discovered were expressed at high levels and that 57.1% of the selected designs were tight binders.

paragraphs: Antibody generation involves choosing both a molecular sequence and the three-dimensional structure associated with it. AbDiffuser tackles these choices jointly with a diffusion model. Its design incorporates physical constraints and domain knowledge, aiming to make the iterative denoising process better suited to proteins and to generate both their backbones and side chains.

The method combines a new protein structure representation, an architecture designed for aligned proteins, and strong diffusion priors. It also accommodates changes in sequence length. The authors report an order-of-magnitude reduction in memory complexity, which enables generation at the backbone and side-chain level. These components connect the model's computational design to the structural detail it can produce.

In the laboratory, all 16 discovered HER2 antibodies were expressed at high levels, and 57.1% of selected designs were tight binders. Those findings demonstrate laboratory function for tested designs while keeping expression and binding success as distinct outcomes.
summary.tldr: AbDiffuser jointly generates antibody sequences and full-atom structures, with computational validation and laboratory evidence of expression and binding.

title: AbDiffuser: full-atom generation of in-vitro functioning antibodies

abstract: The ability to discern and comprehend pragmatic meanings is a cornerstone of social and emotional intelligence, referred to as pragmatic reasoning. Despite the strides made in the development of Large Language Models (LLMs), such as ChatGPT, these models grapple with capturing the nuanced and ambiguous facets of language, falling short of the aspiration to build human-like conversational agents. In this work, we introduce a novel benchmark, the **DiPlomat**, which delves into the fundamental components of conversational pragmatic reasoning, encompassing situational context reasoning, open-world knowledge acquisition, and unified figurative language understanding. We start by collecting a new human-annotated dialogue dataset, composed of 4,177 multi-turn dialogues and a vocabulary of 48,900 words. Along with the dataset, two tasks are proposed to evaluate machines' pragmatic reasoning capabilities, namely, Pragmatic Reasoning and Identification(PIR) and Conversational Question Answering (CQA). Furthermore, we probe into a zero-shot natural language inference task, where the significance of context in pragmatic reasoning is underscored. Experimental findings illustrate the existing limitations of current prevailing LLMs in the realm of pragmatic reasoning, shedding light on the pressing need for further research to facilitate the emergence of emotional intelligence within human-like conversational agents.

paragraphs: Understanding conversation involves more than recognizing the literal meaning of individual sentences. A listener must interpret what a speaker means in a particular situation, using context and knowledge to resolve ambiguity or figurative language. DiPlomat turns this pragmatic reasoning problem into a benchmark for conversational language models.

The authors collect a human-annotated dataset containing 4,177 multi-turn dialogues and a vocabulary of 48,900 words. The benchmark covers reasoning about situational context, acquiring open-world knowledge, and understanding figurative language. These provide ways to examine interpretation within conversations rather than treating utterances as isolated text.

Experiments reveal limitations in the evaluated leading language models’ handling of these conversational demands. The dataset and tasks provide concrete evaluation targets for improving nuanced language understanding, while the findings motivate further work toward conversational agents that better recognize socially and emotionally meaningful intent.
summary.tldr: DiPlomat evaluates whether language models can interpret conversational meaning using context, outside knowledge, and figurative-language understanding.

title: Diplomat: A Dialogue Dataset for Situated PragMATic Reasoning

abstract: While Transformers have shown remarkable success in natural language processing, their attention mechanism's large memory requirements have limited their ability to handle longer contexts. Prior approaches, such as recurrent memory or retrieval-based augmentation, have either compromised the random-access flexibility of attention (i.e., the capability to select any token in the entire context) or relied on separate mechanisms for relevant context retrieval, which may not be compatible with the model's attention. In this paper, we present a novel approach that allows access to the complete context while retaining random-access flexibility, closely resembling running attention on the entire context. Our method uses a landmark token to represent each block of the input and trains the attention to use it for selecting relevant blocks, enabling retrieval of blocks directly through the attention mechanism instead of by relying on a separate mechanism. Our approach seamlessly integrates with specialized data structures and the system's memory hierarchy, enabling processing of arbitrarily long context lengths. We demonstrate that our method can obtain comparable performance with Transformer-XL while significantly reducing the number of retrieved tokens in each step. Finally, we show that fine-tuning LLaMA 7B with our method successfully extends its context length capacity to over 32k tokens, allowing for inference at the context lengths of GPT-4. We release the implementation of landmark attention and the code to reproduce our experiments at https://github.com/epfml/landmark-attention/.

paragraphs: Transformer attention becomes memory-intensive as context grows. Ways of extending context can restrict access to earlier tokens or introduce a separate retrieval system whose choices may not fit the model's attention. This paper introduces landmark attention to retain flexible access to the full context while selecting only relevant blocks for retrieval.

Each input block receives a landmark token that represents it. The model learns to use attention over these landmarks to select relevant blocks, bringing retrieval into the attention mechanism itself. The approach also integrates with specialized data structures and the system's memory hierarchy, enabling support for arbitrarily long contexts while preserving access across the context.

summary.tldr: Landmark attention retrieves context blocks through learned attention, preserving flexible access and extending demonstrated LLaMA 7B context beyond 32,000 tokens.

title: Random-Access Infinite Context Length for Transformers

abstract: Neural radiance fields (NeRFs) have become a ubiquitous tool for modeling scene appearance and geometry from multiview imagery. Recent work has also begun to explore how to use additional supervision from lidar or depth sensor measurements in the NeRF framework. However, previous lidar-supervised NeRFs focus on rendering conventional camera imagery and use lidar-derived point cloud data as auxiliary supervision; thus, they fail to incorporate the underlying image formation model of the lidar. Here, we propose a novel method for rendering transient NeRFs that take as input the raw, time-resolved photon count histograms measured by a single-photon lidar system, and we seek to render such histograms from novel views. Different from conventional NeRFs, the approach relies on a time-resolved version of the volume rendering equation to render the lidar measurements and capture transient light transport phenomena at picosecond timescales. We evaluate our method on a first-of-its-kind dataset of simulated and captured transient multiview scans from a prototype single-photon lidar. Overall, our work brings NeRFs to a new dimension of imaging at transient timescales, newly enabling rendering of transient imagery from novel views. Additionally, we show that our approach recovers improved geometry and conventional appearance compared to point cloud-based supervision when training on few input viewpoints. Transient NeRFs may be especially useful for applications which seek to simulate raw lidar measurements for downstream tasks in autonomous driving, robotics, and remote sensing.

This paper instead models the raw measurements from a single-photon lidar and predicts them from new viewpoints.

The results demonstrate novel-view rendering of transient imagery. When training from few viewpoints, the approach also recovers better geometry and conventional appearance than point-cloud-based supervision. These findings show the value of incorporating the lidar measurement process directly into scene learning. The authors identify simulation of raw lidar signals for autonomous driving, robotics, and remote sensing as possible applications of the approach.
summary.tldr: Transient NeRFs learn from raw photon-arrival histograms to render lidar measurements from new views and improve reconstruction with few input viewpoints.

title: Transient Neural Radiance Fields for Lidar View Synthesis and 3D Reconstruction

abstract: A central aim in computational neuroscience is to relate the activity of large populations of neurons to an underlying dynamical system. Models of these neural dynamics should ideally be both interpretable and fit the observed data well. Low-rank recurrent neural networks (RNNs) exhibit such interpretability by having tractable dynamics. However, it is unclear how to best fit low-rank RNNs to data consisting of noisy observations of an underlying stochastic system. Here, we propose to fit stochastic low-rank RNNs with variational sequential Monte Carlo methods. We validate our method on several datasets consisting of both continuous and spiking neural data, where we obtain lower dimensional latent dynamics than current state of the art methods. Additionally, for low-rank models with piecewise linear nonlinearities, we show how to efficiently identify all fixed points in polynomial rather than exponential cost in the number of units, making analysis of the inferred dynamics tractable for large RNNs. Our method both elucidates the dynamical systems underlying experimental recordings and provides a generative model whose trajectories match observed variability.

paragraphs: Neural recordings capture noisy activity from many neurons, while researchers often seek a simpler dynamical system that explains their collective behavior. Low-rank recurrent neural networks offer interpretable dynamics, but fitting them must account for both noisy observations and randomness in the underlying system. This paper proposes fitting stochastic low-rank networks using variational sequential Monte Carlo methods.

Across datasets containing continuous and spiking neural activity, the method obtains lower-dimensional latent dynamics than the compared state-of-the-art methods. It also produces a generative model whose trajectories reproduce observed variability. These findings support using a compact dynamical description while still representing the variation present in recordings.

In that setting, it identifies all fixed points with polynomial rather than exponential computational cost in the number of units. Because fixed points help characterize a dynamical system, this result makes analysis of large fitted networks more tractable. The work therefore addresses both learning the model and interpreting its dynamics.
summary.tldr: Stochastic low-rank recurrent networks fit compact neural dynamics, with an efficient fixed-point analysis available for piecewise-linear models.

title: Inferring stochastic low-rank recurrent neural networks from neural data

abstract: Generative learning, recognized for its effective modeling of data distributions, offers inherent advantages in handling out-of-distribution instances, especially for enhancing robustness to adversarial attacks. Among these, diffusion classifiers, utilizing powerful diffusion models, have demonstrated superior empirical robustness. However, a comprehensive theoretical understanding of their robustness is still lacking, raising concerns about their vulnerability to stronger future attacks. In this study, we prove that diffusion classifiers possess $O(1)$ Lipschitzness, and establish their certified robustness, demonstrating their inherent resilience. To achieve non-constant Lipschitzness, thereby obtaining much tighter certified robustness, we generalize diffusion classifiers to classify Gaussian-corrupted data. This involves deriving the evidence lower bounds (ELBOs) for these distributions, approximating the likelihood using the ELBO, and calculating classification probabilities via Bayes' theorem. Experimental results show the superior certified robustness of these Noised Diffusion Classifiers (NDCs). Notably, we achieve over 80\% and 70\% certified robustness on CIFAR-10 under adversarial perturbations with \(\ell_2\) norms less than 0.25 and 0.5, respectively, using a single off-the-shelf diffusion model without any additional data.

Among these, diffusion classifiers, utilizing powerful diffusion models, have demonstrated superior empirical robustness. However, a comprehensive theoretical understanding of their robustness is still lacking, raising concerns about their vulnerability to stronger future attacks. In this study, we prove that diffusion classifiers possess $O(1)$ Lipschitzness, and establish their certified robustness, demonstrating their inherent resilience. To achieve non-constant Lipschitzness, thereby obtaining much tighter certified robustness, we generalize diffusion classifiers to classify Gaussian-corrupted data. This involves deriving the evidence lower bounds (ELBOs) for these distributions, approximating the likelihood using the ELBO, and calculating classification probabilities via Bayes' theorem. Experimental results show the superior certified robustness of these Noised Diffusion Classifiers (NDCs). Notably, we achieve over 80\% and 70\% certified robustness on CIFAR-10 under adversarial perturbations with \(\ell_2\) norms less than 0.25 and 0.5, respectively, using a single off-the-shelf diffusion model without any additional data.

Their observed resistance to adversarial attacks motivates this paper’s central question: can that resistance be supported by mathematical guarantees? The authors prove an O(1) Lipschitz bound, which constrains how much the classifier can change as its input changes, and establish certified robustness.

To obtain tighter certificates, they extend the classifiers to operate on Gaussian-corrupted data. They derive evidence lower bounds for the relevant distributions, use those bounds to approximate likelihoods, and apply Bayes’ theorem to calculate class probabilities. The resulting Noised Diffusion Classifiers connect noise-aware generative modeling with stronger robustness certification.

On CIFAR-10, the reported certified robustness exceeds 80% for adversarial perturbations with ℓ2 norms below 0.25 and 70% for norms below 0.5. These results use one off-the-shelf diffusion model and no additional data. The certificates concern the specified perturbation sizes, providing a stronger form of evidence within those bounds than success against a particular collection of attacks alone.
summary.tldr: The paper proves robustness guarantees for diffusion classifiers and tightens certification through classifiers designed for Gaussian-corrupted inputs.

title: Diffusion Models are Certifiably Robust Classifiers

abstract: Peptide design plays a pivotal role in therapeutics, allowing brand new possibility to leverage target binding sites that are previously undruggable. Most existing methods are either inefficient or only concerned with the target-agnostic design of 1D sequences. In this paper, we propose a generative model for full-atom Peptide design with Geometric LAtent Diffusion (PepGLAD) given the binding site. We first establish a benchmark consisting of both 1D sequences and 3D structures from Protein Data Bank (PDB) and literature for systematic evaluation. We then identify two major challenges of leveraging current diffusion-based models for peptide design: the full-atom geometry and the variable binding geometry. To tackle the first challenge, PepGLAD derives a variational autoencoder that first encodes full-atom residues of variable size into fixed-dimensional latent representations, and then decodes back to the residue space after conducting the diffusion process in the latent space. For the second issue, PepGLAD explores a receptor-specific affine transformation to convert the 3D coordinates into a shared standard space, enabling better generalization ability across different binding shapes. Experimental Results show that our method not only improves diversity and binding affinity significantly in the task of sequence-structure co-design, but also excels at recovering reference structures for binding conformation generation.

summary.tldr: PepGLAD combines latent diffusion and geometric normalization to design full-atom peptides for specified binding sites.

title: Full-Atom Peptide Design with Geometric Latent Diffusion

abstract: Distributionally robust offline reinforcement learning (RL), which seeks robust policy training against environment perturbation by modeling dynamics uncertainty, calls for function approximations when facing large state-action spaces. However, the consideration of dynamics uncertainty introduces essential nonlinearity and computational burden, posing unique challenges for analyzing and practically employing function approximation. Focusing on a basic setting where the nominal model and perturbed models are linearly parameterized, we propose minimax optimal and computationally efficient algorithms realizing function approximation and initiate the study on instance-dependent suboptimality analysis in the context of robust offline RL. Our results uncover that function approximation in robust offline RL is essentially distinct from and probably harder than that in standard offline RL. Our algorithms and theoretical results crucially depend on a novel function approximation mechanism incorporating variance information, a new procedure of suboptimality and estimation uncertainty decomposition, a quantification of the robust value function shrinkage, and a meticulously designed family of hard instances, which might be of independent interest.

paragraphs: Distributionally robust offline reinforcement learning seeks policies that withstand changes in environment dynamics while learning from existing data. Large state and action spaces require function approximation, but accounting for uncertain dynamics adds nonlinearity and computational difficulty. This paper studies how to obtain efficient algorithms and sharp guarantees despite those complications.

The analysis focuses on a setting where both the nominal dynamics and their perturbed alternatives have linear parameterizations. Within that setting, the authors propose computationally efficient, minimax-optimal algorithms. They also begin an instance-dependent analysis of suboptimality, examining how performance shortfalls depend on the particular problem rather than only a general worst-case description.

The results rely on variance-aware function approximation, a decomposition of suboptimality and estimation uncertainty, an analysis of robust value-function shrinkage, and carefully constructed hard instances. Together, these tools reveal that approximation in robust offline learning is fundamentally different from its standard counterpart and is plausibly harder. The linear parameterization is central to the setting covered by these guarantees.
summary.tldr: For linearly parameterized dynamics, the paper develops efficient, minimax-optimal robust offline learning algorithms and problem-dependent performance analysis.

title: Minimax Optimal and Computationally Efficient Algorithms for Distributionally Robust Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Anchoring is a recent, architecture-agnostic principle for training deep neural networks that has been shown to significantly improve uncertainty estimation, calibration, and extrapolation capabilities. In this paper, we systematically explore anchoring as a general protocol for training vision models, providing fundamental insights into its training and inference processes and their implications for generalization and safety. Despite its promise, we identify a critical problem in anchored training that can lead to an increased risk of learning undesirable shortcuts, thereby limiting its generalization capabilities. To address this, we introduce a new anchored training protocol that employs a simple regularizer to mitigate this issue and significantly enhances generalization. We empirically evaluate our proposed approach across datasets and architectures of varying scales and complexities, demonstrating substantial performance gains in generalization and safety metrics compared to the standard training protocol. The open-source code is available at https://software.llnl.gov/anchoring.

paragraphs: Anchoring is a training principle that can be used across neural-network architectures and has shown benefits for uncertainty estimation, calibration, and extrapolation. This paper examines its use as a general protocol for vision models. The authors study both training and inference, asking how the protocol affects generalization and safety.

Their analysis identifies a problem in anchored training that can increase the risk of learning undesirable shortcuts. Such shortcuts can limit generalization, so the benefits previously associated with anchoring do not remove the need to examine how it is trained. The authors introduce a revised anchored-training protocol with a simple regularizer designed to mitigate this issue.

They evaluate the approach across datasets and architectures with different scales and levels of complexity. The reported results show substantial gains in generalization and safety metrics compared with standard training. The contribution therefore includes both identifying a failure mode of anchored training and modifying the protocol to address it, with empirical evidence that the revised approach improves the evaluated outcomes.
summary.tldr: A revised anchoring protocol uses a simple regularizer to mitigate shortcut learning and improve vision models' measured generalization and safety.

title: On the Use of Anchoring for Training Vision Models

abstract: Transformer based large-language models (LLMs) display extreme proficiency with language yet a precise understanding of how they work remains elusive. One way of demystifying transformer predictions would be to describe how they depend on their context in terms of simple template functions. This paper takes a first step in this direction by considering families of functions (i.e. rules) formed out of simple N-gram based statistics of the training data. By studying how well these rulesets approximate transformer predictions, we obtain a variety of novel discoveries: a simple method to detect overfitting during training without using a holdout set, a quantitative measure of how transformers progress from learning simple to more complex statistical rules over the course of training, a model-variance criterion governing when transformer predictions tend to be described by N-gram rules, and insights into how well transformers can be approximated by N-gram rulesets in the limit where these rulesets become increasingly complex. In this latter direction, we find that for 79% and 68% of LLM next-token distributions on TinyStories and Wikipedia, respectively, their top-1 predictions agree with those provided by our N-gram rulesets.

paragraphs: This paper explores whether Transformer predictions can be understood through simpler statistical rules. It constructs families of rules from N-gram statistics in the training data and measures how well they approximate the model's predictions. This provides a concrete way to study dependence on context through progressively more complex statistical templates.

The analysis yields a method for detecting overfitting during training without a holdout set and a quantitative measure of progression from simple to more complex rules. It also identifies a model-variance criterion governing when predictions tend to be described by N-gram rules. These results use approximation as a tool for studying both training behavior and prediction structure.

As the rulesets become increasingly complex, their top-ranked token agrees with the language model's top-ranked token for 79% of next-token distributions on TinyStories and 68% on Wikipedia. These figures measure agreement on the top prediction, rather than equality of entire probability distributions. The findings demonstrate substantial descriptive power for the studied rulesets while retaining that specific meaning of agreement.
summary.tldr: N-gram rules approximate many Transformer top-token predictions and provide tools for analyzing statistical learning and detecting overfitting.

title: Understanding Transformers via N-Gram Statistics

abstract: Language models as intelligent agents push the boundaries of sequential decision-making agents but struggle with limited knowledge of environmental dynamics and exponentially huge action space. Recent efforts like GLAM and TWOSOME manually constrain the action space to a restricted subset and employ reinforcement learning to align agents' knowledge with specific environments. However, they overlook fine-grained credit assignments for intra-action tokens, which is essential for efficient language agent optimization, and rely on human's prior knowledge to restrict action space. This paper proposes decomposing language agent optimization from the action level to the token level, offering finer supervision for each intra-action token and manageable optimization complexity in environments with unrestricted action spaces. Beginning with the simplification of flattening all actions, we theoretically explore the discrepancies between action-level optimization and this naive token-level optimization. We then derive the Bellman backup with Action Decomposition (BAD) to integrate credit assignments for both intra-action and inter-action tokens, effectively eliminating the discrepancies. Implementing BAD within the PPO algorithm, we introduce Policy Optimization with Action Decomposition (POAD). POAD benefits from a finer-grained credit assignment process and lower optimization complexity, leading to enhanced learning efficiency and generalization abilities in aligning language agents with interactive environments. We validate POAD across diverse testbeds, with results affirming the advantages of our approach and the correctness of our theoretical analysis. The source code can be accessed directly with this link: https://github.com/morning9393/ADRL.

paragraphs: Language-model agents face enormous action spaces because each action can consist of many possible token sequences. Prior approaches constrain available actions using human knowledge, but they also miss opportunities to assign learning credit to individual tokens. This paper studies how token-level optimization can provide finer supervision without requiring a restricted action set.

Simply flattening actions into a token sequence introduces discrepancies relative to action-level optimization. The authors analyze these differences and derive Bellman backup with Action Decomposition, or BAD, to account for credit both within actions and between actions. This preserves the relationship between tokens that form an action and the larger sequence of environmental decisions.

Integrating BAD into PPO produces Policy Optimization with Action Decomposition, or POAD. The method combines finer credit assignment with lower optimization complexity. Evaluations across diverse interactive testbeds support improved learning efficiency and generalization, as well as the theoretical analysis. The contribution makes token-level learning consistent with the decision structure the agent is meant to optimize.
summary.tldr: POAD improves language-agent reinforcement learning by assigning token-level credit while preserving dependencies within and between actions.

title: Reinforcing LLM Agents via Policy Optimization with Action Decomposition

abstract: Smoke segmentation is of great importance in precisely identifying the smoke location, enabling timely fire rescue and gas leak detection. However, due to the visual diversity and blurry edges of the non-grid smoke, noisy labels are almost inevitable in large-scale pixel-level smoke datasets. Noisy labels significantly impact the robustness of the model and may lead to serious accidents. Nevertheless, currently, there are no specific methods for addressing noisy labels in smoke segmentation. Smoke differs from regular objects as its transparency varies, causing inconsistent features in the noisy labels. In this paper, we propose a conditional sample weighting (CoSW). CoSW utilizes a multi-prototype framework, where prototypes serve as prior information to apply different weighting criteria to the different feature clusters. A novel regularized within-prototype entropy (RWE) is introduced to achieve CoSW and stable prototype update. The experiments show that our approach achieves SOTA performance on both real-world and synthetic noisy smoke segmentation datasets.

paragraphs: Smoke segmentation identifies which image pixels belong to smoke, supporting applications such as fire response and gas-leak detection. Producing reliable training labels is difficult because smoke has blurry boundaries, diverse appearances, and varying transparency. These properties also mean that incorrectly labeled examples can have inconsistent visual features, complicating efforts to reduce their influence during training.

CoSW addresses this problem by making sample weighting conditional on feature clusters. It uses multiple prototypes as reference information, allowing different clusters to follow different weighting criteria. Instead of applying one shared rule across all appearances, the method uses the prototype structure to guide how training samples contribute to learning.

The paper also introduces regularized within-prototype entropy to implement the weighting approach and keep prototype updates stable. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on both real-world and synthetic datasets with noisy smoke labels. The findings support adapting noise-handling rules to the different visual patterns within smoke data, with the prototype framework connecting those patterns to the training process.
summary.tldr: CoSW uses prototype-dependent sample weighting to improve smoke segmentation when pixel labels are noisy.

title: CoSW: Conditional Sample Weighting for Smoke Segmentation with Label Noise

abstract: With high-dimensional state spaces, visual reinforcement learning (RL) faces significant challenges in exploitation and exploration, resulting in low sample efficiency and training stability. As a time-efficient diffusion model, although consistency models have been validated in online state-based RL, it is still an open question whether it can be extended to visual RL. In this paper, we investigate the impact of non-stationary distribution and the actor-critic framework on consistency policy in online RL, and find that consistency policy was unstable during the training, especially in visual RL with the high-dimensional state space. To this end, we suggest sample-based entropy regularization to stabilize the policy training, and propose a consistency policy with prioritized proximal experience regularization (CP3ER) to improve sample efficiency. CP3ER achieves new state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance in 21 tasks across DeepMind control suite and Meta-world. To our knowledge, CP3ER is the first method to apply diffusion/consistency models to visual RL and demonstrates the potential of consistency models in visual RL.

paragraphs: Learning actions from visual observations creates difficult exploration and exploitation problems because the state information is high-dimensional. Consistency models offer a time-efficient diffusion approach and had already been used in online reinforcement learning with state inputs. This paper investigates whether consistency policies can also work effectively when the agent learns from visual inputs.

The authors examine how changing data distributions and the actor-critic framework affect consistency-policy training. They find instability, particularly in visual reinforcement learning. To address it, they introduce sample-based entropy regularization for training stability and propose prioritized proximal experience regularization to improve sample efficiency. The combined method is called CP3ER.

The authors describe it as the first application of diffusion or consistency models to visual reinforcement learning to their knowledge, and present the findings as evidence of these models' potential in that setting.
summary.tldr: CP3ER stabilizes consistency-policy training and improves sample efficiency, reporting leading results across 21 visual reinforcement learning tasks.

title: Generalizing Consistency Policy to Visual RL with Prioritized Proximal Experience Regularization

abstract: Despite the success of Large Language Models (LLMs) on various tasks following human instructions, controlling model generation to follow strict constraints at inference time poses a persistent challenge. In this paper, we introduce Ctrl-G, a neuro-symbolic framework that enables tractable and adaptable control of LLM generation to follow logical constraints reliably. Ctrl-G combines any production-ready LLM with a Hidden Markov Model (HMM), guiding LLM outputs to adhere to logical constraints represented as deterministic finite automata. We show that Ctrl-G, when a TULU2-7B model is coupled with a 2B-parameter HMM, outperforms GPT4 in text editing: on the task of generating text insertions/continuations following logical constraints, our approach achieves over 30% higher satisfaction rate in human evaluation. When applied to medium-size language models (e.g., GPT2-large), Ctrl-G also beats its counterparts on standard benchmarks by large margins. Additionally, as a proof-of-concept study, we use Ctrl-G to assist LLM reasoning on the GSM benchmark, foreshadowing the application of Ctrl-G, as well as other constrained generation approaches, beyond traditional language generation tasks.

paragraphs: Ctrl-G addresses a gap between following an instruction broadly and satisfying precise logical requirements during text generation. The paper introduces a framework that combines a language model with a Hidden Markov Model, using the latter to guide generation. The requirements are represented as deterministic finite automata, giving the system an explicit representation of the constraints it should follow.

The approach brings together a neural text generator and a structured control mechanism. Its purpose is to make constraint handling tractable and adaptable while working with production-ready language models. This matters for tasks such as inserting or continuing text, where an otherwise fluent response may still fail the requested conditions.

In human evaluation of constrained text editing, TULU2-7B paired with a 2B-parameter Hidden Markov Model achieved a satisfaction rate over 30% higher than GPT4. Experiments with medium-size models also showed substantial benchmark gains. A separate GSM reasoning demonstration provides preliminary evidence for broader applications, rather than establishing a general reasoning improvement.
summary.tldr: Ctrl-G combines language models with a structured probabilistic controller to improve adherence to logical generation constraints.

title: Adaptable Logical Control for Large Language Models

abstract: The ability to perform fast and accurate atomistic simulations is crucial for advancing the chemical sciences. By learning from high-quality data, machine-learned interatomic potentials achieve accuracy on par with ab initio and first-principles methods at a fraction of their computational cost. The success of machine-learned interatomic potentials arises from integrating inductive biases such as equivariance to group actions on an atomic system, e.g., equivariance to rotations and reflections. In particular, the field has notably advanced with the emergence of equivariant message passing. Most of these models represent an atomic system using spherical tensors, tensor products of which require complicated numerical coefficients and can be computationally demanding. Cartesian tensors offer a promising alternative, though state-of-the-art methods lack flexibility in message-passing mechanisms, restricting their architectures and expressive power. This work explores higher-rank irreducible Cartesian tensors to address these limitations. We integrate irreducible Cartesian tensor products into message-passing neural networks and prove the equivariance and traceless property of the resulting layers. Through empirical evaluations on various benchmark data sets, we consistently observe on-par or better performance than that of state-of-the-art spherical and Cartesian models.

A key design principle is equivariance: model representations should transform consistently when an atomic system is rotated or reflected. Many successful message-passing models implement this principle with spherical tensors, whose products involve complicated numerical coefficients and can be computationally demanding.

This paper develops an alternative using higher-rank irreducible Cartesian tensors. Existing Cartesian approaches offer promise but constrain how messages can be constructed, limiting architectural flexibility and expressive power. The authors integrate irreducible Cartesian tensor products into message-passing networks to address those restrictions and broaden the available mechanisms for representing atomic interactions.

The work combines formal and empirical evidence. It proves that the resulting layers preserve equivariance and the required traceless property. Across several benchmark datasets, the models consistently match or outperform state-of-the-art spherical and Cartesian models. These results support the proposed tensor construction as a flexible, competitive foundation for interatomic modeling, without establishing a universal advantage for every simulation setting.
summary.tldr: Higher-rank Cartesian tensor products enable flexible equivariant message-passing layers that match or improve on leading atomistic models.

title: Higher-Rank Irreducible Cartesian Tensors for Equivariant Message Passing

abstract: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) provides a principled framework for aligning AI systems with human preference data. For various reasons, e.g., personal bias, context ambiguity, lack of training, etc, human annotators may give incorrect or inconsistent preference labels. To tackle this challenge, we propose a robust RLHF approach -- $R^3M$, which models the potentially corrupted preference label as sparse outliers. Accordingly, we formulate the robust reward learning as an $\ell_1$-regularized maximum likelihood estimation problem. Computationally, we develop an efficient alternating optimization algorithm, which only incurs negligible computational overhead compared with the standard RLHF approach. Theoretically, we prove that under proper regularity conditions, $R^3M$ can consistently learn the underlying reward and identify outliers, provided that the number of outlier labels scales sublinearly with the preference sample size. Furthermore, we remark that $R^3M$ is versatile and can be extended to various preference optimization methods, including direct preference optimization (DPO). Our experiments on robotic control and natural language generation with large language models (LLMs) show that $R^3M$ improves robustness of the reward against several types of perturbations to the preference data.

These errors can distort reward learning in reinforcement learning from human feedback. R³M addresses the problem by treating potentially corrupted labels as sparse outliers within the preference data.

The method expresses robust reward estimation as maximum likelihood with an ℓ1 regularization term. An alternating optimization algorithm solves the resulting problem with negligible additional computational overhead relative to standard RLHF. The framework can also be extended to preference optimization methods such as direct preference optimization, broadening where the outlier model can be used.

The theoretical guarantee is conditional: under appropriate regularity conditions, R³M consistently learns the underlying reward and identifies outliers when the number of corrupted labels grows sublinearly with the sample size. Experiments in robotic control and language generation show improved reward robustness under several forms of preference-data perturbation. Together, the results support explicitly modeling sparse corruption while specifying the regime in which reliable recovery is guaranteed.
summary.tldr: R³M models corrupted preference labels as sparse outliers to improve reward robustness, with recovery guarantees under stated conditions.

title: Robust Reinforcement Learning from Corrupted Human Feedback

abstract: We introduce a new task called Adaptable Error Detection (AED), which aims to identify behavior errors in few-shot imitation (FSI) policies based on visual observations in novel environments. The potential to cause serious damage to surrounding areas limits the application of FSI policies in real-world scenarios. Thus, a robust system is necessary to notify operators when FSI policies are inconsistent with the intent of demonstrations. This task introduces three challenges: (1) detecting behavior errors in novel environments, (2) identifying behavior errors that occur without revealing notable changes, and (3) lacking complete temporal information of the rollout due to the necessity of online detection. However, the existing benchmarks cannot support the development of AED because their tasks do not present all these challenges. To this end, we develop a cross-domain AED benchmark, consisting of 322 base and 153 novel environments. Additionally, we propose Pattern Observer (PrObe) to address these challenges. PrObe is equipped with a powerful pattern extractor and guided by novel learning objectives to parse discernible patterns in the policy feature representations of normal or error states. Through our comprehensive evaluation, PrObe demonstrates superior capability to detect errors arising from a wide range of FSI policies, consistently surpassing strong baselines. Moreover, we conduct detailed ablations and a pilot study on error correction to validate the effectiveness of the proposed architecture design and the practicality of the AED task, respectively. The AED project page can be found at https://aed-neurips.github.io/.
