paragraphs: A policy learned from a few demonstrations can behave inconsistently with what those demonstrations intended. This paper defines Adaptable Error Detection as recognizing such behavior from visual observations in new environments. The detector must work online, meaning it cannot wait to see the entire rollout, and some errors may produce only subtle visible changes.

To study these challenges together, the authors create a benchmark containing 322 base environments and 153 novel environments. They introduce Pattern Observer, or PrObe, which extracts patterns from the policy's internal feature representations. Its learning objectives help distinguish representations associated with normal behavior from those associated with errors, supporting detection beyond conspicuous changes in the observed scene.

Across the evaluated few-shot imitation policies, PrObe detects errors more effectively than strong baselines. Ablation experiments examine the contribution of its architectural choices, while a pilot error-correction study explores the practical usefulness of the task. The findings support adaptable monitoring as a way to identify deviations from demonstrated intent before an operator has access to a completed execution.
summary.tldr: PrObe detects behavior errors in few-shot imitation policies using visual observations and learned patterns that transfer to new environments.

title: AED: Adaptable Error Detection for Few-shot Imitation Policy

abstract: Federated learning has become a pivotal distributed learning paradigm, involving collaborative model updates across multiple nodes with private data. However, handling non-i.i.d. (not identically and independently distributed) data and ensuring model consistency across heterogeneous environments present significant challenges. These challenges often lead to model performance degradation and increased difficulty in achieving effective communication among participant models. In this work, we propose Confusion-Resistant Federated Learning via Consistent Diffusion (CRFed), a novel framework designed to address these issues. Our approach introduces a new diffusion-based data harmonization mechanism that includes data augmentation, noise injection, and iterative denoising to ensure consistent model updates across non-i.i.d. data distributions. This mechanism aims to reduce data distribution disparities among participating nodes, enhancing the coordination and consistency of model updates. Moreover, we design a confusion-resistant strategy leveraging an indicator function and adaptive learning rate adjustment to mitigate the adverse effects of data heterogeneity and model inconsistency. Specifically, we calculate importance sampling weights based on the optimal sampling probability, which guides the selection of clients and the sampling of their data, ensuring that model updates are robust and aligned across different nodes. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets, including MNIST, FashionMNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and NIPD, demonstrate the effectiveness of CRFed in improving accuracy, convergence speed, and overall robustness in federated learning scenarios with severe data heterogeneity.

paragraphs: Federated learning combines model updates from participants that hold private data. When their data distributions differ substantially, those updates can become inconsistent and learning can deteriorate. CRFed addresses this coordination problem through a framework that combines diffusion-based data harmonization with a strategy for managing the effects of inconsistent updates.

The harmonization mechanism uses data augmentation, noise injection, and repeated denoising to reduce differences between participants’ data distributions. A complementary strategy uses an indicator function and adaptive learning rates to mitigate heterogeneity. The method also calculates importance sampling weights from an optimal sampling probability, guiding both which clients participate and how their data are sampled.

Experiments on MNIST, FashionMNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and NIPD report improvements in accuracy, convergence speed, and robustness under severe data heterogeneity. The approach matters because it treats inconsistency as a problem involving both the data seen by participants and the selection and weighting of their contributions to shared learning.
summary.tldr: CRFed combines diffusion-based data harmonization and adaptive sampling to improve federated learning when participants have strongly differing data.

title: Confusion-Resistant Federated Learning via Diffusion-Based Data Harmonization on Non-IID Data

abstract: In this paper, we study an object synthesis task that combines an object text with an object image to create a new object image. However, most diffusion models struggle with this task, \textit{i.e.}, often generating an object that predominantly reflects either the text or the image due to an imbalance between their inputs. To address this issue, we propose a simple yet effective method called Adaptive Text-Image Harmony (ATIH) to generate novel and surprising objects.First, we introduce a scale factor and an injection step to balance text and image features in cross-attention and to preserve image information in self-attention during the text-image inversion diffusion process, respectively. Second, to better integrate object text and image, we design a balanced loss function with a noise parameter, ensuring both optimal editability and fidelity of the object image. Third, to adaptively adjust these parameters, we present a novel similarity score function that not only maximizes the similarities between the generated object image and the input text/image but also balances these similarities to harmonize text and image integration. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, showcasing remarkable object creations such as colobus-glass jar. https://xzr52.github.io/ATIH/

paragraphs: Adaptive Text-Image Harmony tackles the creation of a new object image from an object description and an existing object image. Diffusion models can struggle to combine these inputs because one dominates the output. The paper aims to preserve meaningful contributions from both, producing an object that integrates the textual concept with information from the reference image.

ATIH introduces controls at several points in generation. A scale factor balances text and image features in cross-attention, while an injection step preserves image information in self-attention during inversion. A balanced loss with a noise parameter addresses the tension between making the image editable and retaining fidelity to it. These controls target different parts of the same integration problem.

The method adjusts its parameters using a similarity score that rewards agreement with both inputs while also balancing those agreements. This makes harmony between the two inputs an explicit selection criterion. Extensive experiments support the approach’s effectiveness, including unusual creations such as a colobus–glass jar combination. The stated outcome is more successful integration of the supplied object text and image.
summary.tldr: ATIH adaptively balances text and image influences in diffusion generation to create novel objects that reflect both inputs.

title: Novel Object Synthesis via Adaptive Text-Image Harmony

abstract: Optimizing discrete black-box functions is key in several domains, e.g. protein engineering and drug design. Due to the lack of gradient information and the need for sample efficiency, Bayesian optimization is an ideal candidate for these tasks. Several methods for high-dimensional continuous and categorical Bayesian optimization have been proposed recently. However, our survey of the field reveals highly heterogeneous experimental set-ups across methods and technical barriers for the replicability and application of published algorithms to real-world tasks. To address these issues, we develop a unified framework to test a vast array of high-dimensional Bayesian optimization methods and a collection of standardized black-box functions representing real-world application domains in chemistry and biology. These two components of the benchmark are each supported by flexible, scalable, and easily extendable software libraries (poli and poli-baselines), allowing practitioners to readily incorporate new optimization objectives or discrete optimizers. Project website: https://machinelearninglifescience.github.io/hdbo_benchmark.

paragraphs: Searching for useful discrete sequences is important in areas such as protein engineering and drug design. These problems can require choosing among many possibilities without gradients that indicate how to improve a candidate. Bayesian optimization is attractive because it aims to make effective use of a limited number of evaluations of the unknown objective.

The paper surveys high-dimensional Bayesian optimization and identifies obstacles to comparing existing methods. Published approaches use substantially different experimental setups, while technical barriers make algorithms difficult to reproduce or apply to practical problems. Consequently, evaluating methods together requires a common framework and a consistent collection of objectives.

The authors provide both: a unified environment for testing a broad range of optimizers and standardized black-box functions representing chemistry and biology applications. Two extensible software libraries, poli and poli-baselines, support these components and allow new objectives or optimizers to be added. The contribution is infrastructure for more reproducible comparisons and practical experimentation; the abstract does not identify a universally best optimization method.
summary.tldr: This survey and benchmark standardize evaluation of high-dimensional discrete Bayesian optimization through shared objectives and extensible software.

title: A survey and benchmark of high-dimensional Bayesian optimization of discrete sequences

abstract: Aligning neural dynamics with movements is a fundamental goal in neuroscience and brain-machine interfaces. However, there is still a lack of dimensionality reduction methods that can effectively align low-dimensional latent dynamics with movements. To address this gap, we propose Neural Embeddings Rank (NER), a technique that embeds neural dynamics into a 3D latent space and contrasts the embeddings based on movement ranks. NER learns to regress continuous representations of neural dynamics (i.e., embeddings) on continuous movements. We apply NER and six other dimensionality reduction techniques to neurons in the primary motor cortex (M1), dorsal premotor cortex (PMd), and primary somatosensory cortex (S1) as monkeys perform reaching tasks. Only NER aligns latent dynamics with both hand position and direction, visualizable in 3D. NER reveals consistent latent dynamics in M1 and PMd across sixteen sessions over a year. Using a linear regression decoder, NER explains 86\% and 97\% of the variance in velocity and position, respectively. Linear models trained on data from one session successfully decode velocity, position, and direction in held-out test data from different dates and cortical areas (64\%, 88\%, and 90\%). NER also reveals distinct latent dynamics in S1 during consistent movements and in M1 during curved reaching tasks. The code is available at https://github.com/NeuroscienceAI/NER.

paragraphs: Neural Embeddings Rank, or NER, seeks a compact representation of neural activity that aligns with movement. It maps neural dynamics into three dimensions and contrasts those embeddings using movement ranks. This connects continuous neural representations to continuous movements while producing a space that can be directly visualized.

The researchers compare NER with six other dimensionality reduction techniques using recordings from three cortical areas while monkeys perform reaching tasks. Among the tested methods, only NER aligns the latent dynamics with both hand position and direction. It also reveals consistent dynamics in primary motor and dorsal premotor cortex across sixteen sessions spanning a year.

A linear decoder using NER explains 86% of velocity variance and 97% of position variance. Models trained on one session also decode velocity, position, and direction in held-out data from other dates and cortical areas. NER additionally reveals distinct patterns in somatosensory cortex during consistent movements and in motor cortex during curved reaches. These results show that the representation can expose both shared and differing relationships between neural activity and movement.
summary.tldr: NER creates three-dimensional neural representations aligned with movement and supports decoding across recording sessions and cortical areas.

title: Neural Embeddings Rank: Aligning 3D latent dynamics with movements

abstract: Most digital music tools emphasize precision and control, but often lack support for tactile, improvisational workflows grounded in environmental interaction. Lumia addresses this by enabling users to "compose through looking", transforming visual scenes into musical phrases using a handheld, camera-based interface and large multimodal models. A vision-language model (GPT-4V) analyzes captured imagery to generate structured prompts, which, combined with user-selected instrumentation, guide a text-to-music pipeline (Stable Audio). This real-time process allows users to frame, capture, and layer audio interactively, producing loopable musical segments through embodied interaction. The system supports a co-creative workflow where human intent and model inference shape the musical outcome. By embedding generative AI within a physical device, Lumia bridges perception and composition, introducing a new modality for creative exploration that merges vision, language, and sound. It repositions generative music not as a task of parameter tuning, but as an improvisational practice driven by contextual, sensory engagement.

paragraphs: LUMIA turns looking at the surrounding environment into an input for musical composition. Its handheld camera interface lets people frame and capture visual scenes, then use those scenes to generate musical phrases. The project is designed around tactile improvisation and environmental interaction rather than a workflow centered on detailed parameter adjustment.

GPT-4V analyzes captured images and produces structured prompts. Those prompts are combined with the user’s chosen instrumentation and passed to Stable Audio to generate music. Users can interactively capture material and layer the resulting loopable segments, connecting visual selection with the development of a musical composition.

The division of creative influence is explicit: the person chooses what to look at and which instruments to use, while the models interpret the scene and generate audio. The system demonstrates a physical interface linking vision, language, and sound. Its contribution is a mode of co-creation in which sensory attention and bodily interaction with the environment help guide the musical result.
summary.tldr: LUMIA converts camera-captured scenes and user-selected instrumentation into loopable music through a handheld, interactive workflow.

title: LUMIA: A Handheld Vision-to-Music System for Real-Time, Embodied Composition

abstract: Estimating treatment effects is crucial for personalized decision-making in medicine, but this task faces unique challenges in clinical practice. At training time, models for estimating treatment effects are typically trained on well-structured medical datasets that contain detailed patient information. However, at inference time, predictions are often made using textual descriptions (e.g., descriptions with self-reported symptoms), which are incomplete representations of the original patient information. In this work, we make three contributions. (1) We show that the discrepancy between the data available during training time and inference time can lead to biased estimates of treatment effects. We formalize this issue as an \emph{inference time text confounding} problem, where confounders are fully observed during training time but only partially available through text at inference time. (2) To address this problem, we propose a novel framework for estimating treatment effects that explicitly accounts for inference time text confounding. Our framework leverages large language models (LLMs) together with a custom doubly robust learner to mitigate biases caused by the inference time text confounding. (3) Through a series of experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework in real-world applications.

paragraphs: Treatment-effect models may be trained on detailed, structured patient information but later receive only a textual description, such as self-reported symptoms. These descriptions can omit information present during training. The paper shows that this mismatch can bias treatment-effect estimates, making the representation available at prediction time a central part of the estimation problem.

The authors formalize the mismatch as inference-time text confounding. In their setting, confounders are fully observed during training but only partially represented in the text available during inference. The issue therefore persists even when the training dataset contains the relevant variables: the prediction interface supplies an incomplete account of them.

To address this, the proposed framework combines language models with a custom doubly robust learner that explicitly accounts for the text-confounding problem. Experiments demonstrate effectiveness in real-world applications. The contribution is both a formal description of an overlooked source of bias and a method intended to mitigate it when structured training information must support predictions from incomplete text.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies bias from incomplete inference-time patient text and proposes an LLM-assisted doubly robust framework to mitigate it.

title: LLM-Driven Treatment Effect Estimation Under Inference Time Text Confounding

abstract: Current Vision-Language Models (VLMs) struggle with fine-grained spatial reasoning, particularly when multi-step logic and precise spatial alignment are required. In this work, we introduce SpatialReasoner-R1, a vision-language reasoning model designed to address these limitations. To construct high-quality supervision for spatial reasoning, we design a Multi-Model Monte Carlo Tree Search (M3CTS) method that generates diverse, logically consistent Long Chain-of-Thought (LongCoT) reasoning trajectories. In addition, we propose a fine-grained Direct Preference Optimization (fDPO) method that introduces segment-specific preference granularity for descriptive grounding and logical reasoning, guided by a spatial reward mechanism that evaluates candidate responses based on visual consistency, spatial grounding, and logical coherence. Experimental results demonstrate that fDPO achieves relative performance gains of 4.1% and 9.0% over standard DPO on spatial quality and spatial quantity tasks, respectively. SpatialReasoner-R1, trained with fDPO, sets a new SoTA on SpatialRGPT-Bench, outperforming the strongest baseline by 9.8% in average accuracy, while maintaining competitive performance on general vision-language tasks.

paragraphs: Spatial questions can require a vision-language model to connect precise visual observations with several reasoning steps. SpatialReasoner-R1 targets weaknesses in that combination. The paper develops both a method for generating detailed reasoning supervision and a training objective that distinguishes different parts of a response.

Its Multi-Model Monte Carlo Tree Search generates diverse, logically consistent long reasoning trajectories. Fine-grained Direct Preference Optimization then applies segment-specific preferences to descriptive grounding and logical reasoning. A spatial reward evaluates visual consistency, spatial grounding, and logical coherence, allowing the training signal to reflect these different requirements within an answer.

Compared with standard preference optimization, the fine-grained method delivers relative gains of 4.1% on spatial quality tasks and 9.0% on spatial quantity tasks. The resulting model sets a new best result on SpatialRGPT-Bench, outperforming the strongest baseline by 9.8% in average accuracy, while remaining competitive on general vision-language tasks. These findings support supervising the distinct descriptive and reasoning portions of spatial responses rather than treating their quality as a single undifferentiated judgment.
summary.tldr: SpatialReasoner-R1 improves spatial reasoning through searched reasoning examples and preference training that separately evaluates descriptive and logical segments.

title: Fine-Grained Preference Optimization Improves Spatial Reasoning in VLMs

abstract: Neural networks are valuable intellectual property due to the significant computational cost, expert labor, and proprietary data involved in their development. Consequently, protecting their parameters is critical not only for maintaining a competitive advantage but also for enhancing the model's security and privacy. Prior works have demonstrated the growing capability of cryptanalytic attacks to scale to deeper models. In this paper, we present the first defense mechanism against cryptanalytic parameter extraction attacks. Our key insight is to eliminate the neuron uniqueness necessary for these attacks to succeed. We achieve this by a novel, extraction-aware training method. Specifically, we augment the standard loss function with an additional regularization term that minimizes the distance between neuron weights within a layer. Therefore, the proposed defense has zero area-delay overhead during inference. We evaluate the effectiveness of our approach in mitigating extraction attacks while analyzing the model accuracy across different architectures and datasets. When re-trained with the same model architecture, the results show that our defense incurs a marginal accuracy change of less than 1\% with the modified loss function. Moreover, we present a theoretical framework to quantify the success probability of the attack. When tested comprehensively with prior attack settings, our defense demonstrated empirical success for sustained periods of extraction, whereas unprotected networks are extracted between 14 minutes to 4 hours.

paragraphs: Cryptanalytic parameter-extraction attacks try to recover a neural network's weights, threatening the investment embodied in its training. This paper introduces a defense aimed at the neuron uniqueness that these attacks need. The approach modifies training so neurons within a layer become less distinguishable in their weight structure.

Specifically, the authors add a regularization term to the usual training loss that reduces distances between neuron weights in the same layer. Because this changes the learned parameters rather than adding inference machinery, the defense has no inference area-delay overhead. The paper also develops a theoretical framework for quantifying an attack's probability of success.

Evaluations across architectures and datasets examine both resistance to extraction and model accuracy. Retraining the same architecture with the modified loss changes accuracy by less than 1% in the reported results. Under prior attack settings, defended networks resist extraction over sustained testing periods, while unprotected networks are extracted within 14 minutes to four hours. These results demonstrate empirical protection against the tested attacks while preserving accuracy closely, rather than establishing unconditional immunity.
summary.tldr: Extraction-aware training makes neuron weights less distinctive, resisting tested cryptanalytic extraction attacks with less than 1% reported accuracy change.

title: Train to Defend: First Defense Against Cryptanalytic Neural Network Parameter Extraction Attacks

abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) addresses large language model (LLM) hallucinations by grounding responses in external knowledge, but its effectiveness is compromised by poor-quality retrieved contexts containing irrelevant or noisy information. While existing approaches attempt to improve performance through context selection based on predefined context quality assessment metrics, they show limited gains over standard RAG. We attribute this limitation to their failure in holistically utilizing available information (query, context list, and generator) for comprehensive quality assessment. Inspired by recent advances in data selection, we reconceptualize context quality assessment as an inference-time data valuation problem and introduce the Contextual Influence Value (CI value). This novel metric quantifies context quality by measuring the performance degradation when removing each context from the list, effectively integrating query-aware relevance, list-aware uniqueness, and generator-aware alignment. Moreover, CI value eliminates complex selection hyperparameter tuning by simply retaining contexts with positive CI values. To address practical challenges of label dependency and computational overhead, we develop a parameterized surrogate model for CI value prediction during inference. The model employs a hierarchical architecture that captures both local query-context relevance and global inter-context interactions, trained through oracle CI value supervision and end-to-end generator feedback. Extensive experiments across 8 NLP tasks and multiple LLMs demonstrate that our context selection method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, effectively filtering poor-quality contexts while preserving critical information. Code is available at https://github.com/SJTU-DMTai/RAG-CSM.

We attribute this limitation to their failure in holistically utilizing available information (query, context list, and generator) for comprehensive quality assessment. Inspired by recent advances in data selection, we reconceptualize context quality assessment as an inference-time data valuation problem and introduce the Contextual Influence Value (CI value). This novel metric quantifies context quality by measuring the performance degradation when removing each context from the list, effectively integrating query-aware relevance, list-aware uniqueness, and generator-aware alignment. Moreover, CI value eliminates complex selection hyperparameter tuning by simply retaining contexts with positive CI values. To address practical challenges of label dependency and computational overhead, we develop a parameterized surrogate model for CI value prediction during inference. The model employs a hierarchical architecture that captures both local query-context relevance and global inter-context interactions, trained through oracle CI value supervision and end-to-end generator feedback. Extensive experiments across 8 NLP tasks and multiple LLMs demonstrate that our context selection method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, effectively filtering poor-quality contexts while preserving critical information. Code is available at https://github.com/SJTU-DMTai/RAG-CSM.

paragraphs: Retrieval-augmented generation can suffer when the retrieved material contains irrelevant or noisy information. This paper argues that selecting useful context requires considering the query, the other retrieved passages, and the generator together. A passage's value therefore depends on how it contributes to the particular answer being produced.

The proposed Contextual Influence Value measures how much performance deteriorates when a context is removed from the retrieved list. This incorporates relevance to the query, uniqueness relative to other contexts, and compatibility with the generator. Selection then retains contexts with positive values, avoiding a complicated search over selection hyperparameters.

Directly obtaining these values creates label and computation demands, so the authors train a surrogate to predict them during inference. Its hierarchical architecture captures individual query-context relationships and interactions across the context list, using oracle influence supervision and generator feedback. Experiments across eight NLP tasks and multiple language models report improvements over state-of-the-art baselines, supporting context selection based on contribution to generation rather than isolated passage quality alone.
summary.tldr: The method selects retrieved contexts by predicting their contribution to generation quality, accounting for the query, other contexts, and generator.

title: Influence Guided Context Selection for Effective Retrieval-Augmented Generation

abstract: Refusal mechanisms in large language models (LLMs) are essential for ensuring safety. Recent research has revealed that refusal behavior can be mediated by a single direction in activation space, enabling targeted interventions to bypass refusals. While this is primarily demonstrated in an English-centric context, appropriate refusal behavior is important for any language, but poorly understood. In this paper, we investigate the refusal behavior in LLMs across 14 languages using \textit{PolyRefuse}, a multilingual safety dataset created by translating malicious and benign English prompts into these languages. We uncover the surprising cross-lingual universality of the refusal direction: a vector extracted from English can bypass refusals in other languages with near-perfect effectiveness, without any additional fine-tuning. Even more remarkably, refusal directions derived from any safety-aligned language transfer seamlessly to others. We attribute this transferability to the parallelism of refusal vectors across languages in the embedding space and identify the underlying mechanism behind cross-lingual jailbreaks. These findings provide actionable insights for building more robust multilingual safety defenses and pave the way for a deeper mechanistic understanding of cross-lingual vulnerabilities in LLMs.

paragraphs: This paper examines whether the internal mechanisms behind language-model refusals are shared across languages. Prior work found that a single direction in activation space can mediate refusal behavior, mainly in English-focused settings. The authors investigate the multilingual case using PolyRefuse, a dataset of malicious and benign English prompts translated into 14 languages.

They find that a refusal direction extracted from English can bypass refusals in other languages with near-perfect effectiveness and without additional fine-tuning. They also report transfer between directions derived from other safety-aligned languages. This suggests that the studied models share a closely related internal refusal mechanism across their aligned languages.

The authors attribute this transfer to refusal vectors being parallel across languages in the model’s representation space. That geometric relationship provides an explanation for the cross-language behavior observed in their study. The findings expose a multilingual safety vulnerability and offer a mechanistic basis for developing stronger defenses. The empirical scope remains the investigated languages and models, despite the broad transfer reported within that setting.
summary.tldr: Across 14 studied languages, refusal directions transfer strongly between safety-aligned languages, revealing a shared multilingual safety vulnerability.

title: Refusal Direction is Universal Across Safety-Aligned Languages

abstract: We introduce ROGR, a novel approach that reconstructs a relightable 3D model of an object captured from multiple views, driven by a generative relighting model that simulates the effects of placing the object under novel environment illuminations. Our method samples the appearance of the object under multiple lighting environments, creating a dataset that is used to train a lighting-conditioned Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) that outputs the object's appearance under any input environmental lighting. The lighting-conditioned NeRF uses a novel dual-branch architecture to encode the general lighting effects and specularities separately. The optimized lighting-conditioned NeRF enables efficient feed-forward relighting under arbitrary environment maps without requiring per-illumination optimization or light transport simulation. We evaluate our approach on the established TensoIR and Stanford-ORB datasets, where it improves upon the state-of-the-art on most metrics, and showcase our approach on real-world object captures.

paragraphs: ROGR reconstructs a three-dimensional object model that can display the object under different lighting conditions. Starting from multiple captured views, it uses a generative relighting model to simulate how the object would appear under new environmental illumination. Those generated appearances supply a dataset for learning a representation whose output depends on the requested lighting.

The representation is a lighting-conditioned Neural Radiance Field, or NeRF. Its dual-branch architecture separately encodes general illumination effects and specular appearance. This separation gives the model dedicated components for these aspects of relighting while retaining a single representation that responds to an input environment map.

Once optimized, the model produces relit appearances through a feed-forward computation, without additional optimization for each illumination or light-transport simulation. Evaluations on TensoIR and Stanford-ORB improve on the state of the art on most metrics, and the authors also demonstrate real-world captures. The result connects generative relighting with a reusable 3D representation that supports efficient changes of illumination after training.
summary.tldr: ROGR uses generated lighting variations to train a 3D object representation that supports efficient relighting under new environment maps.

title: ROGR: Relightable 3D Objects using Generative Relighting

abstract: To learn approximately optimal acting policies for decision problems, modern Actor Critic algorithms rely on deep Neural Networks (DNNs) to parameterize the acting policy and greedification operators to iteratively improve it. The reliance on DNNs suggests an improvement that is gradient based, which is per step much less greedy than the improvement possible by greedier operators such as the greedy update used by Q-learning algorithms. On the other hand, slow and steady changes to the policy can also be beneficial for the stability of the learning process, resulting in a tradeoff between greedification and stability. To address this tradeoff, we propose to extend the standard framework of actor critic algorithms with value-improvement: a second greedification operator applied only when updating the policy's value estimate. In this framework the agent can evaluate non-parameterized policies and perform much greedier updates while maintaining the steady gradient-based improvement to the parameterized acting policy. We prove that this approach converges in the popular analysis scheme of generalized Policy Iteration in the finite-horizon domain. Empirically, incorporating value-improvement into the popular off-policy actor-critic algorithms TD3 and SAC significantly improves or matches performance over their respective baselines, across different environments from the DeepMind continuous control domain, with negligible compute and implementation cost.

paragraphs: Actor-critic algorithms improve an acting policy while estimating its value. When a neural network parameterizes the policy, gradient updates typically make relatively gradual improvements. Greedier updates can move more aggressively toward high-value actions, but gradual policy changes can help learning remain stable. This paper addresses that trade-off by changing value estimation.

The proposed framework adds a second greedification operator used only when updating the policy’s value estimate. This lets the agent evaluate non-parameterized policies and use more aggressive improvement within value updates, while retaining steady gradient-based changes to the acting policy. The two update processes can therefore use different degrees of greediness.

The authors prove convergence within generalized policy iteration for finite-horizon problems. They also incorporate value improvement into TD3 and SAC, reporting performance that significantly improves on or matches the respective baselines across DeepMind continuous control environments. With negligible reported computation and implementation cost, the approach offers a practical way to exploit greedier value updates while preserving gradual changes in behavior.
summary.tldr: Value improvement adds greedier updates to actor-critic value estimation while keeping acting-policy changes gradual, improving or matching reported TD3 and SAC performance.

title: Value Improved Actor Critic Algorithms

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become the dominant paradigm for improving the performance of language models on complex reasoning tasks. Despite the substantial empirical gains demonstrated by RL-based training methods like GRPO, a granular understanding of why and how RL enhances performance is still lacking. To bridge this gap, we introduce SPARKLE, a fine-grained analytic framework to dissect the effects of RL across three key dimensions: (1) plan following and execution, (2) knowledge integration, and (3) chain of subproblems. Using this framework, we gain insights beyond mere accuracy. For instance, providing models with explicit human-crafted, step-by-step plans can surprisingly degrade performance on the most challenging benchmarks, yet RL-tuned models exhibit greater robustness, experiencing markedly smaller performance drops than base or SFT models. This suggests that RL may not primarily enhance the execution of external plans but rather empower models to formulate and follow internal strategies better suited to their reasoning processes. Conversely, we observe that RL enhances models' ability to integrate provided knowledge into their reasoning process, yielding consistent gains across diverse tasks. Finally, we study whether difficult problems---those yielding no RL signals and mixed-quality reasoning traces---can still be effectively used for training. We introduce SparkleRL-PSS, a multi-stage RL pipeline that reuses hard problems with partial step scaffolding, guiding exploration effectively without additional data generation. Together, our findings provide a principled foundation for understanding how RL shapes model behavior, offering practical insights for building more adaptive, data-efficient, and interpretable RL pipelines for reasoning tasks. Our code, data, and checkpoints are available at: https://sparkle-reasoning.github.io/.

paragraphs: A higher mathematical answer score does not reveal which reasoning abilities improved during training. SPARKLE examines reinforcement learning through three more specific dimensions: following and executing plans, incorporating supplied knowledge, and working through chains of subproblems. This makes it possible to distinguish different behavioral changes behind overall accuracy.

The analysis finds that explicit human-written plans can reduce performance on the hardest benchmarks. Reinforcement-learning-tuned models experience smaller drops than base or supervised-fine-tuned models. The authors interpret this as suggesting that reinforcement learning may strengthen internally developed strategies more than execution of externally supplied plans. Separately, they observe consistent improvements in models' ability to use provided knowledge across diverse tasks.

The paper also investigates how to reuse difficult problems that provide no reinforcement-learning signal and contain mixed-quality reasoning traces. Its SparkleRL-PSS pipeline supplies partial steps across multiple training stages to guide exploration without generating additional data. Together, the analysis and training approach connect finer-grained observations about reasoning behavior to a practical way of making difficult training material useful.
summary.tldr: SPARKLE analyzes how reinforcement learning changes mathematical reasoning and introduces partial-step scaffolding to reuse difficult training problems.

title: Beyond Accuracy: Dissecting Mathematical Reasoning for LLMs Under Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Model-free reinforcement learning (RL) combined with diffusion models has achieved significant progress in addressing complex continuous control tasks. However, a persistent challenge in RL remains the accurate estimation of Q-values, which critically governs the efficacy of policy optimization. Although recent advances employ parametric distributions to model value distributions for enhanced estimation accuracy, current methodologies predominantly rely on unimodal Gaussian assumptions or quantile representations. These constraints introduce distributional bias between the learned and true value distributions, particularly in some tasks with a nonstationary policy, ultimately degrading performance. To address these limitations, we propose value diffusion reinforcement learning (VDRL), a novel model-free online RL method that utilizes the generative capacity of diffusion models to represent multimodal value distributions. The core innovation of VDRL lies in the use of the variational loss of diffusion-based value distribution, which is theoretically proven to be a tight lower bound for the optimization objective under the KL-divergence measurement. Furthermore, we introduce double value diffusion learning with sample selection to enhance training stability and further improve value estimation accuracy. Extensive experiments conducted on the MuJoCo benchmark demonstrate that VDRL significantly outperforms some SOTA model-free online RL baselines, showcasing its effectiveness and robustness.

paragraphs: Accurate value estimation is central to reinforcement learning because it guides policy improvement. Existing distributional approaches often use unimodal Gaussian assumptions or quantile representations. The paper argues that these choices can introduce mismatch with the true value distribution, particularly in some tasks where the policy changes during learning.

Value Diffusion Reinforcement Learning, or VDRL, uses a diffusion model to represent multimodal value distributions in online, model-free reinforcement learning. The results support the usefulness of flexible value distributions in the tested continuous-control tasks. The contribution places diffusion modeling inside value estimation, addressing the quality of the learning signal that determines how a policy is optimized.
summary.tldr: VDRL models multimodal value distributions with diffusion and outperforms some state-of-the-art online reinforcement-learning baselines on MuJoCo.

title: Value Diffusion Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Current Reinforcement Fine-tuning (RFT) paradigms for Large Language Models (LLMs) suffer from sample inefficiency due to the redundant exposure of identical queries under uniform data sampling. While previous work has explored curriculum learning via heuristic difficulty metrics, these strategies exhibit limitations by neglecting the intrinsic learning signals generated by the model itself, thus leading to suboptimal training regimes. In this paper, we identify a model-inherent signal termed *angle concentration* that effectively reflects an LLM's capacity to learn from specific data. We theoretically and empirically demonstrate a correlation between the angular distribution of token hidden state vectors and the resulting gradient, revealing a learning preference for data exhibiting higher angle concentration. Inspired by this finding, we propose GAIN-RL, a Gradient-driven Angle-Informed Navigated RL framework. By leveraging the model's intrinsic angle concentration signal, GAIN-RL dynamically selects training data in each epoch, ensuring consistently impactful gradient updates and thus significantly enhancing overall training efficiency. Empirical evaluations show that GAIN-RL (GRPO) achieves over a 2.5$\times$ acceleration in training efficiency across diverse mathematical and coding tasks and varying model scales. Furthermore, GAIN-RL (GRPO)'s efficient sampling yields data-efficient training, achieving better performance with half the original data compared to vanilla GRPO with full training data.

paragraphs: Reinforcement fine-tuning can spend substantial effort revisiting the same queries under uniform sampling. This paper asks whether a model’s own internal activity can identify data it is better positioned to learn from. Its proposed signal, angle concentration, describes the angular distribution of the hidden-state vectors associated with tokens.

The authors establish a theoretical and empirical correlation between that distribution and the resulting training gradient. Their findings indicate a learning preference for examples with higher angle concentration. GAIN-RL uses this signal to select training data dynamically during each epoch, connecting data selection to the model’s current learning behavior instead of relying only on a heuristic measure of difficulty.

Across the reported mathematical and coding tasks and model scales, GAIN-RL with GRPO achieves more than a 2.5-fold improvement in training efficiency. It also obtains better performance using half the original training data than standard GRPO using the full dataset. These results support internal representation geometry as a useful signal for allocating reinforcement-training effort.
summary.tldr: GAIN-RL selects training examples using hidden-state angle concentration, improving reported GRPO training efficiency by over 2.5 times.

title: Angles Don’t Lie: Unlocking Training‑Efficient RL Through the Model’s Own Signals

abstract: Fitting Gaussian Processes (GPs) provides interpretable aleatoric uncertainty quantification for estimation of spatio-temporal fields. Spatio-temporal deep learning models, while scalable, typically assume a simplistic independent covariance matrix for the response, failing to capture the underlying correlation structure. However, spatio-temporal GPs suffer from issues of scalability and various forms of approximation bias resulting from restrictive assumptions of the covariance kernel function. We propose STACI, a novel framework consisting of a variational Bayesian neural network approximation of non-stationary spatio-temporal GP along with a novel spatio-temporal conformal inference algorithm. STACI is highly scalable, taking advantage of GPU training capabilities for neural network models, and provides statistically valid prediction intervals for uncertainty quantification. STACI outperforms competing GPs and deep methods in accurately approximating spatio-temporal processes and we show it easily scales to datasets with millions of observations.

paragraphs: Predicting a field across space and time requires representing how observations are related, along with uncertainty in their values. Gaussian processes offer interpretable uncertainty estimates but face scaling difficulties and biases from restrictive covariance assumptions. Scalable deep models, meanwhile, often simplify the response covariance by treating components as independent.

STACI combines a variational Bayesian neural network approximation of a non-stationary spatio-temporal Gaussian process with a specialized conformal inference algorithm. The non-stationary formulation allows the modeled dependence structure to vary across the field. The neural network component makes GPU training available, while the conformal component supports statistically valid prediction intervals.

The authors report more accurate approximation of spatio-temporal processes than competing Gaussian-process and deep-learning methods. They also demonstrate scaling to datasets containing millions of observations. The importance of the combination is that uncertainty modeling and computational scale are addressed together: the framework represents correlated spatio-temporal variation through its probabilistic approximation and supplies prediction intervals through conformal inference, while retaining the training advantages of neural networks.
summary.tldr: STACI combines a neural approximation of a spatio-temporal Gaussian process with conformal inference for scalable predictions and statistically valid intervals.

title: STACI: Spatio-Temporal Aleatoric Conformal Inference

abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) can efficiently process text-attributed graphs (TAGs) due to their message-passing mechanisms, but their training heavily relies on the human-annotated labels. Moreover, the complex and diverse local topologies of nodes of real-world TAGs make it challenging for a single mechanism to handle. Large language models (LLMs) perform well in zero-/few-shot learning on TAGs but suffer from a scalability challenge. Therefore, we propose a preference-driven knowledge distillation (PKD) framework to synergize the complementary strengths of LLMs and various GNNs for few-shot node classification. Specifically, we develop a GNN-preference-driven node selector that effectively promotes prediction distillation from LLMs to teacher GNNs. To further tackle nodes' intricate local topologies, we develop a node-preference-driven GNN selector that identifies the most suitable teacher GNN for each node, thereby facilitating tailored knowledge distillation from teacher GNNs to the student GNN. Extensive experiments validate the efficacy of our proposed framework in few-shot node classification on real-world TAGs. Our code can be available at .

paragraphs: Classifying nodes in graphs with textual attributes presents complementary challenges for graph neural networks and language models. Graph networks process connected data efficiently but depend heavily on labeled examples. Language models can work with few or no labels, yet applying them at scale is difficult. Different local graph structures also make it hard for one graph-learning mechanism to suit every node.

The proposed preference-driven distillation framework transfers knowledge in two stages. First, a selector guided by graph-network preferences chooses nodes to support transfer of language-model predictions into teacher graph networks. Then a second selector uses node preferences to identify the most suitable teacher for each node. Those selected teachers provide tailored supervision to a student graph network.

Experiments on real-world text-attributed graphs validate the framework for few-shot node classification. The approach matters because it accounts for variation on both sides of knowledge transfer: which nodes help particular teachers learn, and which teacher best suits a particular node. This brings language-model knowledge and multiple graph-learning approaches into one student.
summary.tldr: Preference-driven distillation transfers language-model knowledge through multiple graph teachers, selecting suitable supervision for each node before training a student.

title: Preference-driven Knowledge Distillation for Few-shot Node Classification

abstract: Inducing-point-based sparse variational Gaussian processes have become the standard workhorse for scaling up GP models. Recent advances show that these methods can be improved by introducing a diagonal scaling matrix to the conditional posterior density given the inducing points. This paper first considers an extension that employs a block-diagonal structure for the scaling matrix, provably tightening the variational lower bound. We then revisit the unifying framework of sparse GPs based on Power Expectation Propagation (PEP) and show that it can leverage and benefit from the new structured approximate posteriors. Through extensive regression experiments, we show that the proposed block-diagonal approximation consistently performs similarly to or better than existing diagonal approximations while maintaining comparable computational costs. Furthermore, the new PEP framework with structured posteriors provides competitive performance across various power hyperparameter settings, offering practitioners flexible alternatives to standard variational approaches.

paragraphs: Sparse Gaussian processes use inducing points to make probabilistic modeling more computationally manageable. Recent methods improve these approximations by applying diagonal scaling to the conditional posterior given the inducing points. This paper replaces that diagonal structure with a block-diagonal one, allowing a richer structured approximation within the same broad framework.

The authors prove that the block-diagonal construction tightens the variational lower bound. This is a theoretical improvement in the approximation objective, distinct from an automatic guarantee about every prediction. They also revisit Power Expectation Propagation, showing how its unifying framework for sparse Gaussian processes can incorporate and benefit from these structured posterior approximations.

Across extensive regression experiments, the block-diagonal method performs similarly to or better than existing diagonal approximations while keeping computational costs comparable. The revised Power-EP framework is also competitive across different settings of its power hyperparameter. Together, these results offer practitioners a richer approximation without the reported experiments showing a corresponding increase in computational cost, alongside flexible alternatives to standard variational inference.
summary.tldr: Block-diagonal posterior approximations tighten a sparse Gaussian-process bound and match or improve regression performance at comparable computational cost.

title: Sparse Gaussian Processes: Structured Approximations and Power-EP Revisited

abstract: Over more than a decade there has been an extensive research effort on how to effectively utilize recurrent models and attention. While recurrent models aim to compress the data into a fixed-size memory (called hidden state), attention allows attending to the entire context window, capturing the direct dependencies of all tokens. This more accurate modeling of dependencies, however, comes with a quadratic cost, limiting the model to a fixed-length context. We present a neural long-term memory module that learns to memorize historical context and helps attention to attend to the current context while utilizing long-past information. We show that this neural memory has the advantage of fast parallelizable training. From a memory perspective, we argue that attention due to its limited context but accurate dependency modeling performs as a short-term memory, while neural memory due to its ability to memorize the data, acts as a long-term, more persistent, memory. Based on these two modules, we introduce a new family of architectures, called Titans, and present three variants to address how one can effectively incorporate memory into this architecture. Our experimental results on language modeling, common-sense reasoning, and time series tasks show that Titans are effective compared to baselines, while they can effectively scale to larger context window in needle-in-haystack tasks.

Based on these two modules, we introduce a new family of architectures, called Titans, and present three variants to address how one can effectively incorporate memory into this architecture. Our experimental results on language modeling, common-sense reasoning, and time series tasks show that Titans are effective compared to baselines, while they can effectively scale to larger context window in needle-in-haystack tasks.

paragraphs: Recurrent models compress history into a fixed-size state, while attention directly models relationships across tokens in its context window. Attention's quadratic cost constrains the length of that window. Titans combines attention with a neural long-term memory module that learns to retain historical context, allowing current-context processing to draw on information from much earlier.

The authors describe attention as short-term memory because it models dependencies accurately within a limited context. The neural module serves as a more persistent memory and supports fast, parallelizable training. They introduce three architectural variants that explore how to incorporate these two components into a single model family.

Experiments evaluate Titans on language modeling, common-sense reasoning, and time-series tasks, reporting effectiveness relative to baselines. Needle-in-haystack experiments also show effective scaling to larger context windows. The central architectural contribution is a division of memory responsibilities: attention handles direct relationships in the current context, while learned neural memory supplies access to historical information beyond that immediate window.
summary.tldr: Titans combines attention with learned long-term neural memory to use historical information and scale effectively to larger contexts in reported tests.

title: Titans: Learning to Memorize at Test Time

abstract: Medical Lay Language Generation (MLLG) plays a vital role in improving the accessibility of complex scientific content for broader audiences. Recent literature to MLLG commonly employ parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods such as Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) to fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) using paired expert-lay language datasets. However, LoRA struggles with the challenges posed by multi-source heterogeneous MLLG datasets. Specifically, through a series of exploratory experiments, we reveal that standard LoRA fail to meet the requirement for semantic fidelity and diverse lay-style generation in MLLG task. To address these limitations, we propose Magical, an asymmetric LoRA architecture tailored for MLLG under heterogeneous data scenarios. Magical employs a shared matrix A for abstractive summarization, along with multiple isolated matrices B for diverse lay-style generation. To preserve semantic fidelity during the lay language generation process, Magical introduces a Semantic Invariance Constraint to mitigate semantic subspace shifts on matrix A. Furthermore, to better adapt to diverse lay-style generation, Magical incorporates the Recommendation-guided Switch, an externally interface to prompt the LLM to switch between different matrices B. Experimental results on three real-world lay language generation datasets demonstrate that Magical consistently outperforms prompt-based methods, vanilla LoRA, and its recent variants, while also reducing trainable parameters by 31.66%. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/tianlwang/Magical.git.

summary.tldr: Magical separates shared medical summarization from selectable lay-language styles to improve fidelity and accessibility with fewer trainable parameters.

title: Magical: Medical Lay Language Generation via Semantic Invariance and Layperson-tailored Adaptation

abstract: Image watermarking embeds imperceptible signals into AI-generated images for deepfake detection and provenance verification. Although recent semantic-level watermarking methods demonstrate strong resistance against conventional pixel-level removal attacks, their robustness against more advanced removal strategies remains underexplored, raising concerns about their reliability in practical scenarios. Existing removal attacks primarily operate in the pixel domain without altering image semantics, which limits their effectiveness against semantic-level watermarks. In this paper, we propose Next Frame Prediction Attack (NFPA), the first semantic-level removal attack. Unlike pixel-level attacks, NFPA formulates watermark removal as a video generation task: it treats the watermarked image as the initial frame and aims to subtly manipulate the image semantics to generate the next-frame image, i.e., the unwatermarked image. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation on eight state-of-the-art image watermarking schemes, demonstrating that NFPA consistently outperforms thirteen removal attack baselines in terms of the trade-off between watermark removal and image quality. Our results reveal the vulnerabilities of current image watermarking methods and highlight the urgent need for more robust watermarks.

The conceptual shift is to use a generated continuation of the image as the transformed output.

The authors evaluate the approach against eight state-of-the-art watermarking schemes and compare it with thirteen removal-attack baselines. They report a consistently better trade-off between removing the watermark and maintaining image quality. These results expose vulnerabilities in the evaluated watermarking methods and motivate stronger designs. The central finding concerns robustness under a different class of transformation, beyond the conventional pixel-level attacks emphasized in earlier evaluations.
summary.tldr: Next-frame prediction exposes vulnerabilities in evaluated image watermarks by improving the trade-off between removal and image quality.

title: The Future Unmarked: Watermark Removal in AI-Generated Images via Next-Frame Prediction

abstract: We propose a novel diffusion-based framework for automatic colorization of Anime-style facial sketches, which preserves the structural fidelity of the input sketch while effectively transferring stylistic attributes from a reference image. Our approach builds upon recent continuous-time diffusion models, but departs from traditional methods that rely on predefined noise schedules, which often fail to maintain perceptual consistency across the generative trajectory. To address this, we introduce SSIMBaD (Sigma Scaling with SSIM-Guided Balanced Diffusion), a sigma-space transformation that ensures linear alignment of perceptual degradation, as measured by structural similarity. This perceptual scaling enforces uniform visual difficulty across timesteps, enabling more balanced and faithful reconstructions. On a large-scale Anime face dataset, SSIMBaD attains state-of-the-art structural fidelity and strong perceptual quality, with robust generalization to diverse styles and structural variations.

paragraphs: Colorizing an anime facial sketch from a reference image requires preserving the sketch’s structure while adopting stylistic attributes from the reference. SSIMBaD tackles this through a continuous-time diffusion framework. Its focus is on how the noise process changes perceived image structure throughout generation.

Predefined noise schedules can create uneven perceptual changes along the diffusion trajectory. SSIMBaD transforms sigma space so that degradation measured by structural similarity follows a linear progression. This scaling aims to distribute visual difficulty uniformly across timesteps, making the reconstruction process more balanced and helping it stay faithful to the input sketch.

The central idea is to organize diffusion around a perceptual measure rather than assume that a conventional noise schedule already produces consistent visual changes. On a large anime-face dataset, the authors report state-of-the-art preservation of structure together with strong perceptual quality. They also report robust generalization across different styles and structural variations, supporting the value of perceptually guided scaling for this colorization task.
summary.tldr: SSIMBaD uses structural-similarity-guided diffusion scaling to color anime face sketches while preserving their structure and transferring reference style.

title: SSIMBaD: Sigma Scaling with SSIM-Guided Balanced Diffusion for AnimeFace Colorization

abstract: We study revenue maximization for agents with additive preferences, subject to downward-closed constraints on the set of feasible allocations. In seminal work,~\citet{alaei2014bayesian} introduced a powerful multi-to-single agent reduction based on an ex-ante relaxation of the multi-agent problem. This reduction employs a rounding procedure which is an online contention resolution scheme (OCRS) in disguise, a now widely-used method for rounding fractional solutions in online Bayesian and stochastic optimization problems. In this paper, we leverage our vantage point, 10 years after the work of Alaei, with a rich OCRS toolkit and modern approaches to analyzing multi-agent mechanisms; we introduce a general framework for designing non-sequential and sequential multi-agent, revenue-maximizing mechanisms, capturing a wide variety of problems Alaei's framework could not address. Our framework uses an \emph{interim} relaxation, that is rounded to a feasible mechanism using what we call a two-level OCRS, which allows for some structured dependence between the activation of its input elements. For a wide family of constraints, we can construct such schemes using existing OCRSs as a black box; for other constraints, such as knapsack, we construct such schemes from scratch. We demonstrate numerous applications of our framework, including a sequential mechanism that guarantees a $\frac{2e}{e-1} \approx 3.16$ approximation to the optimal revenue for the case of additive agents subject to matroid feasibility constraints. Finally, we show how our framework can be easily extended to multi-parameter procurement auctions, where we provide an OCRS for Stochastic Knapsack that might be of independent interest.

The challenge is to turn a more tractable relaxed allocation problem into an actual feasible mechanism. Earlier work used an ex-ante relaxation; the authors introduce an interim relaxation to cover a broader range of mechanism-design problems.

summary.tldr: An interim relaxation and two-level contention resolution framework yield revenue-approximation mechanisms under a broader range of allocation constraints.

title: Mechanism Design via the Interim Relaxation

abstract: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) have been seen as a promising competitor for autoregressive language models (ARs). However, diffusion language models have long been constrained by slow inference. A core challenge is that their non‑autoregressive architecture and bidirectional attention preclude the key–value cache that accelerates decoding. We address this bottleneck by proposing a KV-cache-like mechanism, **d**elayed **KV-Cache**, for the denoising process of DLMs. Our approach is motivated by the observation that different tokens have distinct representation dynamics throughout the diffusion process. Accordingly, we propose a delayed and conditioned caching strategy for key and value states. We design two complementary variants to cache key and value step‑by‑step: (1) dKV-Cache-Decode, which provides almost lossless acceleration, and even improves performance on long sequences, suggesting that existing DLMs may under‑utilise contextual information during inference. (2) dKV-Cache‑Greedy, which has aggressive caching with reduced lifespan, achieving higher speed-ups with quadratic time complexity at the cost of some performance degradation. dKV-Cache, in final, achieves from 2-10$\times$ speedup in inference, largely narrowing the gap between ARs and DLMs. We evaluate our dKV-Cache on several benchmarks, delivering acceleration across general language understanding, mathematical, and code‑generation benchmarks. Experiments demonstrate that cache can also be used in DLMs, even in a training-free manner from current DLMs.

paragraphs: Diffusion language models refine text through repeated denoising steps, but inference can be slow. Their bidirectional attention and non-autoregressive structure prevent straightforward use of the key–value caching that accelerates autoregressive models. This paper develops a caching mechanism specifically for diffusion, motivated by the observation that different tokens change their internal representations differently during generation.

The method delays caching and makes reuse conditional on token behavior. It offers two variants with different efficiency tradeoffs. dKV-Cache-Decode provides almost lossless acceleration and even improves performance on long sequences. dKV-Cache-Greedy uses more aggressive caching with a shorter lifespan, providing larger speedups and quadratic time complexity at the expense of some performance.

The reported inference acceleration ranges from twofold to tenfold across evaluations involving language understanding, mathematics, and code generation. The method can operate on existing diffusion language models without additional training. Improved long-sequence results suggest that these models may underuse contextual information during ordinary inference, while the broader results demonstrate that appropriately designed caching can substantially reduce their computational burden.
summary.tldr: Delayed, conditional key–value caching accelerates diffusion language model inference by twofold to tenfold, with variants offering different performance tradeoffs.

title: dKV-Cache: The Cache for Diffusion Language Models

abstract: Visual grounding in 3D is the key for embodied agents to localize language-referred objects in open-world environments. However, existing benchmarks are limited to indoor focus, single-platform constraints, and small scale. We introduce 3EED, a multi-platform, multi-modal 3D grounding benchmark featuring RGB and LiDAR data from vehicle, drone, and quadruped platforms. We provide over 128,000 objects and 22,000 validated referring expressions across diverse outdoor scenes -- 10x larger than existing datasets. We develop a scalable annotation pipeline combining vision-language model prompting with human verification to ensure high-quality spatial grounding. To support cross-platform learning, we propose platform-aware normalization and cross-modal alignment techniques, and establish benchmark protocols for in-domain and cross-platform evaluations. Our findings reveal significant performance gaps, highlighting the challenges and opportunities of generalizable 3D grounding. The 3EED dataset and benchmark toolkit are released to advance future research in language-driven 3D embodied perception.

paragraphs: An embodied agent needs to connect language with physical objects: a referring expression must identify something at a particular location in three-dimensional space. Existing benchmarks provide a restricted test of this ability because they emphasize indoor environments, individual sensing platforms, and relatively small datasets. 3EED broadens evaluation to outdoor scenes observed from several kinds of platforms.

The benchmark combines RGB images and LiDAR measurements collected from vehicles, drones, and quadrupeds. It contains more than 128,000 objects and 22,000 validated referring expressions, a scale the authors describe as ten times larger than existing datasets. Its annotation pipeline combines vision-language model prompting with human verification, supporting scalable collection while checking the resulting spatial references.

The paper also introduces platform-aware normalization and alignment between sensing modalities to support learning across platforms. Evaluation protocols distinguish performance within a domain from transfer across platforms. The reported performance gaps show that this broader setting remains challenging, making the benchmark useful for studying whether language-based object localization generalizes beyond familiar sensing conditions.
summary.tldr: 3EED expands language-based 3D object localization benchmarks to large outdoor datasets spanning vehicles, drones, and quadrupeds.

title: 3EED: Ground Everything Everywhere in 3D

abstract: Solving time-dependent Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) using a densely discretized spatial domain is a fundamental problem in various scientific and engineering disciplines, including modeling climate phenomena and fluid dynamics. However, performing these computations directly in the physical space often incurs significant computational costs. To address this issue, several neural surrogate models have been developed that operate in a compressed latent space to solve the PDE. While these approaches reduce computational complexity, they often use Transformer-based attention mechanisms to handle irregularly sampled domains, resulting in increased memory consumption. In contrast, convolutional neural networks allow memory-efficient encoding and decoding but are limited to regular discretizations. Motivated by these considerations, we propose CALM-PDE, a model class that efficiently solves arbitrarily discretized PDEs in a compressed latent space. We introduce a novel continuous convolution-based encoder-decoder architecture that uses an epsilon-neighborhood-constrained kernel and learns to apply the convolution operator to adaptive and optimized query points. We demonstrate the effectiveness of CALM-PDE on a diverse set of PDEs with both regularly and irregularly sampled spatial domains. CALM-PDE is competitive with or outperforms existing baseline methods while offering significant improvements in memory and inference time efficiency compared to Transformer-based methods.

paragraphs: Time-dependent partial differential equations describe how spatial systems evolve, including fluids and climate phenomena. Computing their evolution on a dense spatial representation can be expensive. Neural surrogate models reduce this burden by working in a compressed latent representation, but handling irregularly spaced samples often introduces another cost: the memory demands of Transformer attention.

CALM-PDE uses continuous convolutions to encode spatial information into a compressed representation and decode it again. Its convolution kernel only considers an epsilon neighborhood, restricting each operation to nearby locations. The model also learns adaptive query points where those operations are applied. Together, these choices allow convolution-based processing to accommodate spatial discretizations beyond regular grids.

The authors evaluate the approach across several equations with both regular and irregular spatial sampling. CALM-PDE matches or exceeds the performance of existing baselines and improves memory use and inference time relative to Transformer-based methods. The result matters because it combines the flexibility needed for irregular domains with the efficiency advantages motivating convolutional architectures, while retaining the computational savings of modeling evolution in latent space.
summary.tldr: CALM-PDE uses adaptive continuous convolutions to model evolving PDEs in compressed space efficiently across regular and irregular spatial samples.

title: CALM-PDE: Continuous and Adaptive Convolutions for Latent Space Modeling of Time-dependent PDEs

abstract: Existing large video-language models (LVLMs) struggle to comprehend long videos correctly due to limited context. To address this problem, fine-tuning long-context LVLMs and employing GPT-based agents have emerged as promising solutions. However, fine-tuning LVLMs would require extensive high-quality data and substantial GPU resources, while GPT-based agents would rely on proprietary models (e.g., GPT-4o). In this paper, we propose Video Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Video-RAG), a training-free and cost-effective pipeline that employs visually-aligned auxiliary texts to help facilitate cross-modality alignment while providing additional information beyond the visual content. Specifically, we leverage open-source external tools to extract visually-aligned information from pure video data (e.g., audio, optical character, and object detection), and incorporate the extracted information into an existing LVLM as auxiliary texts, alongside video frames and queries, in a plug-and-play manner. Our Video-RAG offers several key advantages: (i) lightweight with low computing overhead due to single-turn retrieval; (ii) easy implementation and compatibility with any LVLM; and (iii) significant, consistent performance gains across long video understanding benchmarks, including Video-MME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench. Notably, our model demonstrates superior performance over proprietary models like Gemini-1.5-Pro and GPT-4o when utilized with a 72B model.

paragraphs: Long videos can exceed the context that a video-language model handles effectively. Video-RAG supplies additional information through retrieved text, offering a training-free approach to this problem. It aims to improve comprehension without the extensive data and GPU resources associated with long-context fine-tuning or reliance on proprietary agent models.

Open-source tools extract information from the video’s audio, visible text, and detected objects. The pipeline supplies visually aligned auxiliary text alongside video frames and the user’s query to an existing model. Single-turn retrieval keeps computing overhead low, and the authors describe the design as compatible with any large video-language model. The added text helps connect modalities while providing information beyond the visual input.

The authors report consistent gains on Video-MME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench. When paired with a 72-billion-parameter model, Video-RAG surpasses Gemini-1.5-Pro and GPT-4o in the reported comparisons. That model-size condition is part of the finding. The broader contribution is a plug-in retrieval pipeline that improves long-video understanding without training the underlying video-language model.
summary.tldr: Video-RAG improves long-video comprehension without training by retrieving auxiliary text from audio, visible text, and object detections.

title: Video-RAG: Visually-aligned Retrieval-Augmented Long Video Comprehension

abstract: State-space models (SSMs) have recently emerged as a compelling alternative to Transformers for sequence modeling tasks. This paper presents a theoretical generalization analysis of selective SSMs, the core architectural component behind the Mamba model. We derive a novel covering number-based generalization bound for selective SSMs, building upon recent theoretical advances in the analysis of Transformer models. Using this result, we analyze how the spectral abscissa of the continuous-time state matrix influences the model’s stability during training and its ability to generalize across sequence lengths. We empirically validate our findings on a synthetic majority task, the IMDb sentiment classification benchmark, and the ListOps task, demonstrating how our theoretical insights translate into practical model behavior.
