paragraphs: Selective state-space models form the central architectural component of Mamba and offer an alternative to Transformers for sequence modeling. This paper develops a theoretical account of their generalization behavior, connecting analysis of this architecture to recent advances in understanding Transformer models.

The main result is a generalization bound based on covering numbers. The authors use that bound to study how a property of the continuous-time state matrix, its spectral abscissa, affects training stability and generalization across sequence lengths. This makes the internal state dynamics central to the analysis of whether behavior learned during training carries over to other sequence lengths.

The theoretical findings are examined empirically on a synthetic majority task, IMDb sentiment classification, and ListOps. These experiments demonstrate how the insights correspond to practical model behavior across the tested settings. The contribution therefore combines a mathematical bound with an architectural interpretation and empirical checks. It provides a way to reason about selective state-space models through their dynamics, while drawing on tools developed for attention-based architectures.
summary.tldr: A new generalization bound connects selective state-space model dynamics to training stability and generalization across sequence lengths.

title: Generalization Error Analysis for Selective State-Space Models Through the Lens of Attention

abstract: We develop new stochastic optimization methods that are applicable to a wide range of structured regularizations. Basically our methods are combinations of basic stochastic optimization techniques and Alternating Direction Multiplier Method (ADMM). ADMM is a general framework for optimizing a composite function, and has a wide range of applications. We propose two types of online variants of ADMM, which correspond to online proximal gradient descent and regularized dual averaging respectively. The proposed algorithms are computationally efficient and easy to implement. Our methods yield O(1/\sqrtT) convergence of the expected risk. Moreover, the online proximal gradient descent type method yields O(\log(T)/T) convergence for a strongly convex loss. Numerical experiments show effectiveness of our methods in learning tasks with structured sparsity such as overlapped group lasso.
originalAbstract: We develop new stochastic optimization methods that are applicable to a wide range of structured regularizations. Basically our methods are combinations of basic stochastic optimization techniques and Alternating Direction Multiplier Method (ADMM). ADMM is a general framework for optimizing a composite function, and has a wide range of applications. We propose two types of online variants of ADMM, which correspond to online proximal gradient descent and regularized dual averaging respectively. The proposed algorithms are computationally efficient and easy to implement. Our methods yield O(1/\sqrtT) convergence of the expected risk. Moreover, the online proximal gradient descent type method yields O(\log(T)/T) convergence for a strongly convex loss. Numerical experiments show effectiveness of our methods in learning tasks with structured sparsity such as overlapped group lasso.

paragraphs: Structured regularization encourages patterns in a learned model, rather than treating every parameter independently. Such objectives can combine components that are awkward to optimize together. This paper develops stochastic optimization methods by combining familiar online learning techniques with the Alternating Direction Multiplier Method, a framework for optimizing composite functions.

The authors propose two online ADMM variants. One corresponds to proximal gradient descent, and the other to regularized dual averaging. Both are described as computationally efficient and straightforward to implement. Their purpose is to bring ADMM's treatment of composite structure into an online optimization setting while retaining theoretical control over learning performance.

Both methods achieve an expected-risk convergence rate of O(1/√T). For a strongly convex loss, the proximal-gradient variant has the faster rate O(log(T)/T). That stronger conclusion belongs to that method and assumption specifically. Numerical experiments demonstrate effectiveness on learning problems with structured sparsity, including overlapping group lasso, connecting the optimization framework to models whose parameter groups can overlap.
summary.tldr: Two online ADMM methods support structured regularization with convergence guarantees, including a faster rate for one variant under strong convexity.

title: Dual Averaging and Proximal Gradient Descent for Online Alternating Direction Multiplier Method

abstract: Automatic image annotation is a difficult and highly relevant machine learning task. Recent advances have significantly improved the state-of-the-art in retrieval accuracy with algorithms based on nearest neighbor classification in carefully learned metric spaces. But this comes at a price of increased computational complexity during training and testing. We propose FastTag, a novel algorithm that achieves comparable results with two simple linear mappings that are co-regularized in a joint convex loss function. The loss function can be efficiently optimized in closed form updates, which allows us to incorporate a large number of image descriptors cheaply. On several standard real-world benchmark data sets, we demonstrate that FastTag matches the current state-of-the-art in tagging quality, yet reduces the training and testing times by several orders of magnitude and has lower asymptotic complexity.

Efficient closed-form updates make optimization inexpensive and allow the method to incorporate many image descriptors at relatively low cost.

The finding supports a substantial efficiency improvement in the evaluated tasks: jointly trained linear mappings can provide competitive tags without the computational expense associated with the compared methods.
summary.tldr: FastTag uses two jointly trained linear mappings to match benchmark tagging quality while greatly reducing training and prediction time.

title: Fast Image Tagging

abstract: Coco (""cooperative/competitive"") values are a solution concept for two-player normal-form games with transferable utility, when binding agreements and side payments between players are possible. In this paper, we show that coco values can also be defined for stochastic games and can be learned using a simple variant of Q-learning that is provably convergent. We provide a set of examples showing how the strategies learned by the Coco-Q algorithm relate to those learned by existing multiagent Q-learning algorithms.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning in games where two players can make binding agreements and transfer utility through side payments. These capabilities shape the problem: players can negotiate an arrangement and redistribute its benefits. The starting point is the cooperative/competitive, or coco, value, a solution concept previously defined for two-player normal-form games with transferable utility.

The authors extend coco values to stochastic games, bringing this solution concept into a setting with ongoing interaction. They then introduce Coco-Q, a simple modification of Q-learning for learning those values. The algorithm is proved convergent, giving the learning procedure theoretical support alongside the extension of the game-theoretic concept.

Examples compare the strategies produced by Coco-Q with those learned by existing multiagent Q-learning methods. These comparisons illustrate how allowing agreements and payments changes the strategies that learning can produce. The contribution therefore depends explicitly on a setting where commitments and transfers are possible; those capabilities are part of the modeled interaction.
summary.tldr: Coco-Q extends cooperative/competitive values to stochastic games and learns them with a provably convergent Q-learning variant.

title: Coco-Q: Learning in Stochastic Games with Side Payments

abstract: The goal of the scene labeling task is to assign a class label to each pixel in an image. To ensure a good visual coherence and a high class accuracy, it is essential for a model to capture long range pixel) label dependencies in images. In a feed-forward architecture, this can be achieved simply by considering a sufficiently large input context patch, around each pixel to be labeled. We propose an approach that consists of a recurrent convolutional neural network which allows us to consider a large input context while limiting the capacity of the model. Contrary to most standard approaches, our method does not rely on any segmentation technique nor any task-specific features. The system is trained in an end-to-end manner over raw pixels, and models complex spatial dependencies with low inference cost. As the context size increases with the built-in recurrence, the system identifies and corrects its own errors. Our approach yields state-of-the-art performance on both the Stanford Background Dataset and the SIFT Flow Dataset, while remaining very fast at test time.

A large surrounding image patch can provide the necessary context, but the paper seeks to capture long-range dependencies while limiting the model’s capacity.

The proposed recurrent convolutional network expands the context it considers through recurrence. As that context grows, the system identifies and corrects its own errors. It learns directly from raw pixels in an end-to-end procedure and does not require a separate segmentation technique or task-specific features. Recurrence therefore supplies a mechanism for incorporating wider spatial information within the learned system.

These findings connect the architectural design to both labeling quality and inference cost. The contribution demonstrates that modeling complex spatial dependencies through recurrence can support accurate, visually coherent scene labeling without making inference expensive in the reported evaluations.
summary.tldr: A recurrent convolutional network expands spatial context to refine pixel labels while maintaining fast inference.

title: Recurrent Convolutional Neural Networks for Scene Labeling

abstract: We study the problem of selecting K arms with the highest expected rewards in a stochastic N-armed bandit game. Instead of using existing evaluation metrics (e.g., misidentification probability or the metric in EXPLORE-K), we propose to use the aggregate regret, which is defined as the gap between the average reward of the optimal solution and that of our solution. Besides being a natural metric by itself, we argue that in many applications, such as our motivating example from crowdsourcing, the aggregate regret bound is more suitable. We propose a new PAC algorithm, which, with probability at least 1-δ, identifies a set of K arms with regret at most ε. We provide the sample complexity bound of our algorithm. To complement, we establish the lower bound and show that the sample complexity of our algorithm matches the lower bound. Finally, we report experimental results on both synthetic and real data sets, which demonstrates the superior performance of the proposed algorithm.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to select K high-reward options from N stochastic bandit arms. It evaluates a selected set through aggregate regret: the difference between its average expected reward and that of the optimal set. This focuses attention on the quality of the selected group, a criterion motivated in part by crowdsourcing.

The authors propose a probably approximately correct algorithm. With probability at least 1−δ, it returns K arms whose aggregate regret is at most ε. The guarantee therefore allows a controlled reward shortfall and a controlled probability of failure, expressing the selection goal in terms of the chosen performance measure.

They establish a sample-complexity upper bound and a matching lower bound, showing optimal sample requirements under the formulation studied. Experiments on synthetic and real data report superior performance for the proposed algorithm. The contribution combines a group-level measure of selection quality, a high-probability guarantee, and evidence that the resulting procedure is useful beyond its theoretical analysis.
summary.tldr: The paper gives a sample-optimal PAC algorithm for selecting K bandit arms whose average expected reward is close to optimal.

title: Optimal PAC Multiple Arm Identification with Applications to Crowdsourcing

abstract: We study a novel spline-like basis, which we name the \it falling factorial basis, bearing many similarities to the classic truncated power basis. The advantage of the falling factorial basis is that it enables rapid, linear-time computations in basis matrix multiplication and basis matrix inversion. The falling factorial functions are not actually splines, but are close enough to splines that they provably retain some of the favorable properties of the latter functions. We examine their application in two problems: trend filtering over arbitrary input points, and a higher-order variant of the two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test.

paragraphs: A basis provides building blocks for representing functions, and the choice of those blocks affects both statistical behavior and computational cost. This paper introduces the falling factorial basis, a spline-like construction with similarities to the classical truncated power basis. The goal is to combine useful function properties with faster calculations.

Its main computational advantage is that multiplication by the basis matrix and basis-matrix inversion can be performed in linear time. The functions are not themselves splines. However, the authors prove that they are sufficiently close to splines to retain some of their favorable properties, giving a theoretical basis for using the new construction.

The paper examines two applications: trend filtering at arbitrary input points and a higher-order version of the two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test. These connect the same representation to function estimation and distribution comparison. The contribution is a basis whose computational structure supports efficient operations while preserving selected properties associated with spline-based methods.
summary.tldr: The falling factorial basis enables linear-time matrix operations while retaining some favorable spline properties for estimation and testing.

title: The Falling Factorial Basis and Its Statistical Applications

abstract: Understanding the geometry of neural network loss surfaces is important for the development of improved optimization algorithms and for building a theoretical understanding of why deep learning works. In this paper, we study the geometry in terms of the distribution of eigenvalues of the Hessian matrix at critical points of varying energy. We introduce an analytical framework and a set of tools from random matrix theory that allow us to compute an approximation of this distribution under a set of simplifying assumptions. The shape of the spectrum depends strongly on the energy and another key parameter, $\phi$, which measures the ratio of parameters to data points. Our analysis predicts and numerical simulations support that for critical points of small index, the number of negative eigenvalues scales like the 3/2 power of the energy. We leave as an open problem an explanation for our observation that, in the context of a certain memorization task, the energy of minimizers is well-approximated by the function $1/2(1-\phi)^2$.

paragraphs: This paper studies the geometry of neural network training objectives through the Hessian matrix at critical points. Its eigenvalues describe local curvature, including directions associated with negative curvature. The authors investigate how the distribution of these eigenvalues changes with the energy, or loss level, of the critical point.

They introduce a random-matrix-theory framework that approximates this distribution under simplifying assumptions. The predicted spectrum depends strongly on both energy and phi, the ratio of network parameters to data points. This links local loss-surface geometry to the relative size of the model and dataset within the proposed analytical framework.

For critical points with few negative eigenvalues, the analysis predicts that their number scales with energy to the three-halves power; numerical simulations support that prediction. The authors also observe that minimizer energy in a particular memorization task is approximated by one-half times the square of one minus phi. They explicitly leave an explanation of this latter observation open, distinguishing the supported scaling prediction from an unexplained empirical relationship.
summary.tldr: A random-matrix framework approximates neural loss-surface curvature and predicts an energy-dependent scaling of negative Hessian eigenvalues.

title: Geometry of Neural Network Loss Surfaces via Random Matrix Theory

abstract: Probabilistic models analyze data by relying on a set of assumptions. Data that exhibit deviations from these assumptions can undermine inference and prediction quality. Robust models offer protection against mismatch between a model’s assumptions and reality. We propose a way to systematically detect and mitigate mismatch of a large class of probabilistic models. The idea is to raise the likelihood of each observation to a weight and then to infer both the latent variables and the weights from data. Inferring the weights allows a model to identify observations that match its assumptions and down-weight others. This enables robust inference and improves predictive accuracy. We study four different forms of mismatch with reality, ranging from missing latent groups to structure misspecification. A Poisson factorization analysis of the Movielens 1M dataset shows the benefits of this approach in a practical scenario.

paragraphs: Probabilistic models depend on assumptions about how observations arise. When real data depart from those assumptions, inference and prediction can deteriorate. This paper proposes a general way to detect and reduce such mismatch across a broad class of models by learning how strongly individual observations should influence the analysis.

The method raises each observation's likelihood contribution to a weight and infers these weights alongside the model's latent variables. Observations that fit the assumptions can retain influence, while others are down-weighted. This makes the treatment of mismatched observations part of Bayesian inference, allowing the model to adjust their contributions based on the data.

The authors investigate four forms of mismatch, including missing latent groups and incorrectly specified structure. They report robust inference and improved predictive accuracy, with a Poisson factorization analysis of Movielens 1M illustrating practical benefits. The contribution is a systematic reweighting mechanism that can reduce the effect of assumption violations without requiring each mismatch to be handled by a separate model redesign.
summary.tldr: Bayesian data reweighting learns which observations to down-weight, improving robustness when probabilistic modeling assumptions mismatch the data.

title: Robust Probabilistic Modeling with Bayesian Data Reweighting

abstract: The Gaussian mechanism is an essential building block used in multitude of differentially private data analysis algorithms. In this paper we revisit the Gaussian mechanism and show that the original analysis has several important limitations. Our analysis reveals that the variance formula for the original mechanism is far from tight in the high privacy regime ($\varepsilon \to 0$) and it cannot be extended to the low privacy regime ($\varepsilon \to \infty$). We address these limitations by developing an optimal Gaussian mechanism whose variance is calibrated directly using the Gaussian cumulative density function instead of a tail bound approximation. We also propose to equip the Gaussian mechanism with a post-processing step based on adaptive estimation techniques by leveraging that the distribution of the perturbation is known. Our experiments show that analytical calibration removes at least a third of the variance of the noise compared to the classical Gaussian mechanism, and that denoising dramatically improves the accuracy of the Gaussian mechanism in the high-dimensional regime.

paragraphs: The Gaussian mechanism supports differentially private analysis by adding Gaussian noise. This paper revisits how much noise it requires. The authors show that the classical variance formula is loose when privacy is strong, as epsilon approaches zero, and that its analysis cannot extend to the low-privacy regime where epsilon becomes arbitrarily large.

They develop an optimal calibration of the Gaussian mechanism using the Gaussian cumulative distribution function directly. This avoids the tail-bound approximation used in the earlier analysis. They also add a denoising step based on adaptive estimation, taking advantage of the fact that the distribution of the added perturbation is known.

Denoising produces substantial accuracy improvements in high-dimensional settings. The two changes address different stages of the same process: calibration determines the perturbation needed for privacy, while post-processing uses knowledge of that perturbation to improve the accuracy of the released result.
summary.tldr: Direct Gaussian calibration reduces unnecessary privacy noise, while adaptive denoising improves accuracy, especially in high dimensions.

title: Improving the Gaussian Mechanism for Differential Privacy: Analytical Calibration and Optimal Denoising

abstract: Two methods are proposed for high-dimensional shape-constrained regression and classification. These methods reshape pre-trained prediction rules to satisfy shape constraints like monotonicity and convexity. The first method can be applied to any pre-trained prediction rule, while the second method deals specifically with random forests. In both cases, efficient algorithms are developed for computing the estimators, and experiments are performed to demonstrate their performance on four datasets. We find that reshaping methods enforce shape constraints without compromising predictive accuracy.

These methods reshape pre-trained prediction rules to satisfy shape constraints like monotonicity and convexity. We find that reshaping methods enforce shape constraints without compromising predictive accuracy.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to make an already trained prediction rule satisfy shape constraints in high-dimensional regression and classification. Examples include monotonicity and convexity. These requirements concern the pattern of predictions as inputs change, so satisfying them is a different objective from obtaining accurate predictions on individual examples.

The authors propose two reshaping methods. One can be applied to any pretrained prediction rule, while the other is designed specifically for random forests. Both begin with an existing predictor and reshape its output behavior to meet the desired constraints. The paper also develops efficient algorithms for computing the resulting estimators, making the reshaping step a concrete computational procedure.

Experiments on four datasets demonstrate the methods’ performance. In these evaluations, the reshaped predictors enforce the constraints without compromising predictive accuracy. This provides evidence that shape requirements and predictive performance can be compatible in the studied settings. The broader contribution is a way to add such requirements after training, with both a general-purpose approach and a forest-specific one.
summary.tldr: Two methods reshape pretrained predictors to satisfy shape constraints while preserving accuracy in the reported experiments.

title: Prediction Rule Reshaping

abstract: Deep reinforcement learning algorithms require large amounts of experience to learn an individual task. While meta-reinforcement learning (meta-RL) algorithms can enable agents to learn new skills from small amounts of experience, several major challenges preclude their practicality. Current methods rely heavily on on-policy experience, limiting their sample efficiency. They also lack mechanisms to reason about task uncertainty when adapting to new tasks, limiting their effectiveness on sparse reward problems. In this paper, we address these challenges by developing an off-policy meta-RL algorithm that disentangles task inference and control. In our approach, we perform online probabilistic filtering of latent task variables to infer how to solve a new task from small amounts of experience. This probabilistic interpretation enables posterior sampling for structured and efficient exploration. We demonstrate how to integrate these task variables with off-policy RL algorithms to achieve both meta-training and adaptation efficiency. Our method outperforms prior algorithms in sample efficiency by 20-100X as well as in asymptotic performance on several meta-RL benchmarks.

paragraphs: Meta-reinforcement learning aims to help an agent acquire new skills from little experience. The paper identifies two obstacles: dependence on experience collected under the current policy, and inadequate reasoning about uncertainty over a new task. The first limits reuse of data; the second makes adaptation difficult when useful rewards are sparse.

The proposed algorithm separates inference about the task from control of the agent. It represents task information through latent variables and updates a probability distribution over them as experience arrives. This online probabilistic filtering maintains uncertainty about what task the agent faces. Sampling from the resulting posterior supports structured exploration guided by possible task explanations.

The authors integrate these task variables with off-policy reinforcement learning, allowing previously collected experience to contribute to learning. They report improved efficiency during both meta-training and adaptation. Across several meta-learning benchmarks, the method achieves 20–100 times better sample efficiency than prior algorithms and better asymptotic performance. These results support combining reusable experience with explicit task uncertainty as a practical route to faster adaptation.
summary.tldr: Separating probabilistic task inference from off-policy control improves meta-reinforcement learning sample efficiency by 20–100 times on the reported benchmarks.

title: Efficient Off-Policy Meta-Reinforcement Learning via Probabilistic Context Variables

abstract: In this paper, we study Combinatorial Semi-Bandits (CSB) that is an extension of classic Multi-Armed Bandits (MAB) under Differential Privacy (DP) and stronger Local Differential Privacy (LDP) setting. Since the server receives more information from users in CSB, it usually causes additional dependence on the dimension of data, which is a notorious side-effect for privacy preserving learning. However for CSB under two common smoothness assumptions, we show it is possible to remove this side-effect. In detail, for $B_{\infty}$-bounded smooth CSB under either $\varepsilon$-LDP or $\varepsilon$-DP, we prove the optimal regret bound is $\Theta(\frac{mB^2_{\infty}\ln T } {\Delta\varepsilon^2})$ or $\tilde{\Theta}(\frac{mB^2_{\infty}\ln T} { \Delta\varepsilon})$ respectively, where $T$ is time period, $\Delta$ is the gap of rewards and $m$ is the number of base arms, by proposing novel algorithms and matching lower bounds. For $B_1$-bounded smooth CSB under $\varepsilon$-DP, we also prove the optimal regret bound is $\tilde{\Theta}(\frac{mKB^2_1\ln T} {\Delta\varepsilon})$ with both upper bound and lower bound, where $K$ is the maximum number of feedback in each round. All above results nearly match corresponding non-private optimal rates, which imply there is no additional price for (locally) differentially private CSB in above common settings.

paragraphs: Combinatorial semi-bandits extend classic bandit learning to decisions involving multiple base arms and richer feedback. Protecting that feedback with differential privacy can introduce an additional dependence on data dimension. This paper asks whether that extra dimensional burden is unavoidable under central differential privacy and the stronger local differential privacy setting.

Under two common smoothness assumptions, the authors show how to avoid the additional dimension-related penalty. For B-infinity-bounded smooth problems, they give algorithms and matching lower bounds for both privacy settings. The local-private rate depends inversely on the square of the privacy parameter, whereas the central-private rate depends inversely on the parameter itself, up to the stated logarithmic qualifications.

For B-one-bounded smooth problems under central privacy, the optimal rate also includes the maximum amount of feedback per round. Across these cases, the bounds nearly match the corresponding non-private optimal rates in the sense described by the paper. The result concerns removing an extra dimensional cost under the specified assumptions; the bounds still explicitly capture dependence on privacy strength.
summary.tldr: Under specified smoothness assumptions, private combinatorial semi-bandits achieve optimal regret bounds without an additional dimension-related privacy penalty.

title: (Locally) Differentially Private Combinatorial Semi-Bandits

abstract: We propose an efficient inference method for switching nonlinear dynamical systems. The key idea is to learn an inference network which can be used as a proposal distribution for the continuous latent variables, while performing exact marginalization of the discrete latent variables. This allows us to use the reparameterization trick, and apply end-to-end training with stochastic gradient descent. We show that the proposed method can successfully segment time series data, including videos and 3D human pose, into meaningful “regimes” by using the piece-wise nonlinear dynamics.
originalAbstract: We propose an efficient inference method for switching nonlinear dynamical systems. The key idea is to learn an inference network which can be used as a proposal distribution for the continuous latent variables, while performing exact marginalization of the discrete latent variables. This allows us to use the reparameterization trick, and apply end-to-end training with stochastic gradient descent. We show that the proposed method can successfully segment time series data, including videos and 3D human pose, into meaningful “regimes” by using the piece-wise nonlinear dynamics.

paragraphs: Switching nonlinear dynamical systems describe sequences whose behavior changes between regimes, with nonlinear dynamics operating within each regime. Inference must account for both continuous hidden variables and discrete variables describing those switches. This paper proposes an efficient way to handle those two kinds of uncertainty together when learning from time series.

The method learns an inference network that supplies a proposal distribution for the continuous latent variables. It handles the discrete latent variables through exact marginalization, summing over their possibilities rather than treating them in the same way as the continuous variables. This combination enables the reparameterization trick and end-to-end training using stochastic gradient descent.

The authors show that the resulting method can divide time series into meaningful regimes, including sequences represented as videos and three-dimensional human poses. These segments are obtained using piecewise nonlinear dynamics. The contribution connects an inference strategy to an interpretable outcome: identifying portions of a sequence governed by different patterns of change while training the overall system jointly.
summary.tldr: A learned proposal for continuous states combined with exact treatment of discrete states enables joint training and meaningful time-series segmentation.

title: Collapsed Amortized Variational Inference for Switching Nonlinear Dynamical Systems

abstract: Submodular function minimization is well studied, and existing algorithms solve it exactly or up to arbitrary accuracy. However, in many applications, such as structured sparse learning or batch Bayesian optimization, the objective function is not exactly submodular, but close. In this case, no theoretical guarantees exist. Indeed, submodular minimization algorithms rely on intricate connections between submodularity and convexity. We show how these relations can be extended to obtain approximation guarantees for minimizing non-submodular functions, characterized by how close the function is to submodular. We also extend this result to noisy function evaluations. Our approximation results are the first for minimizing non-submodular functions, and are optimal, as established by our matching lower bound.

paragraphs: Submodular function minimization has strong algorithmic guarantees, but objectives in applications may only be close to submodular. The paper points to structured sparse learning and batch Bayesian optimization as examples motivating this gap. Existing minimization methods depend on close connections between submodularity and convexity, so their guarantees do not automatically cover these nearby objectives.

The authors extend those connections to obtain approximation guarantees for minimizing non-submodular functions. The guarantees are characterized by how close the objective is to being submodular. This makes the departure from the ideal mathematical property part of the analysis, providing a way to describe solution quality when exact submodularity is unavailable.

The results also extend to situations where function evaluations are noisy. A matching lower bound establishes optimality of the approximation results within the studied formulation. The contribution therefore supplies both a positive guarantee and a corresponding limit, clarifying what approximation quality can be achieved for the characterized non-submodular minimization problems.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes optimal approximation guarantees for non-submodular minimization based on closeness to submodularity, including noisy evaluations.

title: Optimal approximation for unconstrained non-submodular minimization

abstract: Back-door attack poses a severe threat to deep learning systems. It injects hidden malicious behaviors to a model such that any input stamped with a special pattern can trigger such behaviors. Detecting back-door is hence of pressing need. Many existing defense techniques use optimization to generate the smallest input pattern that forces the model to misclassify a set of benign inputs injected with the pattern to a target label. However, the complexity is quadratic to the number of class labels such that they can hardly handle models with many classes. Inspired by Multi-Arm Bandit in Reinforcement Learning, we propose a K-Arm optimization method for backdoor detection. By iteratively and stochastically selecting the most promising labels for optimization with the guidance of an objective function, we substantially reduce the complexity, allowing to handle models with many classes. Moreover, by iteratively refining the selection of labels to optimize, it substantially mitigates the uncertainty in choosing the right labels, improving detection accuracy. At the time of submission, the evaluation of our method on over 4000 models in the IARPA TrojAI competition from round 1 to the latest round 4 achieves top performance on the leaderboard. Our technique also supersedes five state-of-the-art techniques in terms of accuracy and the scanning time needed. The code of our work is available at https://github.com/PurduePAML/K-ARM_Backdoor_Optimization

paragraphs: A backdoored model behaves maliciously when an input contains a particular trigger pattern. One detection strategy searches for small patterns that make otherwise benign inputs receive a chosen target label. The paper addresses the cost of this search: existing optimization-based defenses can require work that grows quadratically with the number of classes.

The proposed K-Arm method borrows the idea of allocating effort among competing options from multi-arm bandits. It repeatedly and stochastically chooses promising labels for further optimization, guided by an objective function. As the search proceeds, it revises those choices. This concentrates computation while reducing uncertainty about which labels deserve attention, supporting both faster scanning and more accurate detection.

The authors evaluate the method on more than 4,000 models from rounds one through four of the IARPA TrojAI competition. They report top leaderboard performance at submission time and better accuracy and scanning time than five compared techniques. These findings support adaptive search as a practical way to scan models with many classes.
summary.tldr: K-Arm backdoor scanning adaptively concentrates trigger-search effort on promising labels, improving detection accuracy and scanning time in the reported evaluations.

title: Backdoor Scanning for Deep Neural Networks through K-Arm Optimization

abstract: Fisher’s Linear Discriminant Analysis (FLDA) is a statistical analysis method that linearly embeds data points to a lower dimensional space to maximize a discrimination criterion such that the variance between classes is maximized while the variance within classes is minimized. We introduce a natural extension of FLDA that employs neural networks, called Neural Fisher Discriminant Analysis (NFDA). This method finds the optimal two-layer neural network that embeds data points to optimize the same discrimination criterion. We use tools from convex optimization to transform the optimal neural network embedding problem into a convex problem. The resulting problem is easy to interpret and solve to global optimality. We evaluate the method’s performance on synthetic and real datasets.

We evaluate the method’s performance on synthetic and real datasets.

paragraphs: Fisher’s Linear Discriminant Analysis seeks a lower-dimensional representation that separates classes while keeping examples within each class close together. This paper extends that discrimination objective to a neural network embedding. The proposed Neural Fisher Discriminant Analysis retains the original criterion while allowing a two-layer network to perform the mapping.

The central technical step is to transform the optimal neural embedding problem into a convex optimization problem. The authors use tools from convex optimization to obtain a formulation that can be interpreted and solved to global optimality. Thus, the contribution concerns both the representation objective and a way to optimize the specified network embedding.

Global optimality here refers to the paper’s discrimination criterion for its two-layer embedding problem. It gives a precise meaning to an optimal representation within that formulation. The authors evaluate the method on synthetic and real datasets, although the abstract does not state a comparative performance outcome. The main stated result is the connection between neural discriminant embeddings and a tractable convex formulation.
summary.tldr: Neural Fisher Discriminant Analysis reformulates optimal two-layer discriminant embeddings as a convex problem solvable to global optimality.

title: Neural Fisher Discriminant Analysis: Optimal Neural Network Embeddings in Polynomial Time

abstract: We consider the regret minimization task in a dueling bandits problem with context information. In every round of the sequential decision problem, the learner makes a context-dependent selection of two choice alternatives (arms) to be compared with each other and receives feedback in the form of noisy preference information. We assume that the feedback process is determined by a linear stochastic transitivity model with contextualized utilities (CoLST), and the learner’s task is to include the best arm (with highest latent context-dependent utility) in the duel. We propose a computationally efficient algorithm, \Algo{CoLSTIM}, which makes its choice based on imitating the feedback process using perturbed context-dependent utility estimates of the underlying CoLST model. If each arm is associated with a $d$-dimensional feature vector, we show that \Algo{CoLSTIM} achieves a regret of order $\tilde O( \sqrt{dT})$ after $T$ learning rounds. Additionally, we also establish the optimality of \Algo{CoLSTIM} by showing a lower bound for the weak regret that refines the existing average regret analysis. Our experiments demonstrate its superiority over state-of-art algorithms for special cases of CoLST models.

paragraphs: In contextual dueling bandits, a learner selects two alternatives each round and observes a noisy preference between them. This paper assumes that feedback follows a linear stochastic transitivity model with context-dependent utilities, called CoLST. The learner’s objective is to include the alternative with the highest latent utility in the selected pair.

The proposed CoLSTIM algorithm imitates the feedback process using perturbed estimates of the alternatives’ contextual utilities. This provides a computationally efficient selection rule within the assumed model. When each alternative has a d-dimensional feature vector, the authors prove regret growing on the order of √(dT), up to logarithmic factors, over T rounds.

The paper also establishes a lower bound for weak regret that refines existing average-regret analysis and supports the algorithm’s optimality claim. This matters because the objective concerns whether the best alternative appears in the duel. Experiments show better performance than state-of-the-art algorithms for special cases of CoLST models. The theoretical and empirical conclusions are therefore anchored to the specified preference-model setting.
summary.tldr: CoLSTIM efficiently chooses contextual duels using perturbed utility estimates and achieves near-optimal regret under the CoLST feedback model.

title: Stochastic Contextual Dueling Bandits under Linear Stochastic Transitivity Models

abstract: It is well-known that deep learning models are vulnerable to adversarial examples. Existing studies of adversarial training have made great progress against this challenge. As a typical trait, they often assume that the class distribution is overall balanced. However, long-tail datasets are ubiquitous in a wide spectrum of applications, where the amount of head class instances is significantly larger than the tail classes. Under such a scenario, AUC is a much more reasonable metric than accuracy since it is insensitive toward class distribution. Motivated by this, we present an early trial to explore adversarial training methods to optimize AUC. The main challenge lies in that the positive and negative examples are tightly coupled in the objective function. As a direct result, one cannot generate adversarial examples without a full scan of the dataset. To address this issue, based on a concavity regularization scheme, we reformulate the AUC optimization problem as a saddle point problem, where the objective becomes an instance-wise function. This leads to an end-to-end training protocol. Furthermore, we provide a convergence guarantee of the proposed training algorithm. Our analysis differs from the existing studies since the algorithm is asked to generate adversarial examples by calculating the gradient of a min-max problem. Finally, the extensive experimental results show the performance and robustness of our algorithm in three long-tail datasets.

paragraphs: Adversarial training seeks to protect models against inputs deliberately altered to cause mistakes. This paper examines that problem when classes are highly uneven: common classes have many examples, while rare classes have few. The authors focus on AUC because its insensitivity to class distribution makes it a more appropriate objective than accuracy for their long-tail setting.

Directly optimizing adversarial AUC creates a computational obstacle. Positive and negative examples are coupled in the objective, so generating adversarial examples would require scanning the complete dataset. AdAUC uses concavity regularization to reformulate the objective as a saddle point problem whose terms operate on individual examples. This reformulation enables an end-to-end training procedure.

The paper also establishes a convergence guarantee for the proposed algorithm. Its analysis addresses the extra complication of producing adversarial examples through gradients of a min-max problem. Experiments on three long-tail datasets provide evidence for the method’s performance and robustness, supporting adversarial AUC optimization as a practical direction for imbalanced learning.
summary.tldr: AdAUC reformulates adversarial AUC optimization to enable end-to-end robust training on datasets with highly imbalanced classes.

title: AdAUC: End-to-end Adversarial AUC Optimization Against Long-tail Problems

abstract: A trained neural network can be interpreted as a structural causal model (SCM) that provides the effect of changing input variables on the model’s output. However, if training data contains both causal and correlational relationships, a model that optimizes prediction accuracy may not necessarily learn the true causal relationships between input and output variables. On the other hand, expert users often have prior knowledge of the causal relationship between certain input variables and output from domain knowledge. Therefore, we propose a regularization method that aligns the learned causal effects of a neural network with domain priors, including both direct and total causal effects. We show that this approach can generalize to different kinds of domain priors, including monotonicity of causal effect of an input variable on output or zero causal effect of a variable on output for purposes of fairness. Our experiments on twelve benchmark datasets show its utility in regularizing a neural network model to maintain desired causal effects, without compromising on accuracy. Importantly, we also show that a model thus trained is robust and gets improved accuracy on noisy inputs.

paragraphs: A neural network can be viewed as a structural causal model describing how changes to its inputs affect its output. However, training for prediction accuracy on data containing both causal and correlational relationships does not ensure that these learned effects match real causal relationships. The paper uses expert knowledge to guide those effects during training.

The proposed regularizer aligns a network’s learned causal effects with supplied domain priors. It accommodates both direct and total effects, as well as different forms of prior knowledge. Examples include requiring an effect to be monotonic or requiring a variable to have zero causal effect on the output for a fairness objective. This makes desired input-output behavior an explicit training consideration.

Experiments on twelve benchmark datasets show that the method can maintain the desired causal effects without sacrificing accuracy in those evaluations. The authors also report robustness and improved accuracy when inputs are noisy. The findings support regularization as a practical way to incorporate causal expertise into neural networks, with the desired behavior determined by the supplied priors.
summary.tldr: A causal-effect regularizer incorporates domain priors into neural networks while preserving accuracy and improving performance on noisy inputs in the reported experiments.

title: Matching Learned Causal Effects of Neural Networks with Domain Priors

abstract: The goal of community detection over graphs is to recover underlying labels/attributes of users (e.g., political affiliation) given the connectivity between users. There has been significant recent progress on understanding the fundamental limits of community detection when the graph is generated from a stochastic block model (SBM). Specifically, sharp information theoretic limits and efficient algorithms have been obtained for SBMs as a function of $p$ and $q$, which represent the intra-community and inter-community connection probabilities. In this paper, we study the community detection problem while preserving the privacy of the individual connections between the vertices. Focusing on the notion of $(\epsilon, \delta)$-edge differential privacy (DP), we seek to understand the fundamental tradeoffs between $(p, q)$, DP budget $(\epsilon, \delta)$, and computational efficiency for exact recovery of community labels. To this end, we present and analyze the associated information-theoretic tradeoffs for three differentially private community recovery mechanisms: a) stability based mechanism; b) sampling based mechanisms; and c) graph perturbation mechanisms. Our main findings are that stability and sampling based mechanisms lead to a superior tradeoff between $(p,q)$ and the privacy budget $(\epsilon, \delta)$; however this comes at the expense of higher computational complexity. On the other hand, albeit low complexity, graph perturbation mechanisms require the privacy budget $\epsilon$ to scale as $\Omega(\log(n))$ for exact recovery.

paragraphs: Community detection uses graph connections to infer which vertices belong to the same underlying group. This paper studies exact recovery of those groups when individual connections must remain private. Its setting is the stochastic block model, where within-community and between-community connection probabilities determine how clearly the groups are separated.

The privacy requirement is edge differential privacy, which concerns individual links in the graph. The authors analyze how the connection probabilities, privacy budget, and computational cost interact. They compare three types of private recovery mechanisms: methods based on stability, methods based on sampling, and methods that perturb the graph.

Stability and sampling mechanisms offer better tradeoffs between the graph’s connection probabilities and the privacy budget, but demand more computation. Graph perturbation has lower computational complexity, yet exact recovery requires its epsilon privacy budget to grow at least logarithmically with the number of vertices. The findings make computational efficiency part of the privacy–recovery tradeoff, rather than treating all private community-detection procedures as interchangeable.
summary.tldr: Private community recovery exposes a tradeoff between computational cost, graph structure, and the privacy budget needed for exact recovery.

title: Differentially Private Community Detection for Stochastic Block Models

abstract: 3D perception, especially point cloud classification, has achieved substantial progress. However, in real-world deployment, point cloud corruptions are inevitable due to the scene complexity, sensor inaccuracy, and processing imprecision. In this work, we aim to rigorously benchmark and analyze point cloud classification under corruptions. To conduct a systematic investigation, we first provide a taxonomy of common 3D corruptions and identify the atomic corruptions. Then, we perform a comprehensive evaluation on a wide range of representative point cloud models to understand their robustness and generalizability. Our benchmark results show that although point cloud classification performance improves over time, the state-of-the-art methods are on the verge of being less robust. Based on the obtained observations, we propose several effective techniques to enhance point cloud classifier robustness. We hope our comprehensive benchmark, in-depth analysis, and proposed techniques could spark future research in robust 3D perception.

paragraphs: Point cloud classification assigns categories to objects represented by collections of points in three-dimensional space. Although classification performance has advanced, deployed systems encounter corrupted inputs caused by complex scenes, inaccurate sensors, and imperfect processing. This paper asks how well representative point cloud models withstand those disruptions.

The authors first organize common three-dimensional corruptions into a taxonomy and identify atomic corruption types. They then use this structure to evaluate a broad range of models systematically. The taxonomy gives the investigation a consistent basis for comparing robustness and generalizability, rather than treating each corruption as an unrelated test case.

The benchmark suggests that improving classification performance over time has not brought matching gains in robustness: leading methods appear close to becoming less robust. Drawing on patterns in the evaluation, the authors propose several techniques that improve classifier robustness. The work makes corruption resilience an explicit dimension of progress in three-dimensional perception and supplies both an assessment framework and practical directions for improving it.
summary.tldr: A systematic corruption benchmark finds that advances in point cloud classification do not necessarily bring stronger robustness and proposes techniques to improve it.

title: Benchmarking and Analyzing Point Cloud Classification under Corruptions

abstract: We consider off-policy evaluation (OPE) in Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs), where the evaluation policy depends only on observable variables and the behavior policy depends on unobservable latent variables. Existing works either assume no unmeasured confounders, or focus on settings where both the observation and the state spaces are tabular. In this work, we first propose novel identification methods for OPE in POMDPs with latent confounders, by introducing bridge functions that link the target policy’s value and the observed data distribution. We next propose minimax estimation methods for learning these bridge functions, and construct three estimators based on these estimated bridge functions, corresponding to a value function-based estimator, a marginalized importance sampling estimator, and a doubly-robust estimator. Our proposal permits general function approximation and is thus applicable to settings with continuous or large observation/state spaces. The nonasymptotic and asymptotic properties of the proposed estimators are investigated in detail. A Python implementation of our proposal is available at https://github.com/jiaweihhuang/ Confounded-POMDP-Exp.

paragraphs: Evaluating a new decision policy from previously collected data becomes difficult when the original decisions depended on information that was never recorded. This paper studies that setting in partially observable Markov decision processes. The policy being evaluated uses observable variables, while the policy that generated the data can depend on hidden variables, creating latent confounding.

The authors introduce bridge functions that connect the target policy’s value to the distribution of observed data. These functions provide the basis for new identification methods: ways of expressing the evaluation target through available observations. The paper then develops minimax estimation methods to learn the bridges rather than requiring them to be known beforehand.

Using the learned bridges, the authors construct value-based, marginalized importance-sampling, and doubly robust estimators. Their framework permits general function approximation, extending its applicability to continuous or large observation and state spaces. They investigate both finite-sample and asymptotic properties, providing a statistical treatment of policy evaluation that explicitly accommodates hidden confounding in this partially observed setting.
summary.tldr: Learned bridge functions support off-policy evaluation with hidden confounders and large or continuous observation and state spaces.

title: A Minimax Learning Approach to Off-Policy Evaluation in Confounded Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes

abstract: Machine learning (ML) robustness and domain generalization are fundamentally correlated: they essentially concern data distribution shifts under adversarial and natural settings, respectively. On one hand, recent studies show that more robust (adversarially trained) models are more generalizable. On the other hand, there is a lack of theoretical understanding of their fundamental connections. In this paper, we explore the relationship between regularization and domain transferability considering different factors such as norm regularization and data augmentations (DA). We propose a general theoretical framework proving that factors involving the model function class regularization are sufficient conditions for relative domain transferability. Our analysis implies that “robustness" is neither necessary nor sufficient for transferability; rather, regularization is a more fundamental perspective for understanding domain transferability. We then discuss popular DA protocols (including adversarial training) and show when they can be viewed as the function class regularization under certain conditions and therefore improve generalization. We conduct extensive experiments to verify our theoretical findings and show several counterexamples where robustness and generalization are negatively correlated on different datasets.

paragraphs: Adversarial robustness and domain generalization both concern changing data distributions, but they address adversarial and natural changes, respectively. This paper asks whether improvements in one explain improvements in the other. It investigates that relationship through regularization, including restrictions on model functions and the effects of data augmentation.

The authors develop a theoretical framework in which factors involving function-class regularization provide sufficient conditions for relative domain transferability. Their analysis implies that robustness itself is neither necessary nor sufficient for transferability. This shifts attention toward how training constrains the functions a model can learn, giving a more fundamental explanation of when transfer improvements can arise.

The paper also examines when augmentation procedures, including adversarial training, can be interpreted as function-class regularization and consequently improve generalization. That connection holds under specified conditions, rather than for every augmentation procedure automatically. Experiments support the theoretical findings and include counterexamples where robustness and generalization are negatively correlated. These results challenge using robustness alone as evidence that a model will transfer better.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies regularization-based sufficient conditions for domain transferability and shows why adversarial robustness alone need not improve transfer.

title: Adversarially Robust Models may not Transfer Better: Sufficient Conditions for Domain Transferability from the View of Regularization

abstract: Recent advances in vision-language pre-training (VLP) have demonstrated impressive performance in a range of vision-language (VL) tasks. However, there exist several challenges for measuring the community’s progress in building general multi-modal intelligence. First, most of the downstream VL datasets are annotated using raw images that are already seen during pre-training, which may result in an overestimation of current VLP models’ generalization ability. Second, recent VLP work mainly focuses on absolute performance but overlooks the efficiency-performance trade-off, which is also an important indicator for measuring progress. To this end, we introduce the Vision-Language Understanding Evaluation (VLUE) benchmark, a multi-task multi-dimension benchmark for evaluating the generalization capabilities and the efficiency-performance trade-off (“Pareto SOTA”) of VLP models. We demonstrate that there is a sizable generalization gap for all VLP models when testing on out-of-distribution test sets annotated on images from a more diverse distribution that spreads across cultures. Moreover, we find that measuring the efficiency-performance trade-off of VLP models leads to complementary insights for several design choices of VLP. We release the VLUE benchmark to promote research on building vision-language models that generalize well to images unseen during pre-training and are practical in terms of efficiency-performance trade-off.

Such overlap may overstate how well the models generalize to unfamiliar images. The paper also identifies a second evaluation gap: focusing on absolute task performance can overlook the efficiency required to achieve it.

VLUE evaluates models across multiple tasks and dimensions, combining generalization testing with the efficiency-performance trade-off. Its out-of-distribution test sets use images from a more diverse distribution spanning cultures. The benchmark's Pareto perspective considers performance alongside efficiency, making resource trade-offs part of how model progress is assessed.

All evaluated vision-language pretraining models show a sizable generalization gap on the out-of-distribution tests. Assessing efficiency together with performance also provides complementary insights into model design choices. The benchmark therefore broadens the evidence used to judge progress: strong results on familiar image distributions are considered alongside transfer to diverse imagery and the practical efficiency of achieving those results.
summary.tldr: VLUE evaluates vision-language models on diverse unseen-image distributions and efficiency-performance trade-offs, revealing substantial generalization gaps.

title: VLUE: A Multi-Task Multi-Dimension Benchmark for Evaluating Vision-Language Pre-training

abstract: Deep learning methods are highly accurate, yet their opaque decision process prevents them from earning full human trust. Concept-based models aim to address this issue by learning tasks based on a set of human-understandable concepts. However, state-of-the-art concept-based models rely on high-dimensional concept embedding representations which lack a clear semantic meaning, thus questioning the interpretability of their decision process. To overcome this limitation, we propose the Deep Concept Reasoner (DCR), the first interpretable concept-based model that builds upon concept embeddings. In DCR, neural networks do not make task predictions directly, but they build syntactic rule structures using concept embeddings. DCR then executes these rules on meaningful concept truth degrees to provide a final interpretable and semantically-consistent prediction in a differentiable manner. Our experiments show that DCR: (i) improves up to +25% w.r.t. state-of-the-art interpretable concept-based models on challenging benchmarks (ii) discovers meaningful logic rules matching known ground truths even in the absence of concept supervision during training, and (iii), facilitates the generation of counterfactual examples providing the learnt rules as guidance.

paragraphs: Concept-based models seek to explain decisions through ideas that people can understand. Yet their internal concept embeddings can be high-dimensional vectors with unclear semantic meaning, weakening that promise. The Deep Concept Reasoner, or DCR, addresses this problem by separating the construction of reasoning rules from the execution of those rules on meaningful concept values.

In DCR, neural networks use concept embeddings to build syntactic rule structures instead of directly producing task predictions. The rules are then evaluated using concept truth degrees, yielding the final prediction. This process remains differentiable, allowing learning while preserving an interpretable reasoning structure. The distinction matters because the learned embeddings help construct an explanation whose execution uses semantically meaningful quantities.

The reported benefits therefore cover predictive performance, recovery of meaningful reasoning, and support for examining how a decision could change.
summary.tldr: DCR turns concept embeddings into explicit logical rules, combining interpretable predictions with improved benchmark performance and guided counterfactual generation.

title: Interpretable Neural-Symbolic Concept Reasoning

abstract: Understanding how convolutional neural networks (CNNs) can efficiently learn high-dimensional functions remains a fundamental challenge. A popular belief is that these models harness the local and hierarchical structure of natural data such as images. Yet, we lack a quantitative understanding of how such structure affects performance, e.g., the rate of decay of the generalisation error with the number of training samples. In this paper, we study infinitely-wide deep CNNs in the kernel regime. First, we show that the spectrum of the corresponding kernel inherits the hierarchical structure of the network, and we characterise its asymptotics. Then, we use this result together with generalisation bounds to prove that deep CNNs adapt to the spatial scale of the target function. In particular, we find that if the target function depends on low-dimensional subsets of adjacent input variables, then the decay of the error is controlled by the effective dimensionality of these subsets. Conversely, if the target function depends on the full set of input variables, then the error decay is controlled by the input dimension. We conclude by computing the generalisation error of a deep CNN trained on the output of another deep CNN with randomly-initialised parameters. Interestingly, we find that, despite their hierarchical structure, the functions generated by infinitely-wide deep CNNs are too rich to be efficiently learnable in high dimension.

paragraphs: Convolutional networks are often said to succeed because they match the local, hierarchical structure of data. This paper asks how that structure quantitatively affects learning as more training samples become available. It studies infinitely wide, deep convolutional networks in the kernel regime and characterizes the spectrum of their associated kernel.

The authors show that this spectrum reflects the network's hierarchy. The findings clarify that hierarchical architecture alone does not ensure efficient learning; the target's particular dependence on the inputs matters.
summary.tldr: Infinite-width convolutional networks benefit from local low-dimensional targets, but hierarchical structure alone does not ensure efficient high-dimensional learning.

title: What Can Be Learnt With Wide Convolutional Neural Networks?

abstract: We consider the problem of decentralized multi-agent reinforcement learning in Markov games. A fundamental question is whether there exist algorithms that, when run independently by all agents, lead to no-regret for each player, analogous to celebrated convergence results for no-regret learning in normal-form games. While recent work has shown that such algorithms exist for restricted settings (notably, when regret is defined with respect to deviations to Markov policies), the question of whether independent no-regret learning can be achieved in the standard Markov game framework was open. We provide a decisive negative resolution to this problem, both from a computational and statistical perspective. We show that: • Under the complexity-theoretic assumption that PPAD $\neq$ P, there is no polynomial-time algorithm that attains no-regret in two-player general-sum Markov games when executed independently by all players, even when the game is known to the algorithm designer. • When the game is unknown, no algorithm, efficient or otherwise, can achieve no-regret without observing exponentially many episodes in the number of players. These results are proven via lower bounds for a simpler problem we refer to as SparseCCE, in which the goal is to compute a coarse correlated equilibrium that is “sparse” in the sense that it can be represented as a mixture of a small number of product policies.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether agents in a Markov game can each run a learning algorithm independently and all achieve no regret. Earlier positive results apply to restricted settings, including particular definitions of allowable policy deviations. The authors examine the standard framework and identify separate computational and statistical barriers.

For two-player general-sum games, they show that a polynomial-time independent no-regret algorithm cannot exist under the complexity assumption PPAD differs from P. This computational obstruction persists even when the algorithm designer knows the game. For unknown games, they establish a different barrier: any such algorithm requires exponentially many observed episodes in the number of players, regardless of its computational efficiency.

The proofs proceed through SparseCCE, a problem of finding a coarse correlated equilibrium representable by a small mixture of product policies. Lower bounds for this simpler representation problem imply the learning barriers. The findings distinguish limitations of independent learning in the standard setting from the restricted cases where positive guarantees remain available, rather than ruling out multi-agent learning generally.
summary.tldr: The paper proves computational and sample-complexity barriers to independent no-regret learning in the standard Markov-game framework.

title: Hardness of Independent Learning and Sparse Equilibrium Computation in Markov Games

abstract: Recent approaches build on implicit neural representations (INRs) to propose generative models over function spaces. However, they are computationally costly when dealing with inference tasks, such as missing data imputation, or directly cannot tackle them. In this work, we propose a novel deep generative model, named VaMoH. VaMoH combines the capabilities of modeling continuous functions using INRs and the inference capabilities of Variational Autoencoders (VAEs). In addition, VaMoH relies on a normalizing flow to define the prior, and a mixture of hypernetworks to parametrize the data log-likelihood. This gives VaMoH a high expressive capability and interpretability. Through experiments on a diverse range of data types, such as images, voxels, and climate data, we show that VaMoH can effectively learn rich distributions over continuous functions. Furthermore, it can perform inference-related tasks, such as conditional super-resolution generation and in-painting, as well or better than previous approaches, while being less computationally demanding.

paragraphs: Implicit neural representations describe data through continuous functions, creating a way to learn distributions over functions rather than only fixed collections of values. Existing generative approaches can make inference tasks such as filling in missing observations expensive or unavailable. This paper introduces VaMoH to combine expressive function modeling with more efficient inference.

It uses a normalizing flow for the prior distribution and a mixture of hypernetworks to parameterize the data likelihood. These results support its usefulness for both generating function-based data and completing inference tasks conditioned on partially observed information.
summary.tldr: VaMoH combines continuous neural representations with variational inference to learn function distributions and perform competitive, less costly conditional generation.

title: Variational Mixture of HyperGenerators for Learning Distributions over Functions

abstract: Stochastic optimization is one of the central problems in Machine Learning and Theoretical Computer Science. In the standard model, the algorithm is given a fixed distribution known in advance. In practice though, one may acquire at a cost extra information to make better decisions. In this paper, we study how to buy information for stochastic optimization and formulate this question as an online learning problem. Assuming the learner has an oracle for the original optimization problem, we design a $2$-competitive deterministic algorithm and a $e/(e-1)$-competitive randomized algorithm for buying information. We show that this ratio is tight as the problem is equivalent to a robust generalization of the ski-rental problem, which we call super-martingale stopping. We also consider an adaptive setting where the learner can choose to buy information after taking some actions for the underlying optimization problem. We focus on the classic optimization problem, Min-Sum Set Cover, where the goal is to quickly find an action that covers a given request drawn from a known distribution. We provide an $8$-competitive algorithm running in polynomial time that chooses actions and decides when to buy information about the underlying request.

paragraphs: Stochastic optimization usually assumes that decisions are made using a probability distribution already known to the algorithm. This paper adds another choice: paying to acquire information that could improve those decisions. The learner must weigh the cost of information against the benefit of resolving uncertainty.

Assuming access to an oracle for the original optimization problem, the authors formulate information purchasing as online learning. They provide a deterministic algorithm with competitive ratio 2 and a randomized algorithm with ratio e/(e−1). These ratios describe worst-case performance relative to a benchmark. They establish tightness through a connection to a robust extension of ski rental called super-martingale stopping.

The paper also studies buying information after some optimization actions have already been taken. For Min-Sum Set Cover, where actions aim to cover a request drawn from a known distribution quickly, it gives a polynomial-time algorithm with competitive ratio 8. This extension makes information acquisition part of the evolving action sequence, rather than a decision that must always happen before the underlying task begins.
summary.tldr: The paper develops competitive algorithms for deciding when paid information is worth acquiring during stochastic optimization.

title: Buying Information for Stochastic Optimization

abstract: Standard MSE or MAE loss function is commonly used in limited field-of-vision depth completion, treating each pixel equally under a basic assumption that all pixels have same contribution during optimization. Recently, with the rapid rise of panoramic photography, panoramic depth completion (PDC) has raised increasing attention in 3D computer vision. However, the assumption is inapplicable to panoramic data due to its latitude-wise distortion and high uncertainty nearby textures and edges. To handle these challenges, we propose distortion and uncertainty aware loss (DUL) that consists of a distortion-aware loss and an uncertainty-aware loss. The distortion-aware loss is designed to tackle the panoramic distortion caused by equirectangular projection, whose coordinate transformation relation is used to adaptively calculate the weight of the latitude-wise distortion, distributing uneven importance instead of the equal treatment for each pixel. The uncertainty-aware loss is presented to handle the inaccuracy in non-smooth regions. Specifically, we characterize uncertainty into PDC solutions under Bayesian deep learning framework, where a novel consistent uncertainty estimation constraint is designed to learn the consistency between multiple uncertainty maps of a single panorama. This consistency constraint allows model to produce more precise uncertainty estimation that is robust to feature deformation. Extensive experiments show the superiority of our method over standard loss functions, reaching the state of the art.

paragraphs: Panoramic depth completion must contend with geometry that standard pixelwise losses do not capture. Treating every pixel equally overlooks distortion that changes with latitude in an equirectangular panorama. The task also has elevated uncertainty near textures and edges, where depth predictions can be less accurate than in smoother regions.

The proposed distortion and uncertainty aware loss addresses these issues through two components. Its distortion component uses the projection's coordinate transformation to assign unequal pixel importance according to latitude. Its uncertainty component uses a Bayesian deep learning framework to account for uncertainty in depth completion, particularly around non-smooth regions.

A further constraint encourages multiple uncertainty maps for the same panorama to agree. The authors report that this improves uncertainty estimation and makes it robust to feature deformation. Extensive experiments show improvements over standard loss functions and state-of-the-art performance. The contribution is a training objective that reflects both panoramic projection geometry and spatial differences in prediction uncertainty.
summary.tldr: A loss combining projection-aware pixel weighting and consistent uncertainty estimation improves panoramic depth completion.

title: Distortion and Uncertainty Aware Loss for Panoramic Depth Completion

abstract: Despite the impressive performance recently achieved by automatic speech recognition (ASR), we observe two primary challenges that hinder its broader applications: (1) The difficulty of introducing scalability into the model to support more languages with limited training, inference, and storage overhead; (2) The low-resource adaptation ability that enables effective low-resource adaptation while avoiding over fitting and catastrophic forgetting issues. Inspired by recent findings, we hypothesize that we can address the above challenges with modules widely shared across languages. To this end, we propose an ASR framework, dubbed Master-ASR, that, for the first time, simultaneously achieves strong multilingual scalability and low-resource adaptation ability thanks to its modularize-then-assemble strategy. Specifically, Master-ASR learns a small set of generalizable sub-modules and adaptively assembles them for different languages to reduce the multilingual overhead and enable effective knowledge transfer for low-resource adaptation. Extensive experiments and visualizations demonstrate that Master-ASR can effectively discover language similarity and improve multilingual and low-resource ASR performance over state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods, e.g., under multilingual-ASR, our framework achieves a 0.13∼2.41 lower character error rate (CER) with 30% smaller inference overhead over SOTA solutions on multilingual ASR and a comparable CER with nearly 100 times fewer trainable parameters over SOTA solutions on low-resource tuning, respectively.

Master-ASR addresses these challenges through a modular architecture built around components shared across languages.

The framework first learns a small collection of generalizable submodules, then adaptively assembles them for different languages.
