paragraphs: A transformer may need to represent several worlds whose rules disagree, but many interpretability studies examine only one setting at a time. MetaOthello creates a controlled way to study this problem through Othello-like games that share syntax while differing in rules or tokenization. The authors train small GPT models on mixtures of these variants.

The models learn shared representations of board state. Linear probes trained on one game can intervene on another game’s board representation nearly as effectively as probes matched to that game. When variants conflict, the researchers identify and steer a localized mechanism that resolves the ambiguity, showing how shared state information can coexist with a specific mechanism for handling disagreement.

For structurally equivalent games with remapped tokens, a single orthogonal rotation aligns their representations across layers. This supports the interpretation that the shared representation reflects abstract game structure rather than just token identities. Within this controlled setting, the results show transformers sharing common structure while localizing conflict, offering a framework for investigating how multiple world models coexist.
summary.tldr: MetaOthello shows small transformers sharing board-state structure across game variants while resolving conflicting rules through a localized mechanism.

title: MetaOthello: A Controlled Study of Multiple World Models in Transformers

abstract: Reward models learned from human preferences are central to aligning large language models (LLMs) via reinforcement learning from human feedback, yet they are often vulnerable to reward hacking due to noisy annotations and systematic biases such as response length or style. We propose Bayesian Non-Negative Reward Model (BNRM), a principled reward modeling framework that integrates non-negative factor analysis into Bradley–Terry (BT) preference model.BNRM represents rewards through a sparse, non-negative latent factor generative process that operates at two complementary levels: instance-specific latent variables induce disentangled reward representations, while sparsity over global latent factors acts as an implicit debiasing mechanism that suppresses spurious correlations. Together, this disentanglement-then-debiasing structure enables robust uncertainty-aware reward learning. To scale BNRM to modern LLMs, we develop an amortized variational inference network conditioned on deep model representations, allowing efficient end-to-end training. Extensive empirical results demonstrate that BNRM substantially mitigates reward over-optimization, improves robustness under distribution shifts, and yields more interpretable reward decompositions than strong baselines.

paragraphs: Reward models trained from human preferences can learn misleading shortcuts, including preferences for particular response lengths or styles. When reinforcement learning strongly optimizes those rewards, such shortcuts can enable reward hacking. BNRM addresses this by changing how a preference model represents reward and uncertainty.

The framework combines the Bradley–Terry preference model with sparse, non-negative latent factors. Instance-specific variables separate reward into distinct components, while sparsity over global factors acts as an implicit mechanism for suppressing spurious correlations. These two levels provide the paper's disentanglement-then-debiasing structure, allowing uncertainty-aware learning with more interpretable reward components.

To make the approach practical for modern language models, the authors develop an amortized variational inference network conditioned on deep model representations, enabling efficient end-to-end training. Extensive experiments report substantially less reward over-optimization, stronger robustness under distribution shifts, and more interpretable decompositions than strong baselines. The results support structured Bayesian reward modeling as a way to mitigate exploitation of imperfect preference signals while making the learned rewards easier to examine.
summary.tldr: BNRM uses sparse non-negative Bayesian reward factors to mitigate reward over-optimization and improve robustness and interpretability.

title: Mitigating Reward Hacking in RLHF via Bayesian Non-negative Reward Modeling

abstract: It is widely recognized that reinforcement learning (RL) fine-tuning of large language models often leads to diversity collapse, where outputs lack variety. Prior work has proposed a range of heuristics to counteract this effect, but these methods are ad hoc: they frequently trade off correctness for diversity, their effectiveness varies across tasks, and in some cases they even contradict one another. In this work, we place these observations on a rigorous foundation. We first provide a formal proof of why RL fine-tuning exhibits diversity collapse via a selection and reinforcement bias. Next, we make a key observation that any reward modification to address diversity collapse only needs to be applied on the correct trajectories. Building directly on this analysis, we introduce a principled method—differential smoothing—that provably improves both correctness and diversity, outperforming vanilla RL as well as widely used entropy-based heuristics. Our theory precisely characterizes when existing heuristics help and why they fail, while showing that differential smoothing is universally superior. Extensive experiments with models from 1B to 7B parameters, across domains including CountDown and real-world mathematical reasoning, demonstrate consistent gains. Differential smoothing improves both Pass@1 and Pass@k, with up to 6.7% improvements on AIME24 dataset.

Existing interventions often trade correctness against variety, and their effects can vary across tasks. This paper develops a theoretical account of the problem, proving how selection and reinforcement bias produce the collapse in diversity.

The analysis identifies a more targeted intervention: reward modifications intended to address diversity collapse only need to affect correct trajectories. The authors build differential smoothing around this observation. Within their theoretical analysis, the method improves both correctness and diversity, and is universally superior to the alternatives considered. The same framework characterizes when existing heuristics help and why they fail.

They report consistent improvements in both Pass@1 and Pass@k, with gains of up to 6.7% on AIME24. Together, the theory and experiments support preserving a broader range of successful reasoning trajectories while also improving answer correctness.
summary.tldr: Differential smoothing targets rewards on correct trajectories to improve both reasoning accuracy and output diversity during reinforcement learning.

title: Differential Smoothing Mitigates Sharpening and Improves LLM Reasoning

abstract: Hypergraphs are graph generalizations with key applications in domains such as healthcare, where strict data privacy requirements apply, or bioinformatics, where testing new compounds is costly. However, due to their combinatorial nature, hypergraph representations are often either intractable or lead to significant information loss. For this reason, research into hypergraph synthesis is limited, and state-of-the-art approaches yield poor generation quality in terms of overall structural patterns and graph-level validity. To address such shortcomings, we introduce SuperHype, an exact and tractable hypergraph diffusion model. The core of SuperHype is the graph-superposition decomposition, a novel representation that embeds a hypergraph into a multi-layer graph, enabling a tractable representation with no loss of generalization. To generate new samples from such representations, we introduce a Graph-Superposition Transformer that treats the superposition as an interconnected sequence of layers. Moreover, we enhance the model’s performance by incorporating hypergraph-specific auxiliary features and aggregating indirect node interactions via triplet pooling. Our evaluation across five datasets shows that SuperHype generally reproduces local and global connectivity patterns with superior fidelity compared to state-of-the-art baselines.

paragraphs: Hypergraphs represent relationships that can involve multiple nodes together, making them useful for complex structured data. Generating synthetic hypergraphs is difficult because their combinatorial structure can make representations computationally unwieldy or cause substantial information loss. SuperHype addresses this representation problem as the foundation of a hypergraph diffusion model.

Its graph-superposition decomposition embeds a hypergraph into a multilayer graph. The authors describe this representation as exact and tractable, retaining generality while enabling manageable computation. A Graph-Superposition Transformer processes the resulting layers as an interconnected sequence. Hypergraph-specific auxiliary features and triplet pooling further help the model incorporate structure and indirect interactions between nodes.

Across five datasets, SuperHype generally reproduces local and global connectivity patterns more faithfully than state-of-the-art baselines. This is a qualified empirical result about structural fidelity, rather than a claim of uniform superiority on every dataset. The broader contribution connects a lossless, tractable representation with a generative architecture designed around that representation, addressing a central obstacle in hypergraph synthesis.
summary.tldr: SuperHype uses an exact multilayer graph representation to generate hypergraphs with generally better local and global structural fidelity.

title: SuperHype: Hypergraph Generation via Graph-Superposition Decomposition

abstract: We introduce a practical, black-box framework termed Detection Augmented Learning (DAL) for the problem of piecewise stationary bandits without knowledge of the underlying non-stationarity. DAL accepts any stationary bandit algorithm with order-optimal regret as input and augments it with a change detector, enabling applicability to all common bandit variants. Extensive experimentation demonstrates that DAL consistently surpasses all state-of-the-art methods across diverse non-stationary scenarios, including synthetic benchmarks and real-world datasets, underscoring its versatility and scalability. We provide theoretical insights into DAL’s strong empirical performance, complemented by thorough empirical validation.

paragraphs: A piecewise stationary bandit problem contains periods of stable reward behavior separated by changes. A learner must choose actions while dealing with those changes, without necessarily knowing when they will occur. This paper introduces Detection Augmented Learning, or DAL, to handle that setting without prior knowledge of the underlying non-stationarity.

DAL combines a change detector with an existing stationary bandit algorithm. The input algorithm must have order-optimal regret, meaning its performance loss has the appropriate optimal scaling for its stationary problem. Treating that algorithm as a black box makes the framework broadly reusable across common bandit variants, rather than requiring a separate learning method for every variant.

Experiments cover synthetic benchmarks and real-world datasets with diverse non-stationary behavior. The authors report that DAL consistently surpasses the state-of-the-art methods in those evaluations and provide theoretical insights into its performance. The approach matters because it connects established stationary learners with explicit change detection, offering a general route to adapting them to environments that change in stages.
summary.tldr: DAL equips order-optimal stationary bandit algorithms with change detection to handle unknown shifts in reward behavior.

title: DAL: A Practical Prior-Free Black-Box Framework for Piecewise Stationary Bandits

abstract: Object insertion aims to seamlessly composite a reference object into a specified region of a background image. Recent diffusion-based methods achieve high visual quality but formulate insertion as a simple 2D inpainting task, providing no explicit control over the object’s 3D pose and limiting their practical applicability. We propose DIRECT (Decomposed Injection for REference Composition and Target-integration), a novel framework that integrates interactive pose manipulation with high-fidelity 2D image synthesis to enable pose-controllable object insertion. Our method decomposes the insertion conditions into three complementary components: appearance guidance capturing visual details from the reference object, geometry guidance derived from the user-adjusted 3D proxy, and context guidance from the target background. By injecting them through separate pathways, DIRECT avoids feature entanglement and simultaneously preserves reference appearance, follows the user-specified pose, and adapts the object to the target scene. We also introduce an automated data construction pipeline to improve the diversity and quality of training data. Experiments show that DIRECT outperforms previous methods in both geometric controllability and visual quality.

title: Direct 3D-Aware Object Insertion via Decomposed Visual Proxies

abstract: Looping, reusing a block of layers across depth, and depth growing, training shallow-to-deep models by duplicating middle layers, have both been linked to stronger reasoning, but their relationship remains unclear. We provide a mechanistic unification: looped and depth-grown models exhibit convergent depth-wise signatures, including increased reliance on late layers and recurring patterns aligned with the looped or grown block. These shared signatures support the view that their gains stem from a common form of iterative computation. Building on this connection, we show that the two techniques are adaptable and composable: applying inference-time looping to the middle blocks of a depth-grown model improves accuracy on some reasoning primitives by up to $2\times$, despite the model never being trained to loop. Both approaches also adapt better than the baseline when given more in-context examples or additional supervised fine-tuning data. Additionally, depth-grown models achieve the largest reasoning gains when using higher-quality, math-heavy cooldown mixtures, which can be further boosted by adapting a middle block to loop. Overall, our results position depth growth and looping as complementary, practical methods for inducing and scaling iterative computation to improve reasoning.

summary.tldr: Depth growth and layer looping show shared iterative-computation signatures and can be combined to improve some reasoning tasks.

title: From Growing to Looping: A Unified View of Iterative Computation in LLMs

abstract: This paper is concerned with learning the input-output mapping of general nonlinear dynamical systems. While the existing literature focuses on Gaussian inputs and benign disturbances, we significantly broaden the scope of admissible control inputs and allow correlated, nonzero-mean, adversarial disturbances. With our reformulation as a linear combination of basis functions, we prove that the $\ell_2$-norm estimator overcomes the challenges posed by an adversary with access to the full information history, provided that the attack times are sparse, i.e., the probability that the system is under adversarial attack at a given time is smaller than a certain threshold. We provide an estimation error bound that decays with the input memory length and prove its optimality by constructing a problem instance that suffers from the same bound under probabilistic adversarial attacks. Our work provides a sharp input-output analysis for a generic nonlinear and partially observed system under significantly generalized assumptions compared to existing works.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to learn the relationship between inputs and outputs in nonlinear dynamical systems when observations can be disturbed adversarially. It broadens the usual setting beyond Gaussian inputs and benign noise, allowing disturbances that are correlated, have nonzero mean, and respond to the full information history.

The analysis reformulates the input-output relationship as a linear combination of basis functions. Within this formulation, the authors prove an estimation guarantee for an ℓ2-norm estimator when attacks are sufficiently sparse. Specifically, the probability of an attack at a given time must stay below a threshold. The adversary's extensive information is therefore allowed alongside an explicit restriction on attack frequency.

The resulting error bound decreases as the input memory length grows. A constructed problem instance under probabilistic adversarial attacks matches that bound, establishing its optimality in the stated analysis. Together, these results explain both what the estimator can achieve and why the bound cannot generally be improved, covering nonlinear and partially observed systems under broader assumptions than the compared literature.
summary.tldr: The paper proves matching estimation-error bounds for nonlinear input-output learning when informed adversarial attacks occur sufficiently infrequently.

title: On the Sharp Input-Output Analysis of Nonlinear Systems under Adversarial Attacks

abstract: Video-based visible-infrared person re-identification (VVI-ReID) aims to learn robust video-level representations under modality discrepancy. However, existing methods typically rely on Euclidean geometry, which is suboptimal for modeling the complex temporal dynamics within visible and infrared tracklets, as it inevitably distorts the intrinsic hierarchical structure inherent in diverse temporal variations (e.g., occlusion, pose). In this paper, we propose Hyperbolic Hierarchical Alignment (HHA), which unifies spatio-temporal modeling and cross-modality alignment on the Poincaré ball. HHA employs a Hyperbolic Hierarchical Spatio-Temporal Aggregator (HHSA) to organize time-varying cues into low-distortion hierarchical representations via Hyperbolic Geometry Interaction (HGI) and Dual-Geometry Fusion (DGF). Furthermore, we introduce Geometry-Aware Modality Alignment (GMA), which integrates Hyperbolic Modality Alignment (HMA) to couple modality centroids for geometric consistency and Hyperbolic Prototype Alignment (HPA) to anchor both modalities to shared identity prototypes for robust discrimination. Experiments on HITSZ-VCM and BUPTCampus demonstrate state-of-the-art performance. The code will be available at https://github.com/Visuang/HHA.

paragraphs: Matching a person across visible-light and infrared videos requires handling both sensor differences and changes over time. The paper argues that conventional Euclidean representations distort the hierarchy in these temporal variations, weakening the representation used for matching identities across modalities.

Hyperbolic Hierarchical Alignment places temporal modeling and modality alignment in the Poincaré ball, a hyperbolic representation space. Its spatio-temporal aggregator organizes changing visual cues hierarchically through geometry interaction and dual-geometry fusion. A second component aligns the modalities in two ways: it couples their centroids to promote geometric consistency and anchors both to shared identity prototypes to support discrimination between people.

Experiments on HITSZ-VCM and BUPTCampus report state-of-the-art performance. The approach joins two closely related requirements: preserving the organization of changes within a person’s video and keeping visible and infrared representations comparable. The stated findings support using a common geometric framework for both requirements in the evaluated cross-modality identification setting.
summary.tldr: HHA uses hyperbolic representations to organize temporal variation and align person identities across visible and infrared videos.

title: Hyperbolic Hierarchical Alignment for Video-Based Visible-Infrared Person Re-Identification

abstract: Fine-tuning large language models for vertical domains remains labor-intensive, requiring practitioners to curate data, configure training, and iteratively diagnose model behavior. Despite growing interest in autonomous machine learning and language agents, end-to-end LLM fine-tuning has not been systematically studied as an interactive agent task. We introduce FT-Dojo, an interactive benchmark environment for autonomous LLM fine-tuning, comprising 13 tasks across 5 domains. Rather than a new collection of static datasets, FT-Dojo standardizes a task interface, shared raw-data repository, sandboxed execution environment, structured feedback protocol, and held-out evaluation procedure. We further develop FT-Agent, a fine-tuning-oriented autonomous framework that uses structured iteration planning, fail-fast validation, and multi-level feedback analysis to refine data and training strategies. Experiments show that FT-Agent provides a strong initial baseline, achieving the best performance on 10 out of 13 tasks, with additional controlled comparisons against frontier agents, open-source planning backbones, and multi-run statistics supporting the main findings. Case studies show that agents can recover from failures through cumulative learning, while still exposing limitations in causal diagnosis and long-horizon planning. The implementation is available at https://github.com/microsoft/rd-agent.

FT-Dojo turns that workflow into an interactive task for autonomous agents. Its benchmark contains 13 tasks across five domains and evaluates the process of adaptation, including how an agent responds to feedback.

It iteratively revises both data choices and training strategies within this common environment.

FT-Agent achieves the best performance on 10 of the 13 tasks in the reported experiments. Controlled comparisons and repeated-run statistics provide additional support for the findings. Case studies show recovery through cumulative learning, while also exposing weaknesses in causal diagnosis and long-term planning. The benchmark therefore supplies both an initial strong baseline and a way to examine where autonomous fine-tuning still breaks down.
summary.tldr: FT-Dojo benchmarks autonomous fine-tuning workflows, and FT-Agent leads on 10 of its 13 tasks while revealing planning and diagnosis limits.

title: FT-Dojo: Towards Autonomous LLM Fine-Tuning with Language Agents

abstract: Conditional independence testing (CIT) is essential for reliable scientific discovery. It prevents spurious findings and enables controlled feature selection. Recent CIT methods have used machine learning (ML) models as surrogates of the underlying distribution. However, model-agnostic approaches require a train-test split, which reduces statistical power. We introduce Semi-knockoffs, a CIT method that can accommodate any pre-trained model, avoids this split, and provides valid p-values and false discovery rate (FDR) control for high-dimensional settings. Unlike methods that rely on the model-$X$ assumption (known input distribution), Semi-knockoffs only require conditional expectations for continuous variables. This makes the procedure less restrictive and more practical for machine learning integration. To ensure validity when these expectations are estimated, we present two new theoretical results: (i) stability for regularized models trained with a null feature and (ii) the double-robustness property.

paragraphs: Conditional independence testing asks whether variables remain related after accounting for other variables. It supports scientific discovery and feature selection by helping distinguish meaningful relationships from spurious ones. Machine learning models can assist these tests, but model-agnostic approaches commonly require splitting data into training and testing portions, reducing statistical power.

Semi-knockoffs accommodates any pretrained model without requiring that split. The method provides valid p-values and false discovery rate control in high-dimensional settings. Its assumptions also differ from approaches that require knowing the full input distribution: for continuous variables, it requires conditional expectations. This narrows the distributional information needed to integrate a predictive model into the testing procedure.

Because conditional expectations may themselves need estimation, the paper develops two theoretical results addressing validity in that situation. One concerns the stability of regularized models trained with a null feature; the other establishes a double-robustness property. The contribution combines model flexibility, avoidance of data splitting, and formal statistical guarantees, while retaining the stated requirements on conditional expectations.
summary.tldr: Semi-knockoffs enables model-agnostic conditional independence testing without a train-test split, with finite-sample guarantees under its stated assumptions.

title: Semi-knockoffs: a model-agnostic conditional independence testing method with finite-sample guarantees

abstract: Model fusion seeks to combine independently trained neural networks into a single model without retraining, but is complicated by representational divergence arising from permutation invariance, random initialization, and heterogeneous training data. Existing methods struggle particularly in zero-shot settings under non-IID data distributions, and are often limited to specific architectures or pairwise fusion. We introduce a neuron-centric family of fusion algorithms that frames fusion as a principled representation-matching problem: intermediate neurons across parent models are grouped into target representations, which the fused model’s corresponding sub-networks are then trained to approximate. Unlike prior work, our approach incorporates neuron attribution scores to bias alignment toward salient features, and can be applied to any architecture modularizable as a DAG of levels—empirically validated on VGGs, ResNets, and ViTs. Experiments across standard benchmarks show consistent improvements over existing fusion methods, with the largest gains in zero-shot and non-IID scenarios. Code is available at https://github.com/AndrewSpano/model-fusion-via-retrofittinghttps://github.com/AndrewSpano/model-fusion-via-retrofitting.

paragraphs: Independently trained networks can encode related capabilities in differently arranged internal representations. Random initialization, neuron permutations, and different training data complicate combining them into one model. This paper approaches fusion as a representation-matching problem, with particular attention to zero-shot settings and parent models trained on differently distributed data.

The proposed algorithms group intermediate neurons from the parent networks into target representations. Corresponding subnetworks in the fused model are then trained to approximate those targets. Neuron attribution scores influence the alignment, giving greater emphasis to salient features. Although the broader goal is fusion without retraining entire parent models, the described retrofitting procedure does include training the fused subnetworks.

The method applies to architectures that can be organized as a directed acyclic graph of levels, and experiments validate it on VGGs, ResNets, and vision transformers. Across standard benchmarks, it consistently improves on existing fusion methods, with the largest gains in zero-shot and non-IID settings. The results support feature-aware alignment as a practical response to representational differences among independently trained models.
summary.tldr: Retrofitting fuses networks by aligning salient neuron representations and training fused subnetworks to reproduce the resulting targets.

title: Model Fusion via Retrofitting

abstract: Domain Adaptive Object Detection (DAOD) addresses the challenge of transferring object detectors from labeled source domains to unlabeled target domains. Existing domain adaptation methods primarily rely on feature distribution alignment, which enhances domain-invariant features (statistical invariance) but also inadvertently increases inherent domain-common spurious factors (e.g., common environmental contexts), which act as shortcut features rather than the true causal factors for object classification. We propose Dynamic Causal Refinement (DCR), a novel framework that establishes a closed-loop feedback mechanism between data augmentation and model optimization to progressively refine causal features. Specifically, we design Semantic Prediction Consistency (SPC) to filter domain-specific spurious factors and establish a robust statistical invariance, and Discrepancy-Guided Causal Refinement (DGCR) to actively suppress the dependence on domain-common spurious factors via spectral perturbation for causal refinement. This process encourages the detector to suppress its reliance on shortcut features and instead prioritize semantically meaningful causal representations. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art counterparts significantly.

paragraphs: Domain-adaptive object detection transfers a detector from labeled source data to an unlabeled target domain. A common strategy aligns feature distributions across the two domains. The paper argues that this can preserve misleading cues shared by both domains, such as environmental context, even when those cues are shortcuts rather than meaningful evidence about the object.

Dynamic Causal Refinement creates a feedback loop between data augmentation and model optimization. Its Semantic Prediction Consistency component filters domain-specific spurious factors and establishes statistical invariance. Its Discrepancy-Guided Causal Refinement component uses spectral perturbation to suppress dependence on spurious factors that the domains have in common.

This division matters because removing differences between domains does not by itself remove shortcuts that both domains share. The framework progressively encourages features tied to object semantics while reducing reliance on those shared cues. Experiments on standard benchmarks show significant improvements over state-of-the-art counterparts. The reported findings support refining the content of invariant representations, alongside making those representations statistically consistent across domains.
summary.tldr: Dynamic Causal Refinement improves cross-domain object detection by targeting both domain-specific shortcuts and misleading cues shared across domains.

title: Domain Adaptive Object Detection via Dynamic Causal Refinement

abstract: The community is increasingly exploring linear RNNs (LRNNs) as language models, motivated by their expressive power and parallelizability. While prior work establishes the expressivity benefits of LRNNs over transformers, it is unclear what makes LRNNs—but not traditional, nonlinear RNNs—as easy to parallelize in practice as transformers. We answer this question by providing a tight connection between types of RNNs and standard complexity classes. We show that LRNNs can be viewed as log-depth (bounded fan-in) arithmetic circuits, which represents only a slight depth overhead relative to log-depth boolean circuits that transformers admit. Furthermore, we show that nonlinear RNNs can solve $\mathsf L$-complete problems (and even $\mathsf P$-complete ones, under polynomial precision), revealing a fundamental barrier to parallelizing them as efficiently as transformers. Our theory also identifies fine-grained expressivity differences between recent popular LRNN variants: permutation-diagonal LRNNs are $\mathsf{NC}^1$-complete whereas diagonal-plus-low-rank LRNNs are more expressive ($\mathsf{PNC}^1$-complete). We provide further insight by associating each type of RNN with a corresponding automata-theoretic model that it can simulate. Together, our results reveal fundamental tradeoffs between nonlinear RNNs and different variants of LRNNs, providing a foundation for designing LLM architectures that achieve an optimal balance between expressivity and parallelism.

paragraphs: Linear recurrent neural networks are attractive language-model architectures partly because their computations can be parallelized efficiently. This paper explains why linear recurrence has that advantage over traditional nonlinear recurrence by connecting network types to computational complexity classes. The analysis treats parallelizability as a property of the computations each architecture can express.

The authors represent linear RNNs as bounded-fan-in arithmetic circuits with logarithmic depth, placing them close to the logarithmic-depth Boolean circuits associated with transformers. Nonlinear RNNs can solve L-complete problems and, with polynomial precision, even P-complete problems. These results expose a fundamental complexity-theoretic barrier to making nonlinear recurrence as parallelizable as transformers.

The analysis also distinguishes linear variants: permutation-diagonal models are NC¹-complete, while diagonal-plus-low-rank models have the greater expressivity characterized by PNC¹-completeness. Corresponding automata models provide another account of what each architecture can simulate. Together, the results explain why recurrence alone does not determine parallel efficiency and give architecture designers a theoretical basis for weighing expressive power against opportunities for parallel computation.
summary.tldr: Complexity-theoretic connections explain linear RNNs' parallel efficiency and distinguish the expressive power of recurrent architectures.

title: Why Are Linear RNNs More Parallelizable?

abstract: Terminal embeddings have emerged as a powerful tool for dimension reduction. Given a set of points $P\subset \mathbb{R}^d$, a terminal embedding is a mapping $f:\mathbb{R}^d\rightarrow \mathbb{R}^t$ that preserves the pairwise distance between any pair of points $p\in P$ and $q\in \mathbb{R}^d$ up to small distortion under this mapping. Terminal embeddings have been particularly fruitful for constructing $k$-means and $k$-median coresets, where the objective is to find a typically weighted subset $\Omega$ of $P$ such that for any candidate solution, the cost of the clustering objective on $\Omega$ approximates the cost of the clustering objective on $P$ up to small distortion. Unfortunately, these techniques have not been extended to more complicated structures such as clustering time-series data under common straight-line interpolation between measurements. The main issue is that terminal embeddings, arguably the central technique in this line of research, cannot be linear and are thus not immediately suitable to preserve linear structures. In this work, we develop a generalization of terminal embeddings to affine line-segments that overcomes this issue. We showcase their applicability by using our lines-preserving terminal embeddings to obtain the first dimension-free coresets for clustering time-series under the Fréchet distance. The underlying dimension reduction uses Johnson-Lindenstrauss embeddings, and our experiments indicate that they compare favorably against PCA for real-world time-series.

paragraphs: Terminal embeddings reduce dimension while preserving distances from every point in a chosen dataset to any possible query point. This supports small weighted summaries, called coresets, whose clustering costs approximate those of the full dataset for every candidate solution. Extending this idea to time series is difficult because straight-line interpolation between measurements introduces structure that ordinary terminal embeddings do not directly preserve.

The paper generalizes terminal embeddings to affine line segments. This overcomes the mismatch between nonlinear terminal mappings and the linear pieces used to represent time-series curves. The resulting construction supports dimension reduction while respecting the segments relevant to these time-series representations.

Using this approach, the authors obtain the first dimension-free coresets for time-series clustering under Fréchet distance. Their dimension-reduction procedure relies on Johnson–Lindenstrauss embeddings, and experiments on real-world time series compare favorably with PCA. The theoretical contribution extends a powerful compression technique from individual points to structured curves, while the experiments indicate practical promise for the underlying reduction.
summary.tldr: Line-segment-preserving terminal embeddings enable the first dimension-free coresets for time-series clustering under Fréchet distance.

title: Terminal Dimension Reduction for Time Series with Applications

abstract: Optimal-transport distributionally robust optimization (OT-DRO) robustifies data-driven decision-making under uncertainty by capturing the sampling-induced statistical error via optimal transport ambiguity sets. The standard OT-DRO pipeline consists of a two-step procedure, where the ambiguity set is first designed and subsequently embedded into the downstream OT-DRO problem. However, this separation between uncertainty quantification and optimization may lead to excessive conservatism. We introduce an end-to-end pipeline to automatically learn decision-focused ambiguity sets for OT-DRO problems, where the loss function informs the shape of the ambiguity set, leading to less conservative decisions whose distributional robustness is enforced via data-driven bootstrapping. We formulate the learning problem as a bilevel optimization program and solve it via a hypergradient-based method. By leveraging the recently introduced nonsmooth conservative implicit function theorem, we establish convergence to a critical point of the bilevel problem. We present experiments validating our method on standard portfolio optimization and linear regression tasks.

paragraphs: Distributionally robust optimization chooses decisions that account for uncertainty about the data distribution. In optimal-transport approaches, an ambiguity set describes plausible distributions around the observed data. The usual workflow designs that set first and then optimizes the decision. This paper argues that separating those steps can make decisions excessively conservative.

The proposed method learns the ambiguity set and the decision process together. The downstream loss informs the set's shape, making the uncertainty description sensitive to what matters for the decision. Data-driven bootstrapping enforces distributional robustness while the learned set supports less conservative choices. This links uncertainty quantification directly to the objective it is intended to protect.

The authors formulate the procedure as a bilevel optimization problem and solve it with hypergradients. Using a nonsmooth conservative implicit function theorem, they establish convergence to a critical point of that problem. Experiments on portfolio optimization and linear regression validate the approach. The theoretical result concerns critical-point convergence, while the practical contribution is learning uncertainty sets around decision-relevant losses.
summary.tldr: Learning optimal-transport ambiguity sets jointly with downstream decisions reduces conservatism while enforcing robustness through bootstrapping.

title: Loss-Aware Distributionally Robust Optimization via Trainable Optimal Transport Ambiguity Sets

abstract: The paradigm of learning from automatic annotations—driven by pre-trained experts and Foundation Models—dominates data-hungry applications. However, it introduces a critical challenge: model-induced label noise. Unlike stochastic noise in classical robust learning, this noise stems from annotator inductive biases, manifesting as systematic errors tightly coupled with local feature manifolds. Existing methods relying on global transition matrices underfit these structural patterns, while learning instance-specific matrices remains mathematically intractable. We propose Model-Induced Noise Decoupling (MIND), a theoretically grounded framework addressing this dilemma. We demonstrate that the high-dimensional noise manifold can be decoupled into tractable, subspace-dependent components via Latent Manifold Disentanglement. Specifically, our Latent Decoupling Estimator (LDE) dynamically projects samples into latent structural clusters with consistent error modes, facilitating noise identifiability without ground-truth anchor points. To rigorously evaluate robustness, we adopt a hierarchical protocol: moving from controlled noise on CIFAR-100 to a structural stress test on large-scale real-world 3D datasets (S3DIS, ScanNet), where error patterns explicitly couple with geometric manifolds. Empirically, MIND significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods on these complex benchmarks and effectively corrects zero-shot hallucinations from Vision-Language Models (e.g., OpenSeg), highlighting its potential as a robust distillation framework for Foundation Models.

paragraphs: Labels produced by pretrained models can contain systematic errors tied to the structure of the inputs. This differs from treating label noise as random corruption. A single global error model can miss these local patterns, while estimating a separate noise-transition matrix for every example presents a tractability problem. MIND addresses the space between those extremes.

The framework decomposes a high-dimensional noise manifold into components associated with latent subspaces. Its Latent Decoupling Estimator dynamically assigns samples to structural clusters with consistent error patterns. This makes the noise structure identifiable without ground-truth anchor points. Evaluation progresses from controlled CIFAR-100 noise to S3DIS and ScanNet, where annotation errors connect directly to three-dimensional geometry. MIND significantly outperforms existing methods on these benchmarks and corrects zero-shot hallucinations from vision-language models such as OpenSeg. These results support its potential for transferring knowledge from foundation models while correcting their structured annotation errors.
summary.tldr: MIND groups structurally related examples with shared error patterns to identify and correct systematic noise in model-generated labels.

title: MIND: Decoupling Model-Induced Label Noise via Latent Manifold Disentanglement

abstract: The problem of domain generalization concerns learning predictive models that are robust to distribution shifts when deployed in new, previously unseen environments. Existing methods typically require labeled data from multiple training environments, limiting their applicability when labeled data are scarce. In this work, we study domain generalization in an anti-causal setting, where the outcome causes the observed covariates. Under this structure, environment perturbations that affect the covariates do not propagate to the outcome, which motivates regularizing the model’s sensitivity to these perturbations. Crucially, estimating these perturbation directions does not require labels, enabling us to leverage unlabeled data from multiple environments. We propose two methods that penalize the model’s sensitivity to variations in the mean and covariance of the covariates across environments, respectively, and prove that these methods have worst-case optimality guarantees under certain classes of environments. Finally, we demonstrate the empirical performance of our approach on a controlled physical system and a physiological signal dataset.

paragraphs: A prediction model can work well in its training environment yet struggle when its inputs change in a new setting. This paper studies how unlabeled data from multiple environments can help prepare for such changes. Its central assumption is an anti-causal structure: the outcome causes the observed features, so environmental disturbances affecting those features do not propagate back to the outcome.

That structure motivates reducing the model’s sensitivity to environmental changes in its inputs. The authors propose two methods, targeting differences in feature means and feature covariances across environments. Crucially, identifying these directions of variation does not require outcome labels. Unlabeled observations can therefore inform which changes the predictor should resist.

The paper proves worst-case optimality guarantees within particular classes of environments and demonstrates the approach on a controlled physical system and physiological signals. The contribution is a way to use environmental variation without requiring labels everywhere. Its theoretical justification depends on the stated causal structure and environment classes, rather than covering arbitrary distribution shifts.
summary.tldr: Under an anti-causal structure, unlabeled data across environments can guide predictors toward robustness to certain distribution shifts.

title: Anti-causal domain generalization: Leveraging unlabeled data

abstract: What do thinking language models learn during training that their base models lack? We first present an unsupervised method that discovers a model’s reasoning behaviors by training small Sparse Autoencoders on sentence-level activations of reasoning traces, yielding interpretable reasoning taxonomies. Building on this, we introduce constructive model diffing, which aims to reconstruct the base-to-fine-tuned difference from interpretable components: reasoning mechanisms (category vectors that can induce a reasoning behavior in the base model) and reasoning heuristics (a classifier determining when a mechanism should fire). Across nine base/thinking pairs (four RL-trained, four SFT-distilled, one mixed), two independent findings agree: category vectors in the base model converge to far lower loss for taxonomies derived from purely RL-trained models, and hybrid models recover roughly 76% of the RL base-to-thinking gap but only 11% of the SFT gap. This indicates RL primarily teaches heuristics for orchestrating pre-existing base mechanisms, whereas SFT-distillation installs new ones, offering a new lens on what training paradigms teach, with implications for efficient reasoning-model development.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether training a thinking model creates new reasoning abilities or teaches it when to use abilities already present. The authors first train small sparse autoencoders on sentence-level internal activations from reasoning traces. This unsupervised procedure produces interpretable categories of reasoning behavior, giving them a way to compare models through specific behaviors.

They then introduce constructive model diffing: attempting to rebuild the difference between a base model and its trained counterpart from understandable components. One component is a vector that can induce a reasoning behavior in the base model. Another is a classifier that decides when to activate that behavior. Together, these separate reasoning mechanisms from the rules governing their use.

Across nine model pairs, these hybrids recover roughly 76% of the improvement from reinforcement learning but only 11% from supervised distillation. A separate analysis of category-vector losses supports the same distinction. The findings indicate that reinforcement learning primarily organizes existing mechanisms, while supervised distillation installs new ones, within the models studied.
summary.tldr: Reconstructing reasoning-model improvements suggests reinforcement learning mainly teaches when to use existing abilities, while supervised distillation adds new mechanisms.

title: Base Models Know How to Reason, Thinking Models Learn When

abstract: The superficial alignment hypothesis (SAH) posits that large language models learn most of their knowledge during pre-training, and that post-training merely surfaces this knowledge. The SAH, however, lacks a precise definition, which has led to (i) different and seemingly orthogonal arguments supporting it, and (ii) important critiques to it. We propose a new metric called task complexity: the length of the shortest program that achieves a target performance on a task. In this framework, the SAH simply claims that pre-trained models drastically reduce the complexity of achieving high performance on many tasks. Our definition unifies prior arguments supporting the SAH, interpreting them as different strategies to find such short programs. Experimentally, we estimate the task complexity of mathematical reasoning, machine translation, and instruction following; we then show that these complexities can be remarkably low when conditioned on a pre-trained model. Further, we find that pre-training enables access to strong performances on our tasks, but it can require programs of gigabytes of length to access them. Post-training, on the other hand, collapses the complexity of reaching this same performance by several orders of magnitude. Overall, our results highlight that task adaptation often requires surprisingly little information—often just a few kilobytes

paragraphs: The superficial alignment hypothesis proposes that pre-training supplies most language-model knowledge and post-training makes it accessible. This paper gives that idea a more precise formulation through task complexity: the length of the shortest program that reaches a chosen performance level. With a pre-trained model available, the question becomes how much additional program information is needed.

This formulation connects earlier arguments for the hypothesis by treating them as different ways to find short programs. The authors estimate task complexity for mathematical reasoning, machine translation, and instruction following. They find that complexity conditioned on a pre-trained model can be remarkably low, giving a concrete interpretation to the idea that adaptation may require little new information.

However, strong performance accessible through pre-training can still require programs gigabytes long. Post-training reduces the program length needed for that same performance by several orders of magnitude. Task adaptation often needs only a few kilobytes in the reported findings. This separates having access to strong capabilities from having a compact, effective way to invoke them.
summary.tldr: Measuring task complexity by program length suggests post-training can drastically shorten the instructions needed to access performance available through pre-trained models.

title: Operationalising the Superficial Alignment Hypothesis via Task Complexity

abstract: Smart contracts on public blockchains now manage large amounts of value, and vulnerabilities in these systems can lead to substantial losses. As AI agents become more capable at reading, writing, and running code, it is natural to ask how well they can already navigate this landscape, both in ways that improve security and in ways that might increase risk. We introduce EVMbench, an evaluation that measures the ability of agents to detect, patch, and exploit smart contract vulnerabilities. EVMbench draws on 117 curated vulnerabilities from 40 repositories and, in the most realistic setting, uses programmatic grading based on tests and blockchain state under a local Ethereum execution environment. We evaluate a range of frontier agents and find that they are capable of discovering and exploiting vulnerabilities end-to-end against live blockchain instances. We release code, tasks, and tooling to support continued measurement of these capabilities and future work on security.

paragraphs: EVMbench measures how well AI agents can work with vulnerabilities in smart contracts. These programs manage value on public blockchains, so an agent’s coding ability has implications for both protection and misuse. The benchmark separates the work into three capabilities: identifying a vulnerability, repairing it, and exploiting it. This gives a broader view of security capability than code reading alone.

The evaluation contains 117 curated vulnerabilities drawn from 40 repositories. In its most realistic setting, it grades agents programmatically using tests and blockchain state in a local Ethereum execution environment. This grounds assessment in observable program behavior and state changes, allowing the benchmark to evaluate whether an attempted action actually achieves its objective.

The authors find that the frontier agents evaluated can discover and exploit vulnerabilities end to end against running blockchain instances. They release the tasks, code, and tooling to support continued measurement. The findings establish demonstrated capabilities in the benchmark setting and provide a concrete framework for tracking both defensive and offensive progress.
summary.tldr: EVMbench tests agents on detecting, repairing, and exploiting curated smart-contract vulnerabilities using executable checks and blockchain state.

title: EVMbench: Evaluating AI Agents on Smart Contract Security

abstract: Audio-visual speaker tracking aims to localize and track active speakers by leveraging auditory and visual cues, enabling fine-grained, human-centric scene understanding. This capability is essential for real-world applications such as intelligent video editing, surveillance, and human–computer interaction. However, existing datasets are largely limited to simple or homogeneous audio-visual scenes with coarse annotations. Such oversimplified settings bias evaluation toward static audio–visual co-occurrence, rather than rigorously assessing robust spatiotemporal modeling and cross-modal reasoning in complex, dynamic scenes. To address these limitations, we introduce AVTrack, a human-centric audio-visual instance segmentation (AVIS) dataset designed for dynamic real-world scenarios. AVTrack features diverse and challenging conditions, including camera motion, visual occlusions, and position changes. Evaluations of representative AVIS methods on AVTrack reveal substantial performance degradation, establishing AVTrack as a challenging benchmark for robust human-centric audio-visual scene understanding in complex environments. We further provide a simple yet effective baseline to facilitate future research. Project website: https://FudanCVL.github.io/AVTrack/

paragraphs: Audio-visual speaker tracking combines sound and video to locate active speakers and follow them over time. Existing datasets often contain simple, uniform scenes and coarse annotations. As a result, a method can look successful by associating visible people with simultaneous audio, without being thoroughly tested on movement, interruptions in visibility, or more demanding reasoning across the two signals.

AVTrack introduces a dataset for human-centered audio-visual instance segmentation in dynamic real-world scenes. Its challenging conditions include camera movement, people becoming visually occluded, and changes in position. These situations make the benchmark more demanding because identifying the speaker requires maintaining an understanding of people and their locations as the scene changes.

Representative methods suffer substantial performance drops when evaluated on AVTrack. The result exposes a gap between performance in simpler settings and robust tracking in complex scenes. The researchers also provide a simple baseline to support further work. The main contribution is therefore an evaluation resource that makes weaknesses in temporal modeling and audio-visual reasoning easier to reveal and study.
summary.tldr: AVTrack tests audio-visual speaker tracking in dynamic scenes and reveals substantial performance drops in representative existing methods.

title: AVTrack: Audio-Visual Tracking in Human-centric Complex Scenes

abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) can yield large reasoning gains from very few training instances, yet its strong sensitivity to which instances are used makes data selection a central bottleneck. Most existing selection pipelines rely on training-time optimization signals and/or require access to verifiable rewards or ground-truth answers over large candidate pools, which is costly and often infeasible in specialized domains. We study RLVR data selection in a setting where selection must be performed before any RL training and without labels or reward evaluation on the full pool. We propose SHIFT, a one-shot, training-free selector based solely on inference-time hidden-state dynamics. For each candidate instance, SHIFT runs a single deterministic reasoning rollout and computes a reasoning-induced representation shift (RIRS) as the start-to-end hidden-state delta. SHIFT uses the RIRS magnitude as a lightweight proxy for instance utility and enforces coverage via a quality-weighted farthest-first CoreSet procedure in an RIRS-augmented feature space, producing compact subsets that scale to large unlabeled pools. Across mathematical reasoning and medical QA benchmarks under ultra-low budgets, SHIFT consistently outperforms training-free diversity and difficulty/uncertainty baselines, improving both in-domain accuracy and transfer to harder evaluation settings. Ablations show that RIRS-based coverage and quality-weighting contribute complementary gains, and analyses indicate that RIRS is not explained by simple input/output length statistics. Code is available at github.com/JianghaoWu/SHIFT.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards can improve reasoning with very few examples, making the choice of examples consequential. SHIFT tackles selection before any reinforcement-learning training, without requiring labels or reward evaluation across the candidate pool. It uses internal model behavior during inference to judge which instances may be useful.

For each candidate, SHIFT generates one deterministic reasoning rollout and measures the change between the starting and ending hidden states. The magnitude of this reasoning-induced representation shift serves as a proxy for utility. A quality-weighted farthest-first selection procedure then promotes coverage in a feature space augmented with these shifts, balancing useful candidates with a compact subset that covers varied instances.

On mathematical reasoning and medical question-answering benchmarks with extremely small training budgets, SHIFT consistently beats the tested training-free diversity and difficulty or uncertainty baselines. Improvements include in-domain accuracy and transfer to harder evaluations. Ablations find complementary benefits from coverage and quality weighting, while further analysis indicates that simple input or output length does not explain the representation-shift signal.
summary.tldr: SHIFT selects compact RLVR training sets using hidden-state changes from one rollout per candidate, improving reported accuracy and transfer without pool-wide labels.

title: Single-Rollout Hidden-State Dynamics for Training-Free RLVR Data Selection

abstract: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) is essential for adapting Large Language Models, yet existing methods struggle to balance capacity with computational efficiency. Standard approaches enforce rigid low-rank constraints, while dynamic alternatives incur significant memory overheads. To resolve this, we propose Spectral Bridge Variational Inference (SBVI), a geometric framework reformulating LoRA as a continuous Wasserstein gradient flow on the manifold of Gaussian measures. Instead of fixing ranks at initialization, SBVI governs singular value evolution via a stochastic differential equation driven by thermodynamic competition between task gradients and adaptive entropic friction. This induces a spectral bifurcation that automatically prunes noise modes while amplifying signal-rich components, discovering an optimal layer-wise rank distribution. We derive a scalable algorithm with linear complexity using factorized Riemannian retractions and Empirical Bayes friction updates. Experiments on reasoning and coding benchmarks show SBVI achieves state-of-the-art performance, offering superior accuracy and memory efficiency over existing static and dynamic methods.

paragraphs: Low-rank adaptation reduces the cost of fine-tuning language models, but fixed ranks constrain how much adaptation each layer can express. Dynamic alternatives can introduce substantial memory costs. Spectral Bridge Variational Inference develops a geometric approach that lets the effective rank change during learning while seeking computational efficiency.

The framework expresses LoRA as a continuous Wasserstein gradient flow over Gaussian distributions. A stochastic differential equation governs singular values through competition between task gradients and adaptive entropic friction. This mechanism suppresses noise-associated modes and strengthens components carrying useful signal, allowing rank allocation to emerge separately for each layer. The authors derive a linear-complexity algorithm using factorized Riemannian retractions and Empirical Bayes updates for friction.

On reasoning and coding benchmarks, SBVI achieves reported state-of-the-art performance with better accuracy and memory efficiency than the evaluated static and dynamic methods. The approach matters because adaptation capacity becomes something shaped by training signals rather than fully fixed at initialization. Its mathematical construction is paired with an algorithm intended to make that flexibility practical without the memory overhead of existing dynamic approaches.
summary.tldr: SBVI dynamically adjusts LoRA’s layer-wise ranks through geometric flows, improving reported accuracy and memory efficiency on reasoning and coding benchmarks.

title: Spectral Bridge Variational Inference: Dynamic LoRA via Bures-Wasserstein Gradient Flows

abstract: Counterfactual generation aims to simulate realistic hypothetical outcomes under causal interventions. Diffusion models have emerged as a powerful tool for this task, combining DDIM inversion with conditional generation and classifier-free guidance (CFG). In this work, we identify a key limitation of CFG for counterfactual generation: it prescribes a global guidance scale for all attributes, leading to significant spurious changes in inferred counterfactuals. To mitigate this, we propose Factored Classifier-Free Guidance (FCFG), a flexible and model-agnostic guidance technique that enables attribute-wise control following a causal graph. FCFG complements recent advances in classifier-free guidance and can be seamlessly extended to advanced guidance schemes such as CFG++ and APG. Our experiments demonstrate that FCFG significantly improves the axiomatic soundness of inferred counterfactuals across both natural and medical image datasets, mitigating spurious amplification effects, and enhancing counterfactual reversibility.

To mitigate this, we propose Factored Classifier-Free Guidance (FCFG), a flexible and model-agnostic guidance technique that enables attribute-wise control following a causal graph. FCFG complements recent advances in classifier-free guidance and can be seamlessly extended to advanced guidance schemes such as CFG++ and APG. Our experiments demonstrate that FCFG significantly improves the axiomatic soundness of inferred counterfactuals across both natural and medical image datasets, mitigating spurious amplification effects, and enhancing counterfactual reversibility.

paragraphs: Counterfactual image generation asks how an image would change under a causal intervention. A useful result must reflect the intended intervention without introducing unrelated changes. The paper identifies a problem with standard classifier-free guidance: one global guidance scale controls all attributes, which can amplify changes that do not belong in the inferred counterfactual.

Factored Classifier-Free Guidance introduces separate control for attributes according to a causal graph. This gives the generation process more precise control over how guidance affects different properties. The method is model-agnostic and can also extend advanced guidance schemes, including CFG++ and APG. Its contribution is a flexible modification to guidance that incorporates causal structure into attribute-level control.

Experiments on natural and medical images show substantial improvements in how well generated counterfactuals satisfy the evaluated axiomatic requirements. The method reduces spurious amplification and improves reversibility of counterfactual changes. These findings concern consistency with counterfactual principles as well as generation behavior: a plausible-looking image is more useful for this task when its changes follow the intended causal intervention.
summary.tldr: Factored Classifier-Free Guidance uses causal structure to control image attributes separately and reduce unintended counterfactual changes.

title: Factored Classifier-Free Guidance

abstract: We present SleepLM, a family of sleep-language foundation models that enable human sleep alignment, interpretation, and interaction with natural language. Despite the critical role of sleep, learning-based sleep analysis systems operate in closed label spaces (e.g., predefined stages or events) and fail to describe, query, or generalize to novel sleep phenomena. SleepLM bridges natural language and multimodal polysomnography, enabling language-grounded representations of sleep physiology. To support this alignment, we introduce a multilevel sleep caption generation pipeline that enables the curation of the first large-scale sleep-text dataset, comprising over 100K hours of data from more than 10,000 individuals. Furthermore, we present a unified pretraining objective that combines contrastive alignment, caption generation, and signal reconstruction to better capture physiological fidelity and cross-modal interactions. Extensive experiments on real-world sleep understanding tasks verify that SleepLM outperforms state-of-the-art in zero-shot and few-shot learning, cross-modal retrieval, and sleep captioning. Importantly, SleepLM also exhibits intriguing capabilities including language-guided event localization, targeted insight generation, and zero-shot generalization to unseen tasks. To support reproducibility and future work, we open-source the captioning pipeline, pretrained checkpoints, and the model architectures at https://github.com/yang-ai-lab/SleepLM.

title: SleepLM: Natural-Language Intelligence for Human Sleep

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have exhibited remarkable performance on complex reasoning tasks, with reinforcement learning under verifiable rewards (RLVR) emerging as a principled framework for aligning model behavior with reasoning chains. Despite its promise, RLVR remains prohibitively resource-intensive, requiring extensive reward signals and incurring substantial rollout costs during training. In this work, we revisit the fundamental question of data and compute efficiency in RLVR. We first establish a theoretical lower bound on the sample complexity required to unlock reasoning capabilities, and empirically validate that strong performance can be achieved with a surprisingly small number of training instances. To tackle the computational burden, we propose Dynamic One-Shot Policy Refinement (DoPR), a uncertainty-aware RL strategy that dynamically selects a single informative training sample per batch for policy updates, guided by reward volatility and exploration-driven acquisition. DoPR reduces rollout overhead by nearly an order of magnitude while preserving competitive reasoning accuracy, offering a scalable and resource-efficient solution for LLM post-training. This approach offers a practical path toward more efficient and accessible RL-based training for reasoning-intensive LLM applications.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards can improve language-model reasoning, but generating training rollouts and collecting reward signals is expensive. This paper examines how much training data is needed and how to concentrate computation on examples that are especially informative for policy updates.

The authors establish a theoretical lower bound on the sample complexity required to unlock reasoning capabilities. Separately, their empirical results show that strong performance can arise from surprisingly few training instances. Selection is uncertainty-aware and uses reward volatility together with exploration-driven acquisition to guide which sample receives the update.

summary.tldr: DoPR selects one informative sample per batch, cutting rollout overhead by nearly an order of magnitude while preserving competitive reasoning accuracy.

title: Resource-Efficient Reinforcement for Reasoning Large Language Models via Dynamic One-Shot Policy Refinement

abstract: Vision–Language–Action (VLA) policies often fail under distribution shift, suggesting that decisions may depend on spurious visual correlations rather than task-relevant causes. We formulate visual–action attribution as an interventional estimation problem. Accordingly, we introduce the Interventional Significance Score (ISS), an interventional masking procedure for estimating the causal influence of visual regions on action predictions, and the Nuisance Mass Ratio (NMR), a scalar measure of attribution to task-irrelevant features. We analyze the statistical properties of ISS and show that it admits unbiased estimation, and we characterize conditions under which action prediction error provides a valid proxy for causal influence. Experiments across diverse manipulation tasks indicate that NMR predicts generalization behavior and that ISS yields more faithful explanations than existing interpretability methods. These results suggest that interventional attribution provides a simple diagnostic approach for identifying causal misalignment in embodied policies.

paragraphs: Vision-language-action policies may fail when their surroundings change because their decisions depend on visual cues unrelated to the task. This paper investigates that possibility by treating visual attribution as an intervention problem: estimating how changing the available visual information affects predicted actions.

The Interventional Significance Score uses masking interventions to estimate the causal influence of image regions. The Nuisance Mass Ratio then summarizes how much attribution falls on task-irrelevant features. The authors analyze ISS statistically, showing that it admits unbiased estimation. They also characterize conditions under which action prediction error can serve as a valid proxy for causal influence, so that connection is explicitly conditional.

Across varied manipulation tasks, the experiments indicate that NMR predicts generalization behavior and that ISS produces more faithful explanations than existing interpretability methods. These findings suggest a diagnostic use: examining which visual features drive actions can help identify policies whose apparent competence depends on irrelevant cues. The reported contribution is a way to detect such misalignment, with empirical evidence connecting the diagnostic to generalization.
summary.tldr: Interventional visual attribution helps diagnose whether robot policies rely on task-irrelevant cues associated with poor generalization.

title: Embodied Interpretability: Linking Causal Understanding to Generalization in Vision-Language-Action Models

abstract: Hypergraph contrastive learning is an effective paradigm for representation learning on higher-order relational data, yet existing methods largely ignore that hyperedges link nodes with multi-level semantics. Standard contrastive objectives emphasize instance discrimination via hyperspherical uniformity and tend to push embeddings apart in an indiscriminate manner. We show that this leads to a Hierarchy–Uniformity Conflict, whose geometric manifestation is Semantic Flattening, where the semantic depth of hyperedges collapses into a nearly flat cloud of instances. To address this issue, we introduce HyperDepth, a hypergraph contrastive learning framework that moves representations towards a hierarchy–uniformity equilibrium by jointly coordinating spectral and geometric signals. HyperDepth employs a decoupled spectral encoding scheme with adaptive gating so that high-frequency components focus on local instance discrimination while low-frequency components capture global hierarchical structure. On top of this, an energy-based hierarchical alignment module attaches a learnable prototype tree to the representation space and minimizes an interpretable energy functional to recover the semantic depth of hyperedges. Theoretically, under a mild frequency-separation assumption, we show that the local contrastive and global hierarchical objectives operate on orthogonal spectral components and admit equilibrium embeddings that preserve semantic depth while still retaining instance-level discrimination. Experiments on 15 hypergraph datasets and 17 supervised and self-supervised baselines, spanning homophilic and heterophilic regimes, show that HyperDepth attains strong performance with the best average rank.

paragraphs: Hyperedges connect groups of nodes whose relationships can contain several semantic levels. Standard contrastive learning pushes individual representations apart, but the paper shows that this can flatten the hierarchy within those groups. HyperDepth addresses the resulting conflict between distinguishing instances and preserving broader semantic organization.

Experiments cover 15 hypergraph datasets and 17 supervised and self-supervised baselines across homophilic and heterophilic settings. HyperDepth achieves strong performance and the best average rank, supporting the proposed coordination of hierarchy and discrimination under varied relational structures.
summary.tldr: HyperDepth separates local discrimination from global hierarchy to preserve semantic depth in hypergraph contrastive learning.

title: Towards Hierarchy–Uniformity Equilibrium: Recovering Semantic Depth in Hypergraph Contrastive Learning

abstract: Conventional patchified Transformers operate on uniform spatial partitions, distributing computational effort evenly across the domain irrespective of local features. This inflexible tokenization scheme is inherently limited in its ability to efficiently represent and process solutions to complex PDEs. To address this, we propose MeshTok, an adaptive mesh refinement (AMR)-inspired tokenization and sequence modeling framework. This method selectively refines spatial regions exhibiting sharp gradients, transient features, or multiscale structures, generating a heterogeneous set of multiscale tokens defined on a fixed simulation grid. These tokens are processed within a unified Transformer sequence, enabling the model to simultaneously capture coarse-grained global context and fine-grained local details without requiring specialized architectural components. Although adaptive refinement moderately increases token count, it promotes a more targeted allocation of computational resources to physically informative regions, which we view as a practical inductive bias rather than a formal optimality guarantee. Experimental evaluations across multiple PDE families and benchmark datasets demonstrate that MeshTok consistently improves the efficiency-accuracy trade-off compared to uniform-grid baselines. This suggests adaptive multiscale tokenization as a scalable and generalizable design principle for neural PDE modeling. Code is available at https://github.com/SCAILab-USTC/MeshTok.

paragraphs: Transformers for partial differential equations often divide space into uniform patches, assigning similar processing effort everywhere. Yet a solution may contain sharp changes, transient features, or structures at several scales. Uniform tokenization can therefore devote detail to relatively uninformative regions while inadequately representing more demanding ones.

MeshTok adapts ideas from adaptive mesh refinement to token construction on a fixed simulation grid. It creates finer tokens in selected regions and coarser tokens elsewhere. All tokens enter one Transformer sequence, allowing global context and local detail to be processed together without specialized architectural components.

Adaptive refinement moderately increases the token count, so the method's rationale is a more targeted allocation of computation rather than an automatic reduction in tokens. The authors explicitly frame this as a practical inductive bias, without a formal optimality guarantee. Across multiple PDE families and benchmark datasets, MeshTok consistently improves the reported efficiency–accuracy trade-off over uniform-grid baselines. These results suggest that choosing spatial representation scales adaptively can improve neural PDE modeling.
summary.tldr: MeshTok allocates finer spatial tokens to informative PDE regions, improving the reported efficiency–accuracy trade-off.

title: MeshTok: Efficient Multi-Scale Tokenization for Scalable PDE Transformers

abstract: Reconstructing spatiotemporal fields from partial observations is fundamental to scientific inference, from inferring atmospheric states from satellite data to recovering fluid states from imaging. When observations are incomplete, the inverse problem is fundamentally ill-posed: even when the underlying PDE dynamics are Markovian in the full state, partial observation operators induce a non-Markovian posterior that cannot be resolved from a single timestep. We propose a history-bootstrapped autoregressive flow matching (HB-ARFM) for spatiotemporal inverse reconstruction under partial observability. Observation history bootstraps the initial reconstruction via conditional flow matching, resolving ambiguities. The same conditional transport model is then applied autoregressively, conditioning on both new observations and past predictions to propagate the reconstruction forward in time. We evaluate the method on boiling dynamics reconstruction, recovering full velocity and temperature fields from interface geometry and motion. Across two inverse tasks with varying observation sparsity, HB-ARFM produces physically and temporally valid reconstructions where other models fail.
