paragraphs: Recovering a full physical system from partial observations can leave several possible explanations for the same measurement. Even when the complete state evolves according to Markovian dynamics, partial observations can make the reconstruction depend on history. This paper addresses that ambiguity by using observation sequences to initialize an evolving reconstruction.

The proposed HB-ARFM method uses conditional flow matching to build the initial reconstruction from observation history. It then reuses the same conditional transport model autoregressively, combining new observations with earlier predictions to advance through time. History therefore helps resolve the starting ambiguity, while past predictions supply continuing context as subsequent states are reconstructed.

The authors evaluate the method on boiling dynamics, recovering full velocity and temperature fields from interface geometry and motion. Across two inverse tasks with different observation sparsity, it produces physically and temporally valid reconstructions where the compared models fail. The findings support using temporal information throughout reconstruction when individual observations do not identify the hidden physical state.
summary.tldr: HB-ARFM uses observation history and past predictions to reconstruct boiling velocity and temperature fields from partial interface observations.

title: History-Bootstrapped Flow Matching for Inverse Boiling Reconstruction

abstract: Sustainability encompasses three key facets: economic, environmental, and social. However, the nascent discourse that is emerging on sustainable artificial intelligence (AI) has predominantly focused on the environmental sustainability of AI, often neglecting the economic and social aspects. Achieving truly sustainable AI necessitates addressing the tension between its climate awareness, which emphasizes the need to mitigate AI’s environmental impacts, and its social sustainability, which hinges on equitable access to AI development resources. The concept of resource awareness advocates for AI sovereignty through broader access to the infrastructure required to develop AI. Yet, this push for improving accessibility often overlooks the environmental costs of expanding such resource usage. This position paper argues that reconciling climate awareness and resource awareness is essential to realizing sustainable AI and neglecting these factors fuelling the global AI arms race. By applying the base-superstructure framework from historical materialism, we analyze how the material conditions are shaping the current AI progress and the discourse surrounding it. We also introduce the Climate and Resource Aware Machine Learning (CARAML) framework to address the conflict between climate and resource awareness of AI, with actionable recommendations spanning individual, community, industry, government, and global levels to achieve sustainable AI.

Considering either side in isolation leaves this conflict unresolved.

The authors examine these tensions through the base-superstructure framework from historical materialism, focusing on how material conditions shape AI development and the discussion around it. They argue that failing to reconcile climate awareness with resource awareness contributes to a global AI arms race. This is the paper’s analytical position about the consequences of the current development pattern.

Its purpose is to bring environmental concerns and equitable access into a shared sustainability agenda. The contribution is a framework for confronting the tradeoff across levels of action, with economic and social sustainability included explicitly.
summary.tldr: The paper argues that sustainable AI must reconcile equitable infrastructure access with environmental costs and proposes CARAML to guide action.

title: Position: Neglecting the Sustainability of AI is Fuelling a Global AI Arms Race

abstract: In recent years, there has been a surge in the application of neural approaches to NP-hard combinatorial problems such as subgraph isomorphism, maximum clique and the travelling salesman problem in graphs. These approaches are often evaluated as complete replacements of established combinatorial solver tools, with emphasis on solution quality and runtime. In this position paper, we argue that such wholesale replacements for touted faster inference or better solution quality should not be considered the primary motivation for neural surrogates, and a systematic evaluation of when neural methods are appropriate is required. Given our observations, we contend that in the absence of system-level requirements dictated by the task at hand, such as vector indexing and retrieval, or without the need for end-to-end differentiability, neural surrogates rarely offer compelling advantages over the standard combinatorial solver. In this vein, we develop a comprehensive report of where current neural methods fall short, and subsequently devise a diagnostic checklist for when neural methods are truly applicable.

paragraphs: This paper questions the motivation for replacing established combinatorial solvers with neural approximations. It discusses hard graph problems including subgraph isomorphism, maximum clique, and the travelling salesman problem. Neural approaches are often presented as complete substitutes and compared mainly on solution quality and runtime, but the authors argue that those ambitions need more systematic scrutiny.

Their central claim is qualified: neural substitutes rarely offer compelling advantages when the task lacks specific system requirements or a need for end-to-end differentiability. Requirements involving vector indexing and retrieval are named as potentially relevant reasons to use neural methods. The suitability of an approach therefore depends on what the larger system needs, beyond a standalone comparison of answers and speed.

The paper develops a report on where current neural methods fall short and proposes a diagnostic checklist for deciding when they are applicable. This reframes method selection around the demands of the task and its surrounding system. The authors advocate evaluating the justification for neural approximation before treating replacement of a conventional solver as the main research objective.
summary.tldr: Neural substitutes for combinatorial solvers are rarely compelling without specific system requirements or a need for end-to-end differentiability.

title: Position: Neural Approximation Is Rarely Justified for Hard Combinatorial Problems

abstract: Modern large language model (LLM) services increasingly rely on complex, often abstract operations, such as multi-step reasoning and multi-agent collaboration, to generate high-quality outputs. While users are billed based on token consumption and API usage, these internal steps are typically not visible. We refer to such systems as Commercial Opaque LLM Services (COLS). This position paper highlights emerging accountability challenges in COLS: users are billed for operations they cannot observe, verify, or contest. We formalize two key risks: quantity inflation, where token and call counts may be artificially inflated, and quality downgrade, where providers might quietly substitute lower-cost models or tools. Addressing these risks requires a diverse set of auditing strategies, including commitment-based, predictive, behavioral, and signature-based methods. We further explore the potential of complementary mechanisms such as watermarking and trusted execution environments to enhance verifiability without compromising provider confidentiality. We also propose a modular three-layer auditing framework for COLS and users that enables trustworthy verification across execution, secure logging, and user-facing auditability without exposing proprietary internals. Our aim is to encourage further research and policy development toward transparency, auditability, and accountability in commercial LLM services.

summary.tldr: The paper proposes auditing hidden LLM-service operations so users can verify billed activity and service quality without exposing proprietary internals.

title: Position: Invisible Tokens, Visible Bills: The Urgent Need to Audit Hidden Operations in Opaque LLM Services

abstract: This position paper argues that LLM inference serving has outgrown generic heuristics and now demands mathematical optimization and algorithmic foundations. Despite rapid advances in serving systems such as vLLM and SGLang, their algorithmic cores remain largely unchanged from classical distributed computing: request routing uses join-shortest-queue or round-robin, scheduling defaults to FIFO, and KV cache eviction follows LRU. These general-purpose policies ignore the distinctive structure of LLM inference—dynamically growing KV cache memory, prefill-decode phase asymmetry, unknown output lengths, and continuous batching constraints. We contend that the field must develop mathematical models capturing these characteristics, enabling the design of algorithms with provable performance guarantees across diverse workloads, rather than heuristics that may succeed in some scenarios but fail unpredictably in others. Emerging work at the intersection of operations research and ML systems demonstrates that principled methods can match or exceed heuristic performance while providing theoretical guarantees. We call on the community to recognize algorithmic design for LLM serving as a research frontier.

paragraphs: Serving language models requires deciding where requests go, when they run, and which cached information stays in memory. This position paper argues that commonly used policies, including shortest-queue routing, first-in-first-out scheduling, and least-recently-used eviction, do not adequately capture the distinctive structure of language-model inference.

The authors highlight growing key-value cache memory, differences between prompt processing and token generation, unknown output lengths, and continuous batching constraints. These characteristics interact with routing, scheduling, and memory decisions. The proposed research direction is to build mathematical models that capture those interactions and use them to design algorithms with provable performance guarantees across diverse workloads.

The paper points to emerging work combining operations research with machine-learning systems as evidence that principled methods can match or exceed heuristic performance while offering theoretical guarantees. It calls for algorithm design to become a central research topic in serving systems. This is a research agenda supported by emerging results, rather than a claim that one optimization method already resolves every serving workload.
summary.tldr: The paper argues for LLM-specific optimization models and algorithms with performance guarantees for routing, scheduling, and cache management.

abstract: The assumptions behind linear classifiers for categorical data are examined and reformulated in the context of the multinomial manifold, the simplex of multinomial models furnished with the Riemannian structureinduced by the Fisher information. This leads to a new view of hyperplaneclassifiers which, together with a generalized margin concept, shows how toadapt existing margin-based hyperplane models to multinomial geometry. Experiments show the new classification framework to be effective for textclassification, where the categorical structure of the data is modelednaturally within the multinomial family.

This leads to a new view of hyperplaneclassifiers which, together with a generalized margin concept, shows how toadapt existing margin-based hyperplane models to multinomial geometry. Experiments show the new classification framework to be effective for textclassification, where the categorical structure of the data is modelednaturally within the multinomial family.

paragraphs: This paper revisits the assumptions behind linear classification of categorical data. It places the problem on the multinomial manifold: the simplex of multinomial probability models equipped with a geometry derived from Fisher information. This gives the classification problem a mathematical setting tied to the probability models used to describe categorical observations.

Within that setting, the authors develop a new interpretation of hyperplane classifiers and a generalized notion of margin. Together, these ideas show how existing margin-based hyperplane models can be adapted to multinomial geometry. The change concerns both the interpretation of the separating classifier and the margin used to describe its separation of classes.

Experiments show that the resulting classification framework is effective for text classification, where multinomial models naturally represent the categorical structure of the data. The contribution connects the choice of probability model with classifier geometry, showing how a familiar margin-based approach can be reformulated to match that structure.
summary.tldr: The paper adapts hyperplane classifiers and their margins to multinomial geometry, with effective text-classification results.

title: Hyperplane margin classifiers on the multinomial manifold

abstract: Well-calibrated probabilities are necessary in many applications like probabilistic frameworks or cost-sensitive tasks. Based on previous success of asymmetric Laplace method in calibrating text classifiers' scores, we propose to use piecewise logistic regression, which is a simple extension of standard logistic regression, as an alternative method in the discriminative family. We show that both methods have the flexibility to be piecewise linear functions in log-odds, but they are based on quite different assumptions. We evaluated asymmetric Laplace method, piecewise logistic regression and standard logistic regression over standard text categorization collections (Reuters-21578 and TREC-AP) with three classifiers (SVM, Naive Bayes and Logistic Regression Classifier), and observed that piecewise logistic regression performs significantly better than the other two methods in the log-loss metric.

Based on previous success of asymmetric Laplace method in calibrating text classifiers' scores, we propose to use piecewise logistic regression, which is a simple extension of standard logistic regression, as an alternative method in the discriminative family. We show that both methods have the flexibility to be piecewise linear functions in log-odds, but they are based on quite different assumptions. We evaluated asymmetric Laplace method, piecewise logistic regression and standard logistic regression over standard text categorization collections (Reuters-21578 and TREC-AP) with three classifiers (SVM, Naive Bayes and Logistic Regression Classifier), and observed that piecewise logistic regression performs significantly better than the other two methods in the log-loss metric.

paragraphs: A classifier's score is not automatically a well-calibrated probability. The paper addresses converting scores into probability estimates for applications such as probabilistic systems and cost-sensitive decisions. It proposes piecewise logistic regression, a simple extension of standard logistic regression, as a discriminative approach to this calibration problem.

The authors compare its structure with the asymmetric Laplace method, which had previously been successful for text-classifier calibration. Both can express piecewise-linear relationships in log-odds, although they rely on different assumptions. This comparison separates their shared representational flexibility from the distinct modeling assumptions used to obtain probability estimates.

The evaluation uses Reuters-21578 and TREC-AP text collections with SVM, Naive Bayes, and logistic regression classifiers. Across this evaluation, piecewise logistic regression performs significantly better in log loss than both asymmetric Laplace calibration and standard logistic regression. The reported advantage concerns the quality of probability estimates under that metric, supporting the additional flexibility for the studied text-classification calibration tasks.
summary.tldr: Piecewise logistic regression improves reported log-loss calibration results over standard logistic regression and an asymmetric Laplace method on text classifiers.

title: Probabilistic score estimation with piecewise logistic regression

abstract: This work provides a framework for learning sequential attention in real-world visual object recognition, using an architecture of three processing stages. The first stage rejects irrelevant local descriptors based on an information theoretic saliency measure, providing candidates for foci of interest (FOI). The second stage investigates the information in the FOI using a codebook matcher and providing weak object hypotheses. The third stage integrates local information via shifts of attention, resulting in chains of descriptor-action pairs that characterize object discrimination. A Q-learner adapts then from explorative search and evaluative feedback from entropy decreases on the attention sequences, eventually prioritizing shifts that lead to a geometry of descriptor-action scanpaths that is highly discriminative with respect to object recognition. The methodology is successfully evaluated on indoors (COIL-20 database) and outdoors (TSG-20 database) imagery, demonstrating significant impact by learning, outperforming standard local descriptor based methods both in recognition accuracy and processing time.

The third stage integrates local information via shifts of attention, resulting in chains of descriptor-action pairs that characterize object discrimination. A Q-learner adapts then from explorative search and evaluative feedback from entropy decreases on the attention sequences, eventually prioritizing shifts that lead to a geometry of descriptor-action scanpaths that is highly discriminative with respect to object recognition. paragraphs: The paper learns how a visual recognition system should move its attention between informative image locations. Its architecture has three stages. First, an information-theoretic saliency measure removes irrelevant local descriptors and identifies candidate locations. Second, a codebook matcher examines those locations and produces weak hypotheses about which object is present.

The third stage combines local evidence through attention shifts, forming sequences of descriptor-action pairs. A Q-learning procedure explores these sequences and receives evaluative feedback from decreases in entropy, reflecting reduced uncertainty. It learns to favor attention shifts whose resulting scanpaths are especially useful for distinguishing objects, including the geometry of those paths.

Evaluations use indoor imagery from COIL-20 and outdoor imagery from TSG-20. The results show a significant contribution from learning and better recognition accuracy and processing time than the standard local-descriptor methods compared. The findings support learning the order and spatial pattern of evidence gathering as part of recognition, alongside selecting informative local image descriptions.
summary.tldr: Q-learning trains visual attention sequences that improve object recognition accuracy and processing time in indoor and outdoor image evaluations.

title: Q-learning of sequential attention for visual object recognition from informative local descriptors

abstract: Tsochantaridis et al 2005 proposed two formulations for maximum margin training of structured spaces: margin scaling and slack scaling. While margin scaling has been extensively used since it requires the same kind of MAP inference as normal structured prediction, slack scaling is believed to be more accurate and better-behaved. We present an efficient variational approximation to the slack scaling method that solves its inference bottleneck while retaining its accuracy advantage over margin scaling. We further argue that existing scaling approaches do not separate the true labeling comprehensively while generating violating constraints. We propose a new max-margin trainer PosLearn that generates violators to ensure separation at each position of a decomposable loss function. Empirical results on real datasets illustrate that PosLearn can reduce test error by up to 25%. Further, PosLearn violators can be generated more efficiently than slack violators; for many structured tasks the time required is just twice that of MAP inference.
originalAbstract: Tsochantaridis et al 2005 proposed two formulations for maximum margin training of structured spaces: margin scaling and slack scaling. While margin scaling has been extensively used since it requires the same kind of MAP inference as normal structured prediction, slack scaling is believed to be more accurate and better-behaved. We present an efficient variational approximation to the slack scaling method that solves its inference bottleneck while retaining its accuracy advantage over margin scaling. We further argue that existing scaling approaches do not separate the true labeling comprehensively while generating violating constraints. We propose a new max-margin trainer PosLearn that generates violators to ensure separation at each position of a decomposable loss function. Empirical results on real datasets illustrate that PosLearn can reduce test error by up to 25%. Further, PosLearn violators can be generated more efficiently than slack violators; for many structured tasks the time required is just twice that of MAP inference.

paragraphs: Training a structured predictor requires comparing a correct output with competing outputs that may contain many linked decisions. Two maximum-margin approaches, margin scaling and slack scaling, handle these comparisons differently. Margin scaling is widely used because its inference resembles ordinary structured prediction; slack scaling is regarded as more accurate and better behaved, but has an inference bottleneck.

The paper first develops an efficient variational approximation to slack scaling that addresses this bottleneck while retaining its reported accuracy advantage. It then raises a separate concern: existing approaches may generate competing outputs without comprehensively separating the correct labeling. The proposed PosLearn trainer generates violations that enforce separation at each position when the loss decomposes across positions.

Experiments on real datasets show test-error reductions of up to 25% with PosLearn. Its competing outputs can also be generated more efficiently than slack-scaling violations; for many structured tasks, the required time is twice that of MAP inference. These findings connect the choice of training constraints to both prediction accuracy and computational effort.
summary.tldr: The paper makes slack scaling more tractable and introduces PosLearn, whose positionwise training constraints improve accuracy and efficiency in reported experiments.

title: Accurate max-margin training for structured output spaces

abstract: This work proposes a learning method for deep architectures that takes advantage of sequential data, in particular from the temporal coherence that naturally exists in unlabeled video recordings. That is, two successive frames are likely to contain the same object or objects. This coherence is used as a supervisory signal over the unlabeled data, and is used to improve the performance on a supervised task of interest. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method on some pose invariant object and face recognition tasks.
originalAbstract: This work proposes a learning method for deep architectures that takes advantage of sequential data, in particular from the temporal coherence that naturally exists in unlabeled video recordings. That is, two successive frames are likely to contain the same object or objects. This coherence is used as a supervisory signal over the unlabeled data, and is used to improve the performance on a supervised task of interest. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method on some pose invariant object and face recognition tasks.

paragraphs: Unlabeled video contains a useful relationship between observations: neighboring frames are likely to show the same objects. This paper proposes a learning method for deep architectures that uses this temporal coherence as a source of supervision. The sequence itself supplies information about related observations, even though the frames have no supplied object labels.

The key idea is to use continuity over time to support a supervised task of interest. Images of an object may vary across successive frames while still depicting that object. Treating nearby frames as related therefore provides a learning signal relevant to recognizing objects despite changes in appearance. The relationship is probabilistic: successive frames are likely to share objects, rather than guaranteed to do so.

The authors demonstrate the method on some object and face recognition tasks requiring robustness to pose. Their reported effectiveness supports using sequential relationships in unlabeled recordings to improve supervised recognition. The contribution centers on how training information is obtained: temporal structure becomes a usable signal for learning deep representations.
summary.tldr: Temporal continuity in unlabeled video supplies a training signal that improves performance on some pose-invariant object and face recognition tasks.

title: Deep learning from temporal coherence in video

abstract: We propose clustering samples given their pairwise similarities by factorizing the similarity matrix into the product of a cluster probability matrix and its transpose. We propose a rotation-based algorithm to compute this left-stochastic decomposition (LSD). Theoretical results link the LSD clustering method to a soft kernel k-means clustering, give conditions for when the factorization and clustering are unique, and provide error bounds. Experimental results on simulated and real similarity datasets show that the proposed method reliably provides accurate clusterings.
originalAbstract: We propose clustering samples given their pairwise similarities by factorizing the similarity matrix into the product of a cluster probability matrix and its transpose. We propose a rotation-based algorithm to compute this left-stochastic decomposition (LSD). Theoretical results link the LSD clustering method to a soft kernel k-means clustering, give conditions for when the factorization and clustering are unique, and provide error bounds. Experimental results on simulated and real similarity datasets show that the proposed method reliably provides accurate clusterings.

paragraphs: The paper clusters samples using their pairwise similarities. It seeks a factorization of the similarity matrix into a cluster-probability matrix multiplied by its transpose. This represents similarities through probabilistic cluster memberships, making the relationship between the observed similarities and the proposed grouping part of a single matrix decomposition.

The authors introduce a rotation-based algorithm to compute this left-stochastic decomposition. They also establish a theoretical connection with soft kernel k-means clustering. That connection relates the proposed factorization to a clustering formulation with soft assignments, giving a second way to understand what the decomposition represents and how it serves the grouping task.

The theoretical results include error bounds and conditions under which both the factorization and the clustering are unique. Uniqueness is therefore conditional rather than a claim about every similarity matrix. Experiments on simulated and real similarity datasets report reliable, accurate clusterings. The paper combines a concrete computational method with analysis of its relationship to clustering, its ambiguity, and its errors.
summary.tldr: Left-stochastic matrix factorization derives probabilistic clusters from pairwise similarities, with conditional uniqueness results, error bounds, and supporting experiments.

title: Clustering by Left-Stochastic Matrix Factorization
